Hypotension is a late sign; assess perfusion using mental state, pulse quality, capillary refill, skin temperature/colour, urine output and trend, not BP alone.
- Classify the phenotype: hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic, distributive, cardiogenic, obstructive or dissociative/mixed. Treat the cause in parallel; POCUS/echocardiography and lactate may refine the phenotype but must not delay resuscitation.
- **Fluid bolus (ERC 2025):** for hypovolaemic, obstructive or distributive shock, give balanced isotonic crystalloid **10 mL/kg** and reassess after each bolus. If balanced crystalloid is unavailable, 0.9% saline is an alternative and may be preferred in DKA or severe traumatic brain injury. Reassess for crackles, increasing liver edge/JVP, worsening work of breathing or other overload after every bolus.
- Repeated 10 mL/kg boluses may be required; ERC 2025 notes that **40--60 mL/kg in the first hour** may be needed in hypovolaemic/distributive shock, but start vasoactive support early and do not continue fluids reflexively. In cardiogenic shock, individualize fluid and, when a bolus is needed, use a more cautious amount such as **5 mL/kg** with immediate reassessment.
- **Vasoactive timing (selected ERC 2025 pathway):** start a continuous vasoactive infusion early according to shock phenotype, via a dedicated central or peripheral line when necessary, and **not later than after 3--4 boluses (30--40 mL/kg)**. Titrate to perfusion (pulse, refill, urine output, mental state, lactate/echo when available), not BP alone; aim for at least the age-specific 5th-centile systolic pressure.
- **Agent position:** ERC 2025 uses noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor, adrenaline as first-line inotrope, and milrinone as first-line inodilator according to shock phenotype. **For pediatric septic shock specifically, SSC 2026 found insufficient evidence to recommend epinephrine versus norepinephrine as the preferred first-line agent**; therefore do not present one universal septic-shock catecholamine as mandatory. Exact local concentrations and mL/h are deliberately deferred to the pediatric infusion/formulary module because decimal/concentration errors are high-risk.
- **Haemorrhagic shock:** control bleeding, activate the local major-haemorrhage protocol, minimize crystalloids (**max 20 mL/kg**) and give blood products/whole blood as soon as available. Do not use a crystalloid-only strategy when major haemorrhage is suspected.
- Seek expert advice early for refractory shock, congenital heart disease or potential extracorporeal support. Route to cause-specific modules as appropriate: `pediatric-dehydration-shock`, `anaphylaxis`, `trauma-major-hemorrhage`, `cardiac-tamponade-pericardial-emergency`, `tension-pneumothorax`, `adrenal-crisis`, or other syndrome-specific care.
- Newborn resuscitation at birth remains outside this module; use neonatal life support.
- **SSC pediatric 2026 boundary:** evidence is insufficient to mandate starting vasoactives before versus after 40 mL/kg, or a MAP target at the 5th versus 50th percentile. Do not attribute the selected ERC timing/SBP target to SSC. In systems without intensive-care availability, SSC recommends against bolus fluids in sepsis without hypotension; with hypotensive septic shock it suggests up to 40 mL/kg in reassessed 10--20 mL/kg aliquots in the first hour. Stop boluses if shock resolves or overload develops; this is not a mandatory volume to complete.

title: Pediatric Arrhythmias
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- Confirm age/weight, pulse and perfusion; use pediatric ABCDE, monitor/defibrillator, vascular access and 12-lead ECG when this will not delay treatment. Correct hypoxia, ventilation failure, shock, fever, pain, electrolytes and toxins. Seek pediatric cardiology/resuscitation support early.
- **Bradycardia with poor perfusion:** optimize oxygenation/ventilation first. If the child remains bradycardic with poor perfusion and HR **<60/min despite adequate respiratory support**, start chest compressions. Once CPR is indicated, use the `pediatric-cardiac-arrest` adrenaline dose **10 micrograms/kg IV/IO (max 1 mg)**, not the small pre-arrest dose. For pre-arrest bradycardia that has not met the CPR criterion, consider adrenaline **1--2 micrograms/kg IV** as small boluses, or an expert-prescribed continuous infusion with an explicit dose/time unit. Atropine is reserved for selected vagal/conduction causes: **20 micrograms/kg IV** (up to age 11: max 0.5 mg; age 12--17: 300--600 micrograms, with larger emergency doses only per expert/local protocol). Pacing is uncommon and etiology-guided (e.g. complete heart block/sick sinus syndrome).
- **Stable SVT:** use vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine with ECG recording/defibrillator readiness. ERC/RCUK 2025: first dose **0.1--0.2 mg/kg IV** (max 6 mg); if SVT persists, **0.3 mg/kg IV** after at least 1 min (maximum 12--18 mg according to age/local chart). Recurrent or refractory SVT requires pediatric cardiology input rather than repeated empiric adult antiarrhythmics.
- **Unstable/decompensated tachyarrhythmia:** perform synchronized cardioversion without delay. Start at **1 J/kg** (ERC text permits 1--2 J/kg), then double the energy with each subsequent attempt up to **4 J/kg**. Use appropriate sedation/analgesia if conscious, but IV access attempts or sedation must not delay cardioversion. For persistent SVT/VT, consider **amiodarone 5 mg/kg by slow IV infusion (>20 min)** before the third cardioversion only with expert guidance.
- **Broad-complex tachycardia:** if uncertain whether VT or SVT, treat as VT. Avoid reflex AV-nodal blockade in irregular/pre-excited rhythms. Torsades de pointes: magnesium **25--50 mg/kg IV** (max 2 g) over 10--15 min, repeat once if necessary per ERC/RCUK 2025.
- If the pulse is lost, switch immediately to `pediatric-cardiac-arrest`. Do not use adult energy or fixed adult drug doses without pediatric weight-based conversion and maximum-dose checks. Newborn resuscitation at birth is excluded.
- Rechecked against RCUK resource folder **February 2026 Version 6**, arrhythmia page 10: distinguish small adrenaline boluses for bradycardia with a pulse from the **10 micrograms/kg** cardiac-arrest dose. Do not treat an infusion as 1–2 micrograms/kg without a time unit; the infusion rate must come from a verified expert prescription and actual concentration.
- Atropine age bands and slow amiodarone here are the arrhythmia-specific chart, not a generic emergency drug table. Severe bradycardia with poor perfusion despite respiratory support follows CPR/arrest care without waiting for all drug trials. Adenosine must be a rapid proximal injection/flush with ECG monitoring and appropriate access; do not give it for compensatory sinus tachycardia or an uncertain irregular broad-complex rhythm.

title: Pediatric Cardiac Arrest
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- Scope: infants/children/adolescents beyond newborn transition. Recognize arrest clinically or from monitored loss of vital signs, call the resuscitation team, start high-quality CPR and ventilation, and attach self-adhesive defibrillator pads as soon as possible. In a child who becomes bradycardic **<60/min with poor perfusion despite adequate respiratory support**, start chest compressions even if a pulse is still detectable.
- Distinguish shockable (VF/pulseless VT) from non-shockable rhythms (PEA/asystole or severe bradycardia with poor perfusion). Use 2-min CPR cycles and keep rhythm/pulse checks under 5 s.
- **Non-shockable arrest:** obtain IV/IO access and give adrenaline **10 micrograms/kg IV/IO (max 1 mg) as soon as possible**, then repeat **every 4 min** (every other 2-min cycle) unless guided by invasive haemodynamics.
- **Shockable VF/pVT:** give a single shock **4 J/kg** (do not exceed the adult device-dependent ceiling, usually 120--200 J for standard initial shocks), immediately resume CPR for 2 min, and repeat the 4 J/kg shock strategy while the rhythm remains shockable. For refractory VF/pVT requiring >5 shocks, ERC 2025 allows stepwise escalation up to **8 J/kg (max 360 J)**.
- **After the 3rd shock:** give adrenaline **10 micrograms/kg (max 1 mg)** plus amiodarone **5 mg/kg (max 300 mg)** IV/IO. **After the 5th shock:** give another adrenaline dose plus amiodarone **5 mg/kg (max 150 mg)**. Lidocaine **1 mg/kg IV** is an alternative if amiodarone is unavailable or local policy uses lidocaine.
- Selected **ERC 2025 detailed pediatric monitored exception**: in a witnessed VF/pVT arrest in a child already attached to a defibrillator, give up to **three stacked shocks**, checking rapidly after each. If the third stacked attempt fails, start CPR and give **amiodarone after the third stacked shock**; give the first **adrenaline after 4 minutes**, then continue single shocks every 2 min/adrenaline every 4 min, with the second amiodarone **after the fifth shock**. Do not move the pediatric doses to a fifth/seventh-shock scheme or import the adult stacked-shock counter. This exception is not for routine unwitnessed arrest.
- Use 100% oxygen during CPR, effective bag-mask ventilation and an advanced airway only when the team can place it without disrupting compressions. Use waveform capnography when an advanced airway is in place. POCUS only during planned pauses and never to prolong the pause.
- Search and treat reversible causes: hypoxia, hypovolaemia/haemorrhage, hyper-/hypokalaemia and other metabolic causes, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins and pulmonary/coronary thrombosis. Major haemorrhage requires early blood products rather than repeated crystalloid.
- After ROSC, transition immediately to pediatric post-resuscitation care: controlled oxygenation/ventilation, haemodynamic support, glucose/temperature/seizure management and PICU/cause-directed evaluation. Newborn resuscitation immediately after birth follows neonatal life support.
- Source reconciliation: this module selects the detailed ERC 2025 sequence (**adrenaline every 4 min**, refractory VF/pVT escalation when **more than 5 shocks** are needed). RCUK February2026V6 uses 3–5 min adrenaline and its simplified diagram says escalation from the 5th shock; 4 min lies within that interval, but shock thresholds must not be silently mixed. Follow one explicitly chosen team algorithm and actual device ceiling, not an average of diagrams.
- When starting pediatric BLS, use 5 initial rescue breaths and 15:2 compressions/ventilations for trained providers without an advanced airway; once secured, continuous compressions with age-appropriate ventilation are used. Confirm estimated versus measured weight and cumulative doses/maxima. The reference review does not certify the local resuscitation cart, neonatal transition pathway or team competency.

title: Pediatric Status Epilepticus
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- Convulsive status: generalized convulsion >=5 min or recurrent seizures without recovery. Time seizure; ABC, lateral position/suction, oxygen/continuous SpO2 and cardiorespiratory monitoring, bedside glucose, temperature, IV/IO access without delaying first benzodiazepine. Pursue cause (febrile infection/meningitis, trauma, toxins, metabolic/electrolytes, missed antiseizure medication). If consciousness does not recover after motor seizure stops, consider nonconvulsive status/EEG.
- **HSE 2025 glucose gate:** if bedside glucose is **<2.6 mmol/L**, give **10% glucose 3 mL/kg** and recheck glucose in **10 min**, while continuing seizure management.
- If an individualized seizure plan exists, follow it. Count prehospital/home benzodiazepines: give no more than **2 total doses** to reduce respiratory depression. First-line options for age >=1 month:
  - buccal midazolam **0.3 mg/kg**; HSE dose bands: 1--3 months 0.3 mg/kg (max 2.5 mg), 3--11 months 2.5 mg, 1--4 y 5 mg, 5--9 y 7.5 mg, 10--17 y 10 mg;
  - IV lorazepam **0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg)**, diluted with an equal volume of 0.9% sodium chloride and given slowly;
  - rectal diazepam **0.5 mg/kg (max 20 mg)** when buccal/IV routes are unavailable, using the local formulation/dose bands.
  If still seizing 5 min after the first benzodiazepine, give the second and final benzodiazepine dose. Monitor ventilation and be ready to support the airway.
- If seizure persists after 2 benzodiazepine doses / around **15 min from onset**, urgently involve senior pediatrics, anesthesia/PICU and give IV levetiracetam **40 mg/kg (max 3 g)**, diluted to **50 mg/mL** and infused over **5 min**, following HSE 2025 and local drug policy. A loading dose may be given even if the child is already taking maintenance levetiracetam.
- Ongoing seizure after levetiracetam: HSE 2025 next step is IV phenytoin **20 mg/kg (max 2 g)** using a large vein with continuous ECG monitoring because of arrhythmia/extravasation risk; then phenobarbital **20 mg/kg (max 1 g)** with anesthesia/airway readiness. Local Portugal/Azores protocols may select a different equivalent second/third-line pathway and must take precedence once verified.
- **Consultant-neurology alternatives in HSE 2025:** lacosamide **10 mg/kg** may be used after specialist discussion; sodium valproate **20 mg/kg IV (max 3 g)** is another option. Avoid valproate in hepatic dysfunction, metabolic disease, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, pregnancy, and in children <2 y with unknown etiology.
- Refractory status requires PICU/critical-care management, airway control when indicated and EEG-guided therapy. Do not stack repeated benzodiazepines or allow medication preparation/access attempts to delay time-critical treatment.
- This HSE pathway covers **1 month--18 years** and explicitly excludes neonates <1 month and children with established epilepsy who have increased seizures from baseline; use neonatal/individualized specialist pathways for those groups.
- Portugal/Azores operational release requires confirmation of local buccal midazolam/lorazepam/diazepam presentations, levetiracetam/phenytoin/phenobarbital concentrations and infusion standards, pediatric transfer/PICU pathway and EEG access.
- Source selection: retain the HSE 2025 pathway as one complete reference. ERC/RCUK 2025/2026 uses different hypoglycemia and antiseizure-loading references in places; do not combine its boluses/maxima with the HSE sequence or add them together. The HSE 50 mg/mL levetiracetam/5 min emergency infusion is a source-specific instruction, not universal product-label compatibility or permission to prepare it without pharmacy verification of the actual product, diluent, container and route.
- Neonates and increased seizure frequency in established epilepsy follow the appropriate separate/individualized pathway; an individualized rescue plan is not a reason to ignore ongoing convulsive status or delay senior airway treatment. Alternative agents require consultant selection and current product/reproductive/metabolic contraindication review. Source/dose verification here does not confirm local presentations, EEG/PICU capability or enable a blocked medication contract.

title: Trauma Major Hemorrhage
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Scope: adult major traumatic haemorrhage. Activate the local massive-haemorrhage protocol early when critical bleeding is present or strongly suspected; control external bleeding immediately and pursue definitive operative/interventional haemostasis without delay.
- **Portugal reference:** DGS Norma 011/2013, most recently identified by DGS as updated **18/07/2017**, remains the national massive-transfusion reference. It should be treated as a local framework, not as the sole evidence source for 2026 trauma care.
- **Blood-component strategy:** do not hard-code the older DGS pack `4 CE + 4 PFC + 1 CPP` as a universal requirement. The 2023 European trauma guideline supports either (a) fibrinogen concentrate/cryoprecipitate with pRBC, or (b) FFP with pRBC at an FFP:pRBC ratio of at least **1:2**, plus a high platelet:pRBC ratio. Exact packs remain local blood-bank protocol.
- Use early and repeated haemostatic monitoring with PT/INR, Clauss fibrinogen and platelet count and/or a validated viscoelastic method (ROTEM/TEG). Do not delay immediately indicated haemorrhage control or TXA while waiting for viscoelastic results.
- **Tranexamic acid:** in a trauma patient who is bleeding or at risk of significant bleeding, give as soon as possible and within 3 hours of injury: **1 g IV over 10 min, followed by 1 g IV over 8 h**. Do not substitute the inconsistent older DGS text implying 1 mg/kg/h or 1 g every 8 h as the standard CRASH-2 regimen. Do not wait for ROTEM/TEG before giving TXA.
- **Fibrinogen:** treat major bleeding with hypofibrinogenaemia when Clauss fibrinogen is **<=1.5 g/L** or VEM shows functional fibrinogen deficit. The 2023 European guideline suggests an initial **3--4 g fibrinogen concentrate** (or equivalent cryoprecipitate), with repeat dosing guided by VEM/laboratory reassessment. The older DGS 25--50 mg/kg / 2--4 g framework is historical/local context rather than the sole current target.
- **Calcium:** monitor ionised calcium during major trauma/massive transfusion and maintain it in the normal range (approximately **1.1--1.3 mmol/L**). Correct hypocalcaemia promptly; the European guideline prefers calcium chloride for this setting. Remember that **10 mL 10% calcium chloride contains substantially more elemental calcium than 10 mL 10% calcium gluconate**; do not substitute equal volumes.
- **Platelets:** target at least **>50 x 10^9/L** in major bleeding; use a higher target around **>100 x 10^9/L** in ongoing bleeding with traumatic brain injury/CNS involvement, according to current local/neurotrauma protocol and viscoelastic/laboratory findings.
- **Temperature and acid-base:** actively prevent/treat hypothermia and monitor pH/base deficit/lactate. Warm blood products and fluids. Minimize excessive crystalloid because dilution, hyperchloraemic acidosis and hypothermia worsen coagulopathy.
- **rFVIIa:** do **not** use recombinant activated factor VII as first-line therapy. Consider off-label rescue only if major bleeding and traumatic coagulopathy persist despite definitive haemorrhage control, blood products/fibrinogen, antifibrinolytic therapy and correction of hypothermia, hypocalcaemia and severe acidosis. It is not supported for isolated traumatic intracranial haemorrhage.
- Reverse anticoagulation using the dedicated `anticoagulation-reversal` pathway. PCC for VKA/DOAC-related bleeding must follow the agent-specific pathway rather than the historical blanket DGS ROTEM/PCC algorithm.
- Identify chest, abdomen, pelvis, retroperitoneum and long-bone sources with examination, POCUS and imaging appropriate to haemodynamic stability. A negative FAST does not exclude haemorrhage. Apply pelvic stabilization and urgent operative/interventional control when indicated.
- **Local release gate (Portugal/Azores/Horta):** owner protocol confirmation recorded 2026-11-13; the owner confirms an activation protocol and accepts alignment with the current guideline after source review. Local pack contents, blood-bank response times, products and transfer resources remain defined by that protocol; no specific composition, ROTEM/TEG availability or independent blood-bank sign-off is inferred. Use conventional laboratory monitoring when appropriate; do not delay haemostasis or TXA awaiting VEM.

title: Major Burns
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Stop exposure safely, remove constricting jewelry and non-adherent clothing, assess ABCDE and associated trauma, and prevent hypothermia. Use cool running water for initial thermal-burn cooling when feasible; never ice or prolonged whole-body cooling. Cover with clean non-adherent material. Brush dry chemicals off before irrigation when appropriate and identify water-reactive exceptions with toxicology; electrical burns may hide deep injury.
- Estimate depth and percentage total body surface area (TBSA) using a body chart/Lund-Browder assessment. Exclude superficial erythema from resuscitation TBSA. A photograph alone cannot establish depth, circumferential compromise or whole-body TBSA; document uncertainty and reassess.
- Consult a burn center immediately for full-thickness burns, partial-thickness burns at least 10% TBSA, deep burns involving critical sites/joints, suspected inhalation injury, major chemical/high-voltage injury, associated trauma, important comorbidity or uncontrolled pain. These referral criteria do not equal the threshold for formula-based fluid resuscitation. Children require a pediatric burn pathway.
- For adults with at least 20% TBSA burns, the ABA 2024 guideline recommends an initial estimate of 2 mL/kg/%TBSA over the first 24 hours. Use lactated Ringer's/balanced crystalloid and the burn-center protocol. In a modified Brooke schedule, half is allocated to the first 8 hours FROM INJURY and half to the next 16 hours. Subtract fluids already given and account for time elapsed; never give a blind catch-up bolus or restart the clock at admission.
- Example only: 80 kg, 30% TBSA, immediately after injury: 2 x 80 x 30 = 4,800 mL/24 h; 2,400/8 = 300 mL/h initially and 2,400/16 = 150 mL/h subsequently, subject to hourly titration. This is an initial estimate, not a fixed prescription. Do not apply this adult formula alone to children, electrical rhabdomyolysis or small burns.
- Monitor hourly urine output (usual adult target about 0.5 mL/kg/h), perfusion, lactate trend, renal function, electrolytes and cumulative balance. Check catheter patency and other causes of oliguria before escalating fluid. Avoid fluid creep, pulmonary edema and abdominal/extremity compartment syndromes. Consider albumin with the burn team, especially in large burns; timing and dose need specialist selection.
- Shock disproportionate to burn size or very early after injury demands a search for hemorrhage, CO/cyanide toxicity, tension pneumothorax or cardiac injury. Do not attribute all hypotension to burn shock.
- Provide titrated IV analgesia through `sedoanalgesia`/`medication-selection-safety`, tetanus prophylaxis as indicated and appropriate wound care. No routine systemic prophylactic antibiotics for an uncomplicated thermal burn. Circumferential deep burns with impaired perfusion or chest excursion require urgent burn-surgical assessment for escharotomy, not automatic intervention from appearance alone.
- Record time, TBSA estimate, weight, prior fluids, hourly rates/output, serial neurovascular findings and airway trajectory for transfer. Stabilization and early burn-center discussion proceed together.

title: Smoke Inhalation Toxic Injury
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Separate upper-airway thermal edema, lower-airway chemical injury, carbon monoxide poisoning and possible cyanide toxicity; they can coexist. Obtain enclosure/exposure history, soot, voice change, stridor, work of breathing, consciousness, ECG, blood gas with co-oximetry and lactate. Do not use a normal initial chest radiograph to exclude inhalation injury.
- Give the highest achievable oxygen concentration immediately for suspected CO poisoning, typically reservoir mask at 15 L/min with an inflated reservoir; if intubated, initially use FiO2 1.0. A normal conventional SpO2 or PaO2 does not exclude CO poisoning. Measure COHb by blood co-oximetry; interpret with exposure-to-sampling delay and oxygen already given, not as a severity score in isolation.
- Intubate early with expert airway support for progressive obstruction/edema, stridor, respiratory failure or inability to protect the airway; consider transfer duration and anticipated progression. Singed hairs alone do not mandate intubation. Route to `airway-rsi`, prepare a difficult-airway rescue plan and reassess frequently. Bronchoscopy/laryngoscopy may define injury in a stabilized patient but must not delay a threatened airway.
- For CO exposure, consult toxicology/hyperbaric services for loss of consciousness, neurologic deficit, cardiac injury, severe acidosis or COHb above about 25--30%; clinical severity can justify consultation below that range. Pregnancy warrants urgent specialist consideration at lower exposure severity. Continue oxygen during consultation/transfer and arrange advice about delayed neurologic symptoms.
- Suspect severe cyanide toxicity after enclosed-space smoke with altered consciousness, shock or marked lactate elevation; lactate at least 10 mmol/L supports suspicion in smoke exposure but is nonspecific and is not required before treating a convincing collapse. Do not wait for a cyanide assay. Seek toxicology support without delaying resuscitation.
- Adult hydroxocobalamin: 5 g IV, prepared to a total of 200 mL with sodium chloride 0.9% as specified by the verified presentation (25 mg/mL; either one 5 g vial or two 2.5 g vials with their corresponding reconstitution volumes), over 15 minutes. If a pump is used, 200 mL/0.25 h = 800 mL/h for that 15-minute dose only; this is not a maintenance infusion. A second 5 g may be given according to severity/response over 15 minutes to 2 hours; adult total maximum 10 g. Pediatric dosing needs the separate weight-based product protocol.
- Do not administer hydroxocobalamin routinely to every smoke-exposed patient. Monitor BP and allergy; EMA advises renal-function monitoring through 7 days after administration; anticipate red discoloration, laboratory interference and interference with some dialysis blood-leak detectors. Obtain samples before treatment if this causes no delay. Use a separate compatible line; nitrite-based antidotes can worsen oxygen delivery with concurrent CO poisoning and require toxicologist direction.
- Manage bronchospasm with inhaled bronchodilator when present; provide secretion clearance and lung-protective ventilation if needed. Do not use systemic steroids or antibiotics routinely solely for inhalation injury. Nebulized heparin/mucolytic regimens are burn-center-specific, not universal standards. Admit/transfer suspected significant inhalation injury and reassess for delayed deterioration. After CO poisoning, provide delayed-neurologic warning instructions and arrange clinical/neurologic reassessment at about 2 weeks (CDC).

title: Obstetric Emergencies
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- Stabilize the pregnant/postpartum patient first while assessing gestational age and fetal needs; involve obstetrics, anesthesia and neonatology early when relevant. Maternal resuscitation takes priority: do not withhold necessary imaging, defibrillation, drugs or procedures solely because of pregnancy.
- Major threats include ectopic pregnancy, obstetric haemorrhage, severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, sepsis, thromboembolism, placental abruption/accreta spectrum and uterine rupture. Postpartum disease remains possible after delivery.
- **Acute severe hypertension:** ACOG continues to define severe-range BP as **SBP >=160 mm Hg and/or DBP >=110 mm Hg**. If persistent (about **15 min**), treat urgently; established guidance targets treatment within 30--60 minutes of confirmation.
- First-line emergency options remain pregnancy-specific: IV labetalol **20 mg over 2 min**, then 40 mg after 10 min and 80 mg after another 10 min if still severe. This sequence totals 140 mg; if still severe, reassess and switch/escalate with specialist support according to the selected algorithm. The ACOG emergency-checklist example separately specifies a **maximum cumulative IV dose of 300 mg in 24 h**; this is a ceiling, not an instruction to continue repeating ineffective boluses; IV hydralazine **5--10 mg** with reassessment per local algorithm; or immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg PO, followed by 20 mg doses when still severe, using the local first-hour ceiling. **Never give nifedipine sublingually.**
- Choose antihypertensive around asthma/bradycardia/heart failure, maternal haemodynamics and fetal status. Magnesium sulfate prevents/treats eclamptic seizures; it is **not** the antihypertensive.
- **Eclampsia/seizure prophylaxis:** magnesium sulfate is first-line. A common IV regimen supported by major obstetric guidance is **4--6 g IV loading over ~20--30 min**, followed by **1--2 g/h** maintenance; local protocol may use a specific variant. For recurrent seizure despite magnesium, give an additional magnesium bolus per obstetric protocol and involve anesthesia/critical care.
- Monitor respiration, deep-tendon reflexes, urine output and renal function during magnesium therapy. With clinically significant magnesium toxicity/respiratory depression, stop magnesium, support ventilation and give **calcium gluconate 1 g IV (10 mL of 10%) slowly** as antidotal therapy.
- Severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia requires definitive obstetric planning; BP control and magnesium stabilize the mother but do not replace assessment for delivery. Use pregnancy-specific haemorrhage, sepsis, thromboembolism and resuscitation pathways after verification.
- Portugal/Azores: the owner accepts the local obstetric circuit and requests GREEN on 2026-11-13. Use the selected maternity/emergency and transfer/delivery pathway. Verify magnesium presentation/pump standard and antihypertensive product for each administration; no new independent product/stock audit or named specialist/pharmacy signature is inferred from circuit acceptance.

title: Hypertensive Emergencies
sharedPreamble:
# Cardiovascular modules

Shared gate: establish ABC status, perfusion, symptom onset, ECG timing, vascular
access, glucose, pregnancy possibility, bleeding risk, renal function and current
antithrombotic therapy. Use serial examinations; a single normal ECG, troponin or
POCUS study does not exclude time-critical disease.
sectionBody:
- Diagnose acute hypertension-mediated organ injury, not a number alone; severe BP without acute organ injury is not by itself a hypertensive emergency. Assess neurologic, cardiac, aortic, renal, retinal and pregnancy complications.
- Select titratable IV therapy and the reduction target for the specific syndrome. For adults without a compelling syndrome-specific condition, AHA/ACC 2025 advises reducing SBP by no more than 25% within the first hour, followed by reassessment. Do not confuse SBP with MAP percentage targets or transfer this rule to aortic dissection, acute stroke, pulmonary edema, ACS or pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, which require their own targets and timing.
- Avoid abrupt uncontrolled reductions. Verify agent-specific contraindications, infusion math and local targets; use continuous monitoring and frequent neurologic/perfusion reassessment.

title: Iv Antihypertensive Selection
sharedPreamble:
# Cardiovascular modules

Shared gate: establish ABC status, perfusion, symptom onset, ECG timing, vascular
access, glucose, pregnancy possibility, bleeding risk, renal function and current
antithrombotic therapy. Use serial examinations; a single normal ECG, troponin or
POCUS study does not exclude time-critical disease.
sectionBody:
- First identify the hypertension-mediated organ injury and its target; there is no universal substitute for nicardipine. State the current BP, desired range, maximum initial reduction, lower perfusion boundary, monitoring and reassessment interval. Severe asymptomatic hypertension without acute organ injury does not justify rapid IV lowering.
- Nimodipine is not an alternative IV antihypertensive. It is disease-modifying enteral treatment after confirmed aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and can itself cause hypotension; do not substitute it for nicardipine in ICH, ischemic stroke, hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic syndrome, ACS or pulmonary edema.
- **Labetalol** is a practical alternative for many neurologic hypertensive emergencies when bradycardia, high-grade AV block, decompensated systolic failure and active bronchospasm are absent. Give 20 mg IV slowly over 2 minutes; if needed, use protocol-based additional 40--80 mg doses at about 10-minute intervals to a usual cumulative ceiling of 300 mg. For a continuous infusion, the labelled preparation 200 mg/200 mL = 1 mg/mL; 0.5 mg/min = 30 mL/h, 1 mg/min = 60 mL/h and 2 mg/min = 120 mL/h. A 100 mg/100 mL bag gives the same concentration and rates only when pharmacy/local compatibility is confirmed. Monitor ECG/BP and hold for hypotension, bradycardia, block, bronchospasm or worsening pump failure.
- **Clevidipine** is a short-acting arterial alternative when available. Use the ready-to-use 0.5 mg/mL lipid emulsion without dilution: 1 mg/h = 2 mL/h and 2 mg/h = 4 mL/h. The product label permits initial doubling at 90-second intervals; as BP approaches target, use smaller increases and extend adjustments to every 5--10 minutes. Most patients in trials received no more than 16 mg/h = 32 mL/h; the label limits 24-hour exposure because of lipid load (no more than 1,000 mL or an average 21 mg/h). Do not use with soy/egg allergy, defective lipid metabolism or severe aortic stenosis; use strict asepsis, discard an opened vial according to the label, and account for lipid calories.
- **Acute aortic syndrome:** reduce impulse first with esmolol or labetalol when beta-blockade is safe. Only if BP remains high after rate/impulse control add nicardipine, clevidipine or another protocol-approved vasodilator. Never start a pure vasodilator first in a tachycardic patient; use IV diltiazem/verapamil for rate control only when beta-blockers are contraindicated and the aortic/cardiac phenotype permits.
- **Hypertensive pulmonary edema or ACS:** a titratable nitrate is usually more syndrome-concordant than nicardipine. If a pharmacy-approved concentration is 20 mg/100 mL or 40 mg/200 mL = 200 micrograms/mL, 5 micrograms/min = 1.5 mL/h and 10 micrograms/min = 3 mL/h; titrate every 3--5 minutes to symptoms, BP and local ceiling. Do not use with hypotension, preload-dependent/right-ventricular infarction, recent PDE-5 inhibitor or critical stenotic/preload-dependent physiology. Higher-dose pulmonary-edema strategies require the local protocol and continuous monitoring.
- **Pregnancy/postpartum severe hypertension:** use the pregnancy pathway. First-line urgent options are IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or immediate-release oral nifedipine; do not use sublingual nifedipine. Magnesium sulfate is for seizure prevention/treatment, not BP lowering.
- **Sympathetic/toxicologic crisis:** treat agitation, pain and the driver first; benzodiazepines and a cause-appropriate vasodilator may be required. Do not use isolated beta-blockade in acute cocaine/amphetamine toxicity or catecholamine excess without specialist/toxicology guidance.
- Reserve sodium nitroprusside for selected monitored rescue situations when preferred agents are unavailable or ineffective. Its toxicity/monitoring burden and potential problems in raised ICP, renal/hepatic failure and pregnancy make it a poor routine substitute. Enalaprilat and hydralazine outside pregnancy have less predictable/prolonged effects and are not default choices when minute-to-minute titration is needed.

title: Acute Respiratory Failure
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Identify whether the dominant problem is **oxygenation failure, ventilation failure, or both**, and treat the cause in parallel: upper-airway obstruction, asthma/COPD, cardiogenic edema, pneumonia/ARDS, PE, pneumothorax, neuromuscular weakness, obesity-hypoventilation, CNS depression or toxicity.
- Record SpO2 target, respiratory rate/work of breathing, mental state, hemodynamics and an early blood gas when severe hypoxemia, suspected hypercapnia/acidosis or escalating support is present. Integrate lung/cardiac POCUS, ECG and imaging according to the suspected cause.
- **Hypoxemic de-novo respiratory failure:** ATS 2026 recommends HFNO over standard oxygen and conditionally supports NIV/CPAP versus standard oxygen with close monitoring; this does not establish universal HFNO superiority over NIV/CPAP. Without an immediate intubation indication, select support by physiology and local capability, using `high-flow-nasal-oxygen` or `noninvasive-ventilation`. A P/F ratio <=200 mmHg signals substantial hypoxemia but is not an isolated intubation rule; consider FiO2, support, effort and trajectory.
- **Hypercapnic respiratory failure:** bilevel NIV is preferred for an appropriate COPD/acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure with respiratory acidosis when no contraindication or immediate intubation indication exists. Use `noninvasive-ventilation`. ATS 2026 allows HFNO conditionally in selected less severe hypercapnia with mild acidemia (e.g. pH >7.25), only with close monitoring and prompt NIV escalation; do not substitute it for indicated NIV in severe/worsening ventilatory failure.
- **Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema:** CPAP or bilevel NIV is appropriate in the absence of shock, immediate airway indication or other contraindication; treat the cardiac cause simultaneously.
- Choose HFNO, NIV or intubation based on physiology, contraindications and trajectory. **Do not use noninvasive support as a delaying maneuver** when there is refractory/worsening hypoxemia, severe fatigue, worsening acidosis, shock, inability to protect the airway, rapidly worsening mental state or another immediate airway indication.
- Reassess within minutes of any escalation and repeatedly thereafter: SpO2/FiO2, respiratory rate and effort, accessory-muscle use, synchrony, pH/PaCO2 when relevant, mental state and blood pressure. Serial trend is more important than a single score.
- If intubation is likely, activate the airway/critical-care pathway early and optimize physiology before induction. Disposition must be to a setting capable of continuous monitoring and rapid invasive escalation. ATS 2026 supports HFNO or NIV for preoxygenation rather than standard oxygen when appropriate.
- **Local circuit acceptance (2026-11-13):** the owner accepts support selection, failure assessment and intubation/ICU escalation and requests GREEN. No specific ventilator settings, staffing roster or independently verified on-site resource is inferred.

title: Acute Severe Asthma
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Treat first while assessing severity. Mark as immediately life-threatening when there is exhaustion, altered consciousness, cyanosis, silent/poorly ventilated chest, bradycardia/hypotension, refractory hypoxemia or impending arrest. PEF at most about 33% of best/predicted supports life-threatening obstruction when the patient can perform it, but inability to perform PEF must not delay treatment or reassure.
- In immediately life-threatening hypoxemia, give rescue oxygen without delay and obtain expert airway help. Once oxygen can be titrated, use the GINA 2026 SpO2 target 92--95% for adults/adolescents and avoid hyperoxia; do not delay oxygen when oximetry is unavailable. Use 88--92% when there is a separate established risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. Obtain an arterial/venous blood gas for life-threatening features, poor response or suspected ventilatory failure; a normal or rising PaCO2 in a distressed patient is dangerous and may indicate fatigue.
- Use the GINA 2026 acute-care severity branches (Box 9-6): for severe presentation, salbutamol 6--10 puffs of 100 micrograms by pMDI/spacer, one puff at a time, or 5 mg nebulized; for moderate presentation, 4--6 puffs or 2.5 mg nebulized. Repeat if needed up to three cycles 20--30 minutes apart and reassess after each. Refractory/life-threatening disease needs immediate expert escalation; do not apply a routine fixed continuous-nebulization dose from this module. ICU rescue dosing/delivery requires its own verified protocol.
- Add ipratropium with the initial salbutamol cycles in moderate/severe presentations: GINA 2026 Box 9-6 uses 4 puffs of 20 micrograms via spacer or 0.25 mg nebulized, up to three cycles 20--30 minutes apart. Reassess rather than automatically continuing after the initial treatment.
- Give systemic corticosteroid early: prednisolone/prednisone 40--50 mg PO once daily for 5--7 days in most adults; if oral treatment is not possible, use an equivalent IV dose according to formulary. Higher IV doses are not routinely superior. Ensure an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing controller and technique/adherence plan before discharge; never discharge an asthma patient on SABA-only treatment.
- For severe obstruction with inadequate initial response, give magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes. Example: 2 g diluted to 100 mL = 20 mg/mL, run at 300 mL/h for 20 minutes; this is a timed intermittent infusion, not continuous therapy. Check hypotension, renal failure and neuromuscular risk; routine repeated magnesium is not established.
- Do not use sedatives, mucolytics, routine antibiotics, routine epinephrine/terbutaline injection or IV aminophylline. Give IM epinephrine when asthma is part of anaphylaxis or angioedema. NIV is not routine in acute asthma and must not delay intubation. If deterioration, exhaustion, reduced consciousness or refractory gas-exchange failure develops, call ICU/anesthesia early and intubate with an experienced operator using a low respiratory rate, long expiratory time, low external PEEP initially, permissive hypercapnia when safe and monitoring for dynamic hyperinflation/hypotension.
- Reassess every 15--30 minutes during the first hour: speech, accessory-muscle use, respiratory rate, air entry, SpO2, HR/BP, PEF/FEV1 when feasible, potassium, glucose and lactate when beta-agonist exposure is high. Rising lactate may be beta-agonist related and must not automatically trigger more bronchodilator or fluid without reassessing airflow and perfusion.
- Admit persistent severe symptoms, oxygen need, low lung function, prior near-fatal asthma, poor social safety or relapse after initial response. ICU for life-threatening features or escalating support. Discharge only after sustained clinical/lung-function improvement, with controller therapy, written action plan, trigger/technique review and follow-up within days.

title: Copd Exacerbation
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Confirm acute worsening beyond usual variation while actively seeking mimics/precipitants: pneumonia, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, ACS/arrhythmia, pleural effusion, medication/sedative effect and metabolic disease. Severe dyspnea, confusion, cyanosis, edema, hemodynamic instability or inability to speak/eat requires monitored resuscitation assessment.
- Give controlled oxygen to SpO2 88--92% pending blood gas when COPD or another hypercapnia risk is present. Obtain an early gas in severe illness or oxygen need and repeat about 30--60 minutes after a material oxygen/support change. Do not withhold oxygen from life-threatening hypoxemia, but titrate promptly because excessive oxygen can worsen hypercapnia/acidosis.
- Start a short-acting beta2-agonist with or without a short-acting anticholinergic. GOLD 2026 advises against routine high SABA doses: one nebulized dose hourly for 2--3 doses, or 1--2 puffs by pMDI/spacer hourly for 2--3 doses, then every 2--4 hours according to response. Verify the specific product dose/concentration and device; do not automatically import the intensive asthma cycle into COPD. Persistent severe distress requires reassessment/escalation rather than unbounded bronchodilator dosing. Use air-driven nebulization when feasible in CO2 retainers and provide controlled supplemental oxygen separately; monitor HR, rhythm, potassium, tremor and lactate.
- Give prednisone/prednisolone 40 mg PO once daily for 5 days; no taper is usually needed for this short course unless the patient is chronically steroid-dependent or at risk of adrenal suppression. If oral therapy is impossible, use an equivalent IV dose and switch to oral promptly. Avoid routine prolonged or high-dose courses.
- Give antibiotics when increased sputum purulence accompanies at least one of increased dyspnea, fever or sputum volume; also consider prior positive exacerbation sputum culture and invasive/noninvasive mechanical ventilation. Usual duration is 5--7 days, with at most 5 days recommended for responding outpatients (GOLD 2026); individualize hospitalized/severe cases. Pneumonia follows the pneumonia pathway rather than this course-length shortcut. Choose agent and dose from local resistance, recent antibiotics/cultures, bronchiectasis/Pseudomonas risk, allergy, renal function and pneumonia severity; load `empiric-antibiotics` rather than inventing a universal regimen.
- Use bilevel NIV early for persistent acute or acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (generally pH at most 7.35 with elevated PaCO2) despite initial treatment, unless there is an immediate airway indication or contraindication. Load `noninvasive-ventilation`, define failure criteria and repeat gas at about 1 hour. HFNO may improve comfort/oxygenation but is not a substitute for NIV in hypercapnic acidosis. Intubate for arrest, inability to protect the airway, worsening consciousness, refractory hypoxemia/acidosis, shock, secretion burden or failed NIV when consistent with goals of care.
- Do not use methylxanthines routinely. Treat fluids, diuresis and anticoagulation only for the demonstrated phenotype; provide VTE prophylaxis to hospitalized immobile patients unless contraindicated. Continue/restart appropriate long-acting bronchodilators, inhaler technique, smoking treatment and pulmonary-rehabilitation/follow-up planning after stabilization.
- Reassess respiratory rate/effort, mental state, SpO2, gas/pH/PaCO2, hemodynamics, secretion clearance and NIV tolerance frequently. Admit for acidosis/hypercapnia, new oxygen or ventilatory support, serious comorbidity, inadequate home support or failure of ED therapy; higher-acuity placement for severe acidosis, altered consciousness, shock or escalating support.

title: Life Threatening Hemoptysis
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Define life-threatening hemoptysis by airway obstruction, impaired gas exchange, hemodynamic instability, rapid ongoing bleeding or limited cardiopulmonary reserve, not by a single volume threshold. Confirm blood is from the lower respiratory tract while simultaneously excluding upper-airway and gastrointestinal bleeding; do not delay resuscitation for source certainty.
- Activate anesthesia/airway, respiratory/interventional bronchoscopy, interventional radiology and thoracic surgery early. Sit upright if the bleeding side is unknown and airway control is adequate; once the side is known, place the bleeding lung dependent to protect the better lung. Give high-concentration oxygen for critical hypoxemia, two large-bore IV lines, continuous monitoring, full blood count, coagulation/fibrinogen, renal function, blood gas/lactate and crossmatched blood.
- Stop and reverse clinically important anticoagulant/antiplatelet effect according to agent, timing, renal function and bleeding severity by loading `anticoagulation-reversal`; correct severe thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia and hypothermia. Do not delay airway/source control while awaiting laboratory normalization.
- Secure the airway early when clearance is failing, oxygenation is deteriorating, bleeding is brisk or transport/procedure is unsafe. Use the most experienced operator, suction immediately available and a large single-lumen endotracheal tube (commonly at least 8.0--8.5 mm internal diameter) to permit therapeutic bronchoscopy. Do not default to a double-lumen tube because narrow lumens obstruct with clot and impede bronchoscopy. Protect the non-bleeding lung: expert bronchoscopic selective mainstem intubation must ventilate the non-bleeding lung; alternatively, occlude the bleeding bronchus with a bronchial blocker when expertise/equipment permit. Confirm which lung is ventilated.
- Use rigid or large-channel flexible bronchoscopy to suction clot, localize bleeding and apply temporary endobronchial control when unstable or the airway is threatened. If stabilized, obtain multidetector CT angiography before definitive embolization to identify bronchial, non-bronchial systemic or pulmonary arterial sources; do not send an unstable patient away from resuscitation solely for imaging.
- Arrange urgent bronchial/non-bronchial systemic artery embolization after stabilization for life-threatening or recurrent hemoptysis when a culprit vessel is present; it is usually first-line definitive control for systemic arterial bleeding. For a pulmonary-artery source, arrange urgent lesion-specific interventional-radiology and surgical review; pulmonary artery embolization may be appropriate, not automatic surgery solely because of arterial origin. Surgery is selected for an injury/lesion requiring repair or resection, failed/unavailable embolization or recurrent bleeding requiring definitive resection.
- Nebulized tranexamic acid may be considered only as an adjunct/bridge in selected non-catastrophic or temporarily controlled bleeding; a commonly studied regimen is 500 mg in 5 mL nebulized every 8 hours. Evidence in actively life-threatening hemoptysis is insufficient, and it must never delay bronchoscopy, embolization or surgery. Verify formulation, thrombosis/seizure risk and local protocol; do not nebulize blindly through an obstructed airway.
- Reassess airway patency, suctioned/estimated bleeding rate, oxygenation/ventilation, hemodynamics, hemoglobin/coagulation and recurrence continuously. After apparent control, manage the cause (bronchiectasis, TB/infection, malignancy, aspergillosis, vasculitis, pulmonary embolic/vascular lesion) and admit to critical care or a monitored procedural center; early rebleeding requires renewed CTA/bronchoscopy and embolization/surgery review.
- **Local circuit acceptance (2026-11-13):** the owner requests GREEN for the airway, bronchoscopy, CTA and embolization/surgery pathway after source review. This records circuit acceptance, not independently audited on-site bronchoscopy/IR staffing or a new specialist signature; activate the accepted referral/transfer route when needed.

title: Oxygen Therapy Emergency
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Prescribe oxygen to a saturation target, not merely a flow. Use SpO2 94--98% for most acutely ill adults and 88--92% pending blood gas results when COPD or another risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure is present. In cardiac arrest/peri-arrest or immediately life-threatening hypoxemia, give the highest available concentration first and titrate promptly once reliable monitoring is available. Do not give routine oxygen to a normoxemic ACS or stroke patient.
- Treat the following low-flow FiO2 values as rough bedside estimates, not measurements. Actual FiO2 changes with inspiratory demand, respiratory rate, tidal volume, mouth breathing, mask seal and equipment:

| Device | Adult flow | Approximate FiO2 | Operational point |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Standard nasal cannula | 1--6 L/min | about 24--44%; rough rule 24% at 1 L/min then +4 percentage points per additional L/min | Comfortable; permits speech/eating; unreliable FiO2 in tachypnea or high inspiratory demand; dryness/epistaxis possible. |
| Simple face mask | 5--10 L/min | about 35--60% | Never run below 5 L/min because of CO2 rebreathing; variable FiO2, poor tolerance/seal and aspiration risk. |
| Reservoir/non-rebreather mask | 15 L/min initially | high concentration, often about 60--95% with good seal | Pre-fill reservoir and keep it from collapsing during inspiration; bridge for critical illness, not a reason to delay HFNO/NIV/intubation. |
| Venturi mask | Use flow printed on the valve/device | fixed labelled FiO2, commonly 24%, 28%, 35%, 40% or 60% | Prefer when controlled FiO2 matters. Valve colours and required flows can vary by manufacturer; never prescribe by colour alone. Increasing source flow above the stated minimum increases total gas flow, not the labelled FiO2. |
| Heated high-flow nasal oxygen | commonly 20--60 L/min in adults | FiO2 set independently from 0.21 to 1.0 | Heated humidification, better matching of inspiratory demand, dead-space washout and modest variable airway pressure; define failure criteria and do not delay intubation. |

- For a common Venturi system only, typical minimum source flows are 24% at 2--4 L/min, 28% at 4--6 L/min, 35% at 8--12 L/min, 40% at 10--15 L/min and 60% at 12--15 L/min. Verify the exact valve label/package and increase total flow when respiratory demand exceeds device output; changing flow does not convert one labelled valve to another FiO2.
- Reassess within minutes after every device/flow change: SpO2 waveform and target, respiratory rate and effort, mental state, hemodynamics, mask/cannula position, reservoir inflation and oxygen supply. Obtain an early blood gas when severe hypoxemia, suspected hypercapnia, reduced consciousness or escalating support is present; repeat within 30--60 minutes after oxygen changes in patients at risk of CO2 retention or sooner if deteriorating.
- Escalate support rather than repeatedly increasing an inadequate low-flow device. Consider HFNO for hypoxemic failure, NIV for an appropriate ventilatory/cardiogenic indication, and intubation for refractory hypoxemia, exhaustion, worsening consciousness, shock, inability to protect the airway or failed noninvasive support.
- Balance benefit against harm: oxygen reverses hypoxemia but excessive exposure can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients, cause absorption atelectasis and oxidative lung injury, and mask deterioration. Interfaces can cause dryness, pressure injury, claustrophobia and aspiration risk. Oxygen supports combustion: prohibit smoking/flames and keep oils/grease away from equipment.
- Record target range, device, flow or set FiO2, SpO2 response and escalation plan. Flow in L/min is not interchangeable with FiO2, and FiO2 from low-flow devices must not be used as an exact denominator for P/F calculations.

title: High Flow Nasal Oxygen
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Use heated humidified high-flow nasal oxygen primarily for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure when conventional oxygen is inadequate and no immediate indication for intubation exists. HFNO does not correct severe ventilatory failure reliably and must not replace bilevel NIV for a COPD exacerbation with acute respiratory acidosis when NIV is appropriate.
- In adults, select an interface sized to avoid complete nare occlusion, commonly start flow around 40--60 L/min according to inspiratory demand and tolerance, and set FiO2 independently to the syndrome-specific SpO2 target. Optimize the cause, positioning, secretion clearance and comfort; do not treat the device as definitive therapy.
- Calculate ROX only from a reliable SpO2, set HFNO FiO2 as a fraction, and simultaneous respiratory rate: `ROX = (SpO2 / FiO2) / respiratory rate`. Use `scripts/respiratory_support.py` for serial calculations. Record baseline and repeat early and at approximately 2, 6 and 12 hours when therapy continues, but reassess clinically within minutes after initiation or any deterioration.
- Treat published ROX cutoffs as context-limited signals from adults with pneumonia, not universal intubation thresholds. In the original validation cohort, ROX at least 4.88 at 2, 6 or 12 hours was associated with lower intubation risk; ROX below 2.85 at 2 hours, 3.47 at 6 hours or 3.85 at 12 hours signaled higher failure risk. The direction of change and the bedside examination matter more than a single borderline value.
- Define failure before starting. Escalate immediately for refractory or worsening hypoxemia, increasing respiratory effort or fatigue, shock, worsening mental state, inability to protect the airway, dangerous acidosis/hypercapnia, or another immediate airway indication. A reassuring ROX must never overrule these findings or delay intubation.
- Monitor continuous SpO2 and frequent respiratory rate, work of breathing, mental state and hemodynamics; obtain blood gas and imaging/POCUS according to physiology. Document flow, FiO2, target, ROX trend, response, ceiling of care and named escalation plan.

title: Noninvasive Ventilation
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Match NIV to a **supported syndrome**. ERS/ATS recommends bilevel NIV for COPD exacerbation with acute or acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (pH <=7.35 with elevated PaCO2 despite initial medical therapy). CPAP or bilevel NIV is supported in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema when shock or an immediate airway indication is absent.
- **ATS 2026 update:** in de-novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, HFNO is strongly recommended over conventional oxygen; NIV/CPAP is conditionally recommended over conventional oxygen. This does not establish universal HFNO superiority over NIV/CPAP. Select support by syndrome, severity, expertise and response; monitor closely for delayed intubation. Hypercapnic failure strongly favors NIV; HFNO is only a conditional alternative in less severe hypercapnia/mild acidemia, with close monitoring and prompt NIV escalation. Do not treat the older ERS 2022 comparator as a universal preference across all phenotypes.
- NIV is not routine treatment for acute asthma. Before a trial, document reversibility, escalation/ceiling plan and contraindications. Do not use NIV for respiratory arrest, inability to protect the airway, uncontrolled vomiting, fixed upper-airway obstruction, undrained pneumothorax, severe facial injury preventing a seal, or rapidly worsening shock.
- Agitation, heavy secretions, reduced consciousness and severe acidosis increase failure risk and require senior critical-care assessment; a low pH alone is neither an automatic exclusion nor permission for an unsupervised trial.
- **Starting reference, acute hypercapnia:** IPAP 10--15 cmH2O and EPAP 4 cmH2O, then increase effective pressure support over the first 10--30 min according to ventilation, work of breathing, leak, synchrony and tolerance; pressures of 20--30 cmH2O may be needed under an experienced team. Set S/T backup rate individually using the selected ventilator protocol, respiratory drive and patient synchrony; no universal device-independent backup rate is assumed.
- If PaCO2 remains high with inadequate ventilation, correct leak/synchrony before increasing IPAP. For hypoxemia, reassess diagnosis/interface and titrate FiO2 and/or EPAP while retaining sufficient pressure support. Avoid an escalating tidal volume/work-of-breathing pattern that delays intubation.
- For acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, a common CPAP starting reference is **5--10 cmH2O**; choose bilevel when ventilation assistance is also needed. These ranges require patient-specific reassessment.
- **Interface/circuit:** select an appropriately sized oronasal/full-face interface for acute support as tolerated, protect pressure areas and reassess leaks, comfort and secretions. Confirm the device's circuit, intentional leak/exhalation port or expiratory valve and vented/nonvented mask match; never obstruct the exhalation route. Helmet and other interfaces need their own validated settings and trained staff; do not copy mask settings blindly.
- Target SpO2 **88--92%** in acute hypercapnic failure unless an individualized target is documented. Initially use continuous SpO2/ECG and frequent BP, respiratory-rate, consciousness and work-of-breathing assessment. Repeat blood gas at approximately **1 hour**, after material changes and immediately if deterioration occurs; improvement must include clinical effort and gas trends.
- Falling pH, non-improving PaCO2/work of breathing, refractory hypoxemia, new confusion, intolerance or hemodynamic decline are failure signals. pH <7.25 despite optimized NIV requires immediate senior/ICU reassessment and preparation for intubation when appropriate; no single number replaces the airway decision. Do not await the scheduled gas or prolong NIV when immediate intubation is indicated.
- Record device/interface, IPAP/EPAP or CPAP, backup rate, FiO2, oxygen target, response trend, ceiling of care and explicit intubation criteria. Owner accepts this reviewed framework; model-specific setup and competent staffing remain bedside checks rather than assumed equipment availability.

title: Tension Pneumothorax
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Suspect tension physiology when acute dyspnea or pleuritic chest pain is accompanied by shock, severe respiratory compromise or rapid deterioration, especially with asymmetric or absent breath sounds. A relatively normal heart rate, absent tracheal deviation or absent neck-vein distension does not establish stability or exclude the diagnosis.
- Treat this as a clinical time-critical diagnosis. Activate resuscitation support, provide monitored oxygen appropriate to hypoxemia, obtain IV/IO access and prepare immediate pleural decompression. Do not send an unstable patient for CT, and do not wait for chest radiography when the clinical probability of tension pneumothorax is high.
- Use lung POCUS only when it is immediately available and does not delay decompression. Absent sliding and B-lines with a compatible pattern support pneumothorax but are not specific; a lung point supports the diagnosis when seen but may be absent in a very large pneumothorax. A technically limited or negative scan does not overrule worsening obstructive-shock physiology.
- Select needle/catheter decompression or open/finger thoracostomy according to patient context, clinician skill, equipment and current local resuscitation protocol. State the intended anatomical site and device before acting, avoid the inferior rib neurovascular bundle, and have an immediate failure/rescue plan. Do not present one technique or site as universally preferred across spontaneous, traumatic and peri-arrest settings.
- Decompression is not the endpoint: reassess blood pressure, oxygenation, work of breathing and bilateral air entry immediately; confirm pleural access/success by clinical response and available imaging, then arrange definitive intercostal drainage and specialist/critical-care involvement. If there is no prompt improvement, check device failure or malposition and reassess for massive PE, tamponade, hemorrhage, dynamic hyperinflation and other causes of shock.
- Use cautious, reassessed circulatory support only as a bridge to source control. Fluids or vasopressors must not delay decompression or be treated as definitive therapy for obstructive shock.

title: Observation Discharge
sharedPreamble: # Disposition and cross-cutting modules
sectionBody:
- Adult observation is active, time-limited evaluation/treatment for a defined unresolved clinical question, not a place to defer necessary admission or source control. Define entry criteria, required serial tests/exams, treatment endpoints, reassessment times and the syndrome/local unit's maximum safe duration. Assign the responsible clinician and nursing team, with explicit handover and escalation criteria; do not impose one observation time for all conditions.
- Match the plan to actual staffing, equipment and rescue capability. Reassess symptoms, vital signs, consciousness, examination, function and treatment response at the required interval and after a material change; abnormal trends require action even if a score is low. Deterioration, unresolved high-risk diagnosis, escalating support needs or inability to complete the plan safely triggers senior reassessment, inpatient care or transfer.
- Apply the condition-specific discharge pathway, including required serial ECG/laboratory/imaging or post-treatment observation where indicated. A normal single test, symptom improvement, completion of a clock interval or a risk score alone is insufficient for discharge. Check oral intake/medication use, mobility, pain control, post-sedation recovery and relevant pregnancy/frailty/safeguarding needs rather than relying on stable BP alone.
- Review available results and reconcile preliminary versus final interpretations before disposition. If a test can safely remain pending, name the clinician/service responsible for reviewing it, the expected timeframe, the contact method, and the action/escalation plan for a significant result. Verify usable contact details and communicate the plan to the patient and next team; electronic release or 'no news means normal' is not closed-loop follow-up. A result essential to an immediate safe decision must not be left unresolved merely because follow-up is planned.
- Provide a clear working diagnosis and uncertainty, reconciled medication changes/duration and precautions, condition-specific deterioration warnings, where/how urgently to return and concrete follow-up arrangements. Use the patient's language, interpreter/accessibility support and teach-back when possible. Check understanding, decision-making capacity, transport, caregiver support and ability to carry out the plan; address barriers before discharge.
- For admission/transfer, communicate the reason, current status, recent interventions, pending tests, monitoring/rescue needs and named receiving responsibility. Document shared decisions or informed refusal/capacity and the safety plan. Local observation capacity, specialist response times and result-callback systems must be confirmed operationally; this reference review does not certify their existence.

title: Status Epilepticus
sharedPreamble:
# Neurologic modules

Shared gate: establish last-known-well/onset, glucose, temperature, oxygenation,
anticoagulants, seizure activity, trauma and baseline function. Perform serial
focused neurologic examinations; protect the airway when needed without obscuring
time-critical diagnosis.
sectionBody:
- Treat generalized convulsive status epilepticus for a seizure **lasting 5 minutes or more (>=5 minutes)** or recurrent seizures without recovery. Do not wait for 30 minutes. Stabilize airway/breathing/circulation, check glucose immediately, obtain IV/IO access, correct hypoxia/electrolytes and investigate toxins, infection, pregnancy/eclampsia, structural lesions and medication nonadherence in parallel.
- **First-line benzodiazepine — give a full effective dose promptly, not repeated small fractions.** If IV access and resuscitation facilities are available: lorazepam **0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg)**, may repeat once if seizure persists. Alternative: diazepam **0.15--0.2 mg/kg IV (max 10 mg)**, may repeat once. If no IV access: the AES studied IM midazolam regimen is **10 mg when >40 kg or 5 mg at 13--40 kg**, as a single initial dose; smaller children require their pediatric pathway. Prepare airway support before/while giving benzodiazepines; respiratory depression risk is real but undertreatment of status is also dangerous.
- **Established benzodiazepine-refractory status:** promptly give one adequately dosed IV second-line antiseizure medication. Current ED evidence supports clinical equipoise among:
  - levetiracetam **60 mg/kg IV, max 4,500 mg**;
  - fosphenytoin **20 mg PE/kg IV, max 1,500 mg PE**;
  - sodium valproate **40 mg/kg IV, max 3,000 mg**.
  ESETT infused each of these trial regimens over **10 minutes**; use the verified local preparation/product and monitored infusion protocol, not the trial vial concentration by assumption. Choose according to contraindications, interactions, pregnancy, liver disease, cardiac conduction disease and local availability; do not delay escalation searching for a theoretically superior agent.
- Where fosphenytoin is unavailable and local protocol uses phenytoin, use the local monitored loading pathway; IV phenytoin carries hypotension/arrhythmia risk and requires ECG/BP monitoring and strict infusion-rate control.
- **Important selection boundaries:** avoid valproate where contraindicated (notably significant hepatic disease and pregnancy/people with childbearing potential unless specialist benefit clearly outweighs risk); use caution with fosphenytoin/phenytoin in bradycardia, AV block or major conduction disease. Levetiracetam is often operationally simpler but is not universally superior.
- If convulsive activity stops but consciousness does not recover as expected, suspect **non-convulsive status** and obtain urgent EEG/neurology input rather than assuming a postictal state.
- **Refractory status epilepticus:** after adequate benzodiazepine plus an adequate second-line load, involve ICU/neurology, secure airway as required, start continuous EEG and use an anesthetic-infusion pathway (e.g. midazolam/propofol/other specialist regimen) with hemodynamic and ventilation support. No single anesthetic strategy has definitive superiority.
- Pregnancy/eclampsia, toxin-mediated seizures, alcohol withdrawal and severe metabolic disturbances require the corresponding cause-specific pathway; do not apply this generic algorithm without modification.
- Portugal/Azores: on 2026-11-13 the owner confirms all requested local requirements (drugs/preparations, EEG access/circuit and neurology/ICU escalation) and accepts the pathway. This declaration does not identify brands/concentrations or prove on-site continuous EEG; verify exact product and pump preparation for each administration and use the confirmed EEG/escalation circuit. No new independent pharmacy/neurology signature or prospective validation is inferred.

title: Altered Consciousness
sharedPreamble:
# Neurologic modules

Shared gate: establish last-known-well/onset, glucose, temperature, oxygenation,
anticoagulants, seizure activity, trauma and baseline function. Perform serial
focused neurologic examinations; protect the airway when needed without obscuring
time-critical diagnosis.
sectionBody:
- **Immediate adult assessment:** stabilize ABCs and check bedside glucose immediately. Treat hypoglycemia promptly through the appropriate protocol; **do not delay glucose for thiamine** in a nutritionally at-risk patient. Assess breathing/oxygenation, perfusion, temperature, AVPU/GCS, pupils and focal signs; protect the cervical spine when trauma is possible.
- **Airway and ventilation:** support ventilation and protect the airway according to reflexes, respiratory failure and trajectory, not an isolated score alone. Use monitoring and early blood gas/capnography when hypoventilation is possible. Record the neurological examination and confounding sedatives when feasible without delaying lifesaving treatment; repeat examinations after interventions.
- **Search reversible and structural causes in parallel:** hypoxia/hypercapnia, glucose/electrolyte disturbance, shock/sepsis, seizure including nonconvulsive status, stroke/hemorrhage, trauma, temperature disorders, renal/hepatic/endocrine disease, toxins and sedative/alcohol withdrawal. Obtain collateral baseline, onset/last-known-well, medication list/last doses, exposure history and anticoagulants. Do not diagnose intoxication or psychiatric illness solely from an initial impression.
- Obtain targeted glucose/CBC/electrolytes/renal-liver tests, ECG, gas/lactate and other tests guided by findings; urine toxicology is not a universal explanation of coma. Treat shock, hypoglycemia, infection, stroke or status through their syndrome pathways while the investigation continues. Consider EEG for unexplained persistent impairment or possible nonconvulsive status and specialist assessment when infection/LP is being considered.
- **Imaging (ACR 2024):** urgent noncontrast head CT is generally appropriate for suspected intracranial pathology/focal deficit; trauma or known structural disease needs its specific pathway. Persistent altered mental status despite treatment of a presumed medical/toxic-metabolic cause also supports noncontrast CT. Do not require routine CT for every fully explained, resolving metabolic episode; select subsequent MRI/vascular imaging by the suspected condition. Deterioration overrides a reassuring earlier investigation.
- **Antidotes are indication-specific:** suspected opioid-related hypoventilation requires airway/ventilation support and naloxone directed at adequate breathing, without delaying resuscitation. Observe for recurrent respiratory depression. **Do not give flumazenil empirically for unexplained coma**: mixed ingestion, chronic benzodiazepine exposure or seizure/arrhythmia risk can make it harmful; reserve it for selected appropriate cases with toxicology/rescue support. Do not use a blanket sedative/antidote cocktail to replace diagnosis.
- **Destination and reassessment:** unexplained/persistent impairment, recurrent events, new deficits, unstable physiology, inadequate airway protection or inability to implement safe treatment requires monitored admission and appropriate neurology/ICU escalation. Full recovery alone is insufficient for discharge without identifying the likely cause, recurrence risk, observation needs and safe supervision/follow-up. Document serial state, response, capacity/safeguarding and handover plan. GREEN validates the reviewed reference scope and owner acceptance, not autonomous diagnosis or guaranteed local resources.

title: Headache Sah
sharedPreamble:
# Neurologic modules

Shared gate: establish last-known-well/onset, glucose, temperature, oxygenation,
anticoagulants, seizure activity, trauma and baseline function. Perform serial
focused neurologic examinations; protect the airway when needed without obscuring
time-critical diagnosis.
sectionBody:
- Identify thunderclap onset, neurologic deficit, meningism, exertional onset, pregnancy/postpartum state, immunosuppression, cancer and anticoagulation.
- Use a validated SAH pathway and document time from onset to CT. In a neurologically intact patient scanned within 6 hours, a technically adequate modern noncontrast CT interpreted by an appropriately experienced reader may complete the rule-out pathway under current local guidance; do not generalize this to late, poor-quality or clinically discordant studies.
- If meaningful residual risk remains after a negative CT, pursue lumbar puncture and/or CTA according to current guidance, local expertise and shared decision-making; explain the different false-positive/incidental-aneurysm and procedural tradeoffs.
- Nimodipine is used after confirmed aneurysmal SAH to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia; it is not a generic treatment for undifferentiated headache or hypertension and must not delay diagnostic imaging or aneurysm-securing pathways.
- Also consider dissection, venous thrombosis, hypertensive emergency, meningitis, glaucoma and pituitary apoplexy. Escalate abnormal examination, persistent high-risk suspicion or clinical deterioration.

title: Cns Infection
sharedPreamble:
# Neurologic modules

Shared gate: establish last-known-well/onset, glucose, temperature, oxygenation,
anticoagulants, seizure activity, trauma and baseline function. Perform serial
focused neurologic examinations; protect the airway when needed without obscuring
time-critical diagnosis.
sectionBody:
- Treat suspected bacterial meningitis/encephalitis as time critical; obtain blood cultures promptly, but never allow cultures, lumbar puncture or CT to delay empiric antimicrobials when delay would be unsafe.
- Determine whether imaging is needed before LP from clinical contraindications rather than ordering CT routinely. Give dexamethasone with or just before the first antibiotic dose when bacterial meningitis is suspected and the applicable protocol recommends it; benefit is less certain once antibiotics are already established.
- Add IV acyclovir promptly when encephalitis is plausible, with renal adjustment and hydration/renal monitoring.
- Use age, immune status, pregnancy, renal function and local resistance to select doses. Apply isolation precautions, manage seizures/shock and involve critical care/infectious diseases early.

title: Traumatic Intracranial Mass Effect
sharedPreamble:
# Neurologic modules

Shared gate: establish last-known-well/onset, glucose, temperature, oxygenation,
anticoagulants, seizure activity, trauma and baseline function. Perform serial
focused neurologic examinations; protect the airway when needed without obscuring
time-critical diagnosis.
sectionBody:
- **2026 TBI characterization:** document serial eye/verbal/motor responses, pupils, loss of consciousness/amnesia, examination confounders, imaging and relevant pre-injury modifiers. CBI-M (Clinical, Biomarkers, Imaging, Modifiers) supplements description; it is not an Emergency-validated CT rule or individual prognosis calculator. Cohort evaluation published 20 October 2026 supports further implementation research, not automatic treatment/withdrawal decisions.
