A non-testable GCS component is **NT**, not 1 or 0; do not report an artificial summed score. See `references/tbi-biomarkers-cbim-2026.md` for source-specific boundaries.
- **Upstream adult mild-TBI assessment / biomarkers:** this section also covers initial adult head-injury triage; the mass-effect emergency pathway below remains immediate. GFAP/UCH-L1 is an adjunct only in selected patients meeting the exact assay instructions and an accepted laboratory/clinical pathway. The verified i-STAT whole-blood label covers **age >=18, GCS 13--15, venous EDTA whole blood within 24 h**; plasma assays can have a different 12 h window. Do not exchange platform, matrix, units, cutoffs or sample windows.
- **No automatic CT avoidance or discharge:** a negative result cannot cancel urgent CT, clinical deterioration, focal findings, fracture signs, an unreliable examination or the accepted Horta/anticoagulation pathway. A positive, invalid or out-of-window result returns to clinical imaging assessment; it is not a universal CT order solely because 12 h have elapsed. Discharge still requires reassessment, safe supervision and written precautions. No local biomarker platform or CT-avoidance service is certified here.
- **Performance boundary:** the 2026 whole-blood study reported sensitivity and observed NPV of **96.5%**, not a universal NPV >99%. Predictive values depend on prevalence and setting. S100B belongs only to a specifically adopted low-risk/time-limited pathway, not a replacement for NICE/Horta criteria; NfL/tau/NSE do not acquire routine acute CT-rule status from this update.
- Treat traumatic extra-axial hematoma with ventricular/cisternal compression, midline displacement, neurologic decline or herniation signs as an immediate neurosurgical emergency. Hyperosmolar therapy is a bridge to definitive evacuation, not a substitute for it.
- **Hospital da Horta local pathway (TCE protocol supplied 02/10/2026):** begin with ABCDE stabilization, trauma history/comorbidity review and complete examination. Avoid hypoxaemia (local card: SpO2 <94% or PaO2 <60 mmHg), avoid arterial hypotension (local card: SBP <90 mmHg), intubate/sedate/ventilate when GCS <=8 as clinically indicated, and watch for intracranial-hypertension signs. Obtain CBC + coagulation + renal function in moderate/severe TBI and in mild TBI with anticoagulation/coagulopathy or abnormal head CT.
- **Local Horta mild-TBI CT routing:** GCS 15 asymptomatic with no listed risk factor -> discharge pathway with competent adult observation >=24 h and written alarm symptoms. GCS 15 symptomatic without listed risk factors -> head CT; if normal, observe in ED >=6 h and discharge only when asymptomatic/symptoms controlled. GCS 15 with >=1 local intracranial-injury risk factor, or GCS 13--14 -> head CT. Local risk factors shown on the card include epilepsy history, previous neurosurgery, age >65 years (context-dependent), coagulopathy/hypocoagulation, antiplatelet therapy, alcohol/drug use, impaired ability to assess clinically, high-energy mechanism, signs of skull fracture and new focal deficit.
- **Local Horta anticoagulation exception:** for an anticoagulated patient with GCS 15 and a normal initial head CT, the card specifies ED surveillance for >=12 h rather than automatic ward admission.
- **Local Horta moderate/severe pathway:** GCS 9--12 -> head CT and contact the receiving neurosurgical service (HDES is named on the historical card; confirm the current regional destination). GCS <=8 -> head CT and neurosurgical contact; add cervical-spine CT in an unconscious patient or when cervical injury is suspected. Disposition is based on neuroimaging/clinical course and local neurosurgical/ICU/transfer capability.
- **Repeat head CT locally without delay** for symptomatic deterioration, a fall of >=2 GCS points, intracranial-hypertension signs or a new focal neurological deficit. Any concerning deterioration warrants immediate reassessment; do not wait for a two-point fall before escalating.
- **Evidence boundary, owner-accepted reconciliation 13/11/2026:** the historical Horta card remains undated and is more CT-intensive than NICE NG232. The local 6 h/12 h observations are retained as conservative service choices, not universal international minima. ACEP 2023 does not require routine repeat CT or admission/observation solely for anticoagulation when the initial CT and baseline neurologic examination are normal and no other admission criterion exists. Provide written delayed-bleeding precautions and reliable supervision. The supplied adult TBI compendium is supporting material, not a newly authenticated institutional protocol.
- **Blood-pressure boundary:** the local card says avoid SBP <90 mmHg. For severe TBI, Brain Trauma Foundation supports higher age-stratified lower safety bounds: SBP >=100 mmHg for ages 50--69 and >=110 mmHg for ages 15--49 or >70. ACS 2024 provides a practical adult moderate/severe-TBI resuscitation goal of SBP >=110 mmHg (MAP >80 mmHg when ICP is unmonitored), individualized to perfusion and associated injuries. The older 90 mmHg red line is not the treatment goal. These lower safety bounds are not automatic upper BP targets. Aim SpO2 >=94%, PaO2 about 80--100 mmHg and PaCO2 35--45 mmHg unless temporary rescue ventilation is specifically required.
- Activate neurosurgery/trauma and operating-room transfer now for mass effect/herniation. Elevate the head about 30 degrees, keep the neck neutral, avoid hypoxemia and fever, correct glucose extremes, provide monitored analgesia/sedation, obtain serial GCS and pupil examinations, and reverse anticoagulation when indicated. Do not give corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury.
- Do not apply the blood-pressure target for spontaneous intraparenchymal hemorrhage, aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage or ischemic stroke to TBI. Hypertension may be a compensatory response to raised intracranial pressure. First treat pain, agitation, hypoxemia and intracranial hypertension while preventing hypotension.
- If ICP is monitored, individualize cerebral perfusion pressure, commonly within 60--70 mmHg. Treat ICP >22 mmHg when appropriate in severe TBI because values above this threshold are associated with increased mortality.
- **Conditional antihypertensive example, not routine TBI treatment:** if a neurocritical-care specialist judges controlled lowering necessary, use explicit cerebral-perfusion/BP safety limits. For the verified CIMA nicardipine 1 mg/mL label (60975, April 2026), a calculated example is 20 mg made up to a final 200 mL with glucose 5% (20 mL drug + 180 mL diluent = 0.1 mg/mL), in compatible glass/polyethylene. Its normal-adult start is 3--5 mg/h = 30--50 mL/h for 15 min (5 mg/h = 50 mL/h); increase by 0.5--1 mg/h = 5--10 mL/h every 15 min, maximum 15 mg/h = 150 mL/h. Older/organ-impaired patients require the label's lower/slower schedule. Monitor BP/HR at least every 5 min, reduce/stop for hypotension or neurologic decline. This foreign product reference does not establish Portuguese authorization, hospital stock or a locally ready-to-use preparation; verify the dispensed RCM and use immediately after preparation unless Pharmacy validates otherwise.
- For adult clinical herniation or acute ICP crisis, ENLS 6.0 lists 3% sodium chloride 5 mL/kg IV over 5--20 minutes. Show the weight calculation and order it as a bolus volume plus administration time, not as a continuous infusion. It lists 23.4% sodium chloride 30 mL over 10--20 minutes as a concentrated specialist/refractory option; verify the local neurocritical-care protocol because concentrations and repeat-dose rules vary.
- Monitor sodium, chloride, renal function, fluid status and acid-base status; repeat neurologic and pupil examinations immediately after treatment. Avoid severe hypernatremia and hyperchloremia; set repeat-dose/stop thresholds according to local neurocritical-care protocol.
- Mannitol is an effective alternative when hypertonic sodium cannot be used, but hypovolemia, hypotension and renal dysfunction may make it hazardous. Brief controlled hyperventilation is a rescue bridge only for active herniation while definitive treatment is being mobilized, not prophylactic therapy.
- **NICE adult CT comparison (age >=16):** scan within 1 h for initial GCS <=12, GCS <15 at 2 h, suspected open/depressed or basal skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal deficit or more than one vomiting episode. With loss of consciousness/amnesia, age >=65, coagulopathy, dangerous mechanism or retrograde amnesia >30 min triggers CT within 8 h (within 1 h if presenting >8 h after injury). Consider the same 8 h/late-1 h window for anticoagulants or antiplatelets other than aspirin monotherapy even without another criterion. The aspirin exception never negates other CT indications or the accepted local pathway.
- **Surgical triage (BTF):** acute SDH thickness >10 mm or midline shift >5 mm requires urgent evacuation regardless of GCS; smaller SDH with coma plus deterioration/pupillary abnormality also needs immediate neurosurgical decision. EDH volume >30 cm3 requires evacuation. Nonoperative EDH care requires all of: volume <30 cm3, thickness <15 mm, shift <5 mm, GCS >8 and no focal deficit, with serial CT and close observation in a neurosurgical center. Failure of an observation criterion requires urgent specialist reassessment, not an invented standalone surgical threshold. Do not delay contact/transfer while waiting for numeric criteria in a deteriorating patient.
- Consider short antiseizure prophylaxis for selected high-risk moderate/severe TBI with the receiving team; when used, generally limit it to <=7 days unless an actual seizure or another indication requires treatment. Do not extend prophylaxis to prevent late post-traumatic epilepsy or apply it routinely to every mild TBI. Treat an active seizure through the seizure/status pathway.
- **Portuguese consensus comparison (Ferreira et al., 20 July 2026; DOI10.20344/amp.24437):** proposes CCHR plus GFAP/UCH-L1 for selected GCS14--15 patients within12h and different antithrombotic follow-up. This is a national professional consensus, not an authenticated Horta protocol or a DGS biomarker mandate. Its selected intermediate-risk negative-test pathway must not be generalized to every negative assay; preserve current Horta/NICE routing until the exact assay and a coherent clinical/laboratory pathway are adopted. Only the primary abstract/recommendation summary was accessible, not a full algorithm audit.

title: Acute Spinal Cord Compression
sharedPreamble:
# Neurologic modules

Shared gate: establish last-known-well/onset, glucose, temperature, oxygenation,
anticoagulants, seizure activity, trauma and baseline function. Perform serial
focused neurologic examinations; protect the airway when needed without obscuring
time-critical diagnosis.
sectionBody:
- Treat new weakness, sensory level, gait loss, sphincter dysfunction, saddle symptoms or severe/progressive spinal pain as possible cord/conus/cauda compression. Stabilize ABCs, use spinal-motion restriction when trauma or instability is plausible, document a serial motor/sensory examination including sacral function when relevant, and assess bladder function. Do not delay escalation for a complete examination in a rapidly deteriorating patient.
- Distinguish the likely mechanism because immediate treatment differs: trauma/instability, malignant spinal cord compression, epidural abscess, epidural hematoma, acute disc/degenerative compression or vascular disease. Obtain urgent MRI of the relevant spine; image the whole spine when malignant compression or multifocal disease is plausible. For suspected malignant spinal cord compression, obtain MRI as soon as possible and within 24 hours; progressive deficits, sepsis or suspected hematoma require immediate specialist discussion and must not be held to a routine clock target.
- With neurologic signs or symptoms of malignant spinal cord compression, give dexamethasone 16 mg PO or equivalent parenteral dose as soon as possible, then continue 16 mg/day while awaiting surgery or radiotherapy and taper under specialist direction. Monitor glucose, GI and infection risk. In suspected lymphoma/myeloma without neurologic deficits, discuss steroids with hematology first because they may obscure tissue diagnosis.
- Do not give dexamethasone automatically for traumatic spinal cord injury, disc-related cauda equina syndrome, epidural abscess or epidural hematoma. Do not use high-dose methylprednisolone routinely in acute traumatic spinal cord injury.
- In suspected spinal epidural abscess, obtain blood cultures and urgent MRI; start empiric IV antibiotics immediately when sepsis, hemodynamic instability or neurologic compromise is present and activate spine surgery/source control. A stable patient may have cultures obtained first, but microbiologic sampling must not delay treatment when deterioration is plausible.
- In suspected spinal epidural hematoma, stop and reverse anticoagulation using the agent-specific pathway and obtain immediate spine/neurosurgical assessment for decompression. Do not perform lumbar puncture before excluding a compressive lesion.
- In acute traumatic spinal cord injury, avoid hypotension and hypoxemia. Current guideline suggestions use a MAP lower limit of 75--80 mm Hg while avoiding active augmentation beyond an upper limit of 90--95 mm Hg for 3--7 days; evidence certainty is very low, so individualize with the spinal/critical-care team and evaluate hemorrhagic, obstructive and distributive shock before diagnosing neurogenic shock. Select vasoactive therapy by physiology and local protocol.
- Definitive care is cause-specific decompression/stabilization, oncologic surgery/radiotherapy, drainage or hematoma evacuation. Arrange ICU and transfer to a spinal/neurosurgical center when local definitive capability is unavailable; reassess neurologic level, respiratory mechanics, perfusion and bladder function during transfer.

title: Cauda Equina Conus Emergency
sharedPreamble:
# Neurologic modules

Shared gate: establish last-known-well/onset, glucose, temperature, oxygenation,
anticoagulants, seizure activity, trauma and baseline function. Perform serial
focused neurologic examinations; protect the airway when needed without obscuring
time-critical diagnosis.
sectionBody:
- Suspect cauda equina or conus compression with new urinary difficulty or retention, altered urinary sensation, saddle/perineal sensory change, fecal dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, bilateral sciatica, bilateral weakness or a severe/progressive neurologic deficit. Absence of a single classic feature does not exclude it.
- Document lower-limb power/reflexes/sensation, perineal sensation and sacral function as clinically appropriate. Measure and record pre-void and post-void residual (PVR) when this does not delay MRI; catheterize retention and record the drained volume. A PVR above 200 mL increases suspicion, but a lower or normal PVR does not exclude cauda equina syndrome in a compatible presentation.
- Request emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine as soon as possible. The 2026 UK national pathway target is certainly within 4 hours of the radiology request; use the faster local emergency standard when available. Clinical examination, rectal tone and bladder scan cannot safely rule out compression or replace MRI.
- Contact the spinal surgical service urgently when the syndrome is suspected and immediately when MRI confirms compression. Decompress as soon as clinically and operationally feasible according to symptoms and imaging. Do not use a nominal 48-hour window as permission to wait or delay referral.
- Consider massive disc prolapse/stenosis, tumor, epidural abscess, epidural hematoma, conus lesion and vascular causes. Reverse anticoagulation urgently for a compressive hematoma; obtain cultures and start sepsis-directed antibiotics without delay for abscess with systemic illness or neurologic compromise.
- Provide analgesia without obscuring serial neurologic assessment. Do not give dexamethasone routinely for disc-related cauda equina syndrome; if malignant compression is suspected, follow `acute-spinal-cord-compression`. Do not perform lumbar puncture before excluding compression.

title: Upper Gi Bleeding
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Primary survey: assess airway protection, shock/ongoing blood loss, cirrhosis/portal hypertension, comorbidity, pregnancy and antithrombotics. Large-bore access, blood group/crossmatch, serial perfusion/lab reassessment and major-hemorrhage support as indicated; do not use a single early hemoglobin to rule out major acute loss. Avoid both delayed blood/source control and indiscriminate crystalloid loading.
- Distinguish suspected nonvariceal from variceal bleeding early; hematochezia with shock can still be a brisk upper source. Use Glasgow–Blatchford (GBS) with clinical judgment; GBS ≤1 can support outpatient care only if stable, no other admission indication and follow-up is reliable. A score never overrides shock, ongoing bleeding or comorbidity.
- Transfusion: in stable adults without cardiovascular disease, a restrictive RBC threshold around Hb 7 g/dL is usual; individualize for ongoing exsanguination, ischemia/cardiovascular disease and the whole clinical picture. ESGE 2026 suggests Hb ≤8 g/dL and post-transfusion ≥10 g/dL for acute UGIB with acute/chronic cardiovascular disease; evidence is low and the target is not a rigid mandate. For major bleeding, hold anticoagulant; reversal is selective for life-threatening or severe ongoing bleeding with plausible residual drug effect. ESGE 2026 considers agent-specific DOAC reversal/PCC in severe ongoing UGIB, while ACG-CAG suggests against routine use (very-low-certainty evidence); use senior GI/hematology/pharmacy input and do not delay endoscopy. For aspirin, distinguish primary from secondary prevention; preserve/restart secondary-prevention aspirin promptly after hemostasis. With DAPT/recent stent, continue aspirin if possible and coordinate P2Y12 interruption/restart with cardiology. Restart anticoagulation after durable control according to thrombotic and rebleeding risks; timing is individualized. See `anticoagulation-reversal`.
- Airway/endoscopy preparation: do not intubate prophylactically in every case. Consider airway protection selectively for active hematemesis, agitation or encephalopathy with inability to protect the airway. Do not routinely place/aspirate a nasogastric tube. In clinically severe or ongoing active bleeding with likely retained blood/clot, give erythromycin 250 mg IV once 30–120 minutes before endoscopy if no contraindication; it improves visualization, not proven survival. If IV erythromycin is unavailable, ESGE 2026 conditionally suggests IV metoclopramide in selected patients (low-quality evidence); assess QT/arrhythmia, interactions and extrapyramidal/serotonergic risks, and do not delay endoscopy. No routine capsule/blood-sensing capsule for acute risk stratification.
- Nonvariceal suspected peptic ulcer: pre-endoscopy IV PPI may be used per local protocol but must not delay endoscopy or resuscitation. Endoscopy within 24 h after presentation and adequate resuscitation; ESGE 2026 does not require routine ultra-urgent ≤6 h or urgent ≤12 h endoscopy in adequately resuscitated stable patients. Continued instability or uncontrolled hemorrhage requires immediate senior GI/anesthesia/IR/surgical coordination.
- At endoscopy, treat peptic-ulcer Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa stigmata. Use an accepted mechanical or thermal modality; dilute epinephrine injection must not be the sole hemostasis method. For IIb adherent clot, ESGE2026 suggests clot removal and endoscopic treatment when the endoscopist can safely manage conversion to active/high-risk bleeding; individualize when that expertise is unavailable; IIc/III generally need no endoscopic hemostasis. For high-risk ulcers after hemostasis (and selected untreated adherent clot), high-dose PPI for 72 h: 80 mg IV loading then 8 mg/h, or a guideline-supported high-dose intermittent IV/oral regimen. If pharmacy verifies the selected PPI's compatibility/stability at 80 mg/100 mL (0.8 mg/mL), 8 mg/h = 10 mL/h; 80 mg/200 mL gives 20 mL/h. Verify loading administration time, diluent and bag replacement interval; never assume a 72-hour bag stability.
- Recurrent peptic-ulcer bleeding: repeat endoscopy and retreat; a cap-mounted/over-the-scope clip is a rescue option. If repeat endoscopic hemostasis fails, transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE); surgery if TAE is unavailable or unsuccessful. Prophylactic TAE is selective for very high rebleeding risk, not routine. Test/treat H. pylori, retest initially negative tests when appropriate (PPI can cause false negatives), and address NSAIDs, antithrombotics, iron deficiency/anemia and follow-up.
- Suspected variceal bleed/cirrhosis: start vasoactive therapy (terlipressin, octreotide or somatostatin) at presentation and continue up to 5 days per specialist/local regimen; give antibiotic prophylaxis promptly (ESGE: ceftriaxone 1 g/day up to 7 days in ACLD, modified for allergy/local resistance). Endoscopy within 12 h after hemodynamic resuscitation; erythromycin 250 mg IV 30–120 min beforehand if safe. Esophageal varices: endoscopic band ligation (EBL). Gastric varices require an experienced team and lesion-specific glue/obliteration or other specialist technique. Identify high-risk candidates for pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h (preferably 24 h; Child–Pugh C ≤13, or Child–Pugh B >7 with active bleeding despite vasoactive therapy, or HVPG >20 mmHg); persistent/recurrent uncontrolled bleed needs urgent rescue TIPS/advanced-center escalation. After control, plan secondary prophylaxis (nonselective beta-blocker plus serial EBL for esophageal varices when appropriate) with hepatology.
- ESGE 2026 peptic-ulcer timing and endoscopic recommendations concern nonvariceal peptic-ulcer hemorrhage; they do not replace the separate variceal timing/source-control pathway. Anticoagulant reversal/restart is agent- and indication-specific; use `anticoagulation-reversal` and specialist input. For lower-source evaluation and suspected small-bowel bleeding after nondiagnostic upper/lower endoscopy use the diagnostic extension in `lower-gi-bleeding`; escalate to gastroenterology/IR as indicated.
- **Baveno VIII2026 focused update:** variceal therapy is distinct from nonvariceal ulcer care. Start vasoactive treatment promptly for suspected variceal bleeding, generally2--5days or until indicated TIPS; selected shorter treatment after durable haemostasis requires specialist selection. Monitor sodium with terlipressin. For refractory oesophageal bleeding, a dedicated covered self-expanding metal stent is preferred over balloon tamponade as a bridge where expertise exists; salvage TIPS needs urgent specialist coordination. GOV2/IGV1 gastric bleeding needs its own endoscopic/EUS and definitive vascular plan, not esophageal banding by default.
- **Restart/reversal reconciliation:** there is no universal restart day. Document the anticoagulant/last dose/renal function, bleed control and thrombotic indication, coordinate GI/hematology/cardiology and select through the accepted reversal pathway. ACG-CAG discourages routine DOAC reversal/PCC; selective rescue in life-threatening bleeding remains a separate decision. For secondary-prevention aspirin, if interrupted, ACG-CAG supports resumption when endoscopic haemostasis is confirmed. Do not infer local availability of endoscopy, TAE or TIPS from GREEN evidence status.

title: Lower Gi Bleeding
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Assess shock and ongoing hematochezia immediately; establish IV access, crossmatch, serial hemoglobin/coagulation and antithrombotic history. Resuscitate and mobilize gastroenterology, interventional radiology and surgery in parallel. Brisk upper-GI hemorrhage can present as hematochezia, especially with instability; consider the upper-GI pathway.
- In stable adults without cardiovascular disease, use a restrictive transfusion threshold around 7 g/dL. Individualize for cardiovascular ischemia or major ongoing hemorrhage; an initially normal hemoglobin does not exclude acute blood loss and must not delay hemorrhage support.
- For ongoing hemodynamically significant bleeding, prioritize CTA to localize the source. Active extravasation warrants prompt interventional-radiology assessment for angiography/embolization. A negative CTA does not exclude intermittent bleeding; reassess ongoing instability, including an upper source.
- Once stabilized, most hospitalized patients can undergo nonurgent colonoscopy after appropriate preparation; routine colonoscopy within 24 hours has not improved major outcomes. Uncontrolled bleeding needs escalation, not waiting for elective preparation. Surgery is a rescue option after multidisciplinary localization/control assessment.
- Do not use tranexamic acid routinely. PPI/octreotide are not treatments for a proven lower source; use them only for a supported upper/variceal indication. Withhold anticoagulation for major bleeding; reserve agent-specific reversal for life-threatening/ongoing bleeding with likely residual effect after individualized risk review and urgent specialist input. ACG-CAG advises against routine DOAC antidote/PCC, whereas ESGE lower-GI guidance considers reversal for ongoing bleeding or recurrent instability with hematology coordination (low/very-low certainty). Continue secondary-prevention aspirin if possible; if held, restart promptly after hemostasis (ESGE: preferably within 5 days or earlier). With DAPT/recent stent, continue aspirin if possible and agree P2Y12 interruption/restart with cardiology. Restart long-term anticoagulation after control with a drug-specific specialist plan. ESGE 2021 discusses restarting VKA from day 7 in lower-thrombotic-risk patients and earlier resumption with heparin bridging, preferably within 72 h, in selected high-risk VKA patients (very-low certainty). This is not a routine bridge or 72-hour restart instruction for DOACs: their onset is rapid, and ESGE suggests resumption from day 7 with low certainty, individualized to hemostasis and thrombosis risk. See `anticoagulation-reversal`.
- If high-quality upper endoscopy and colonoscopy do not identify the source, assess whether either exam was incomplete or outdated; repeat/second-look endoscopy only when clinically indicated, not routinely. With overt suspected small-bowel bleeding after adequate negative bidirectional endoscopy, capsule endoscopy is the preferred first-line small-bowel test when the patient is stable and there is no known/suspected obstruction or stenosis. Arrange urgently with gastroenterology; ESGE recommends as soon as possible, ideally within 48 h of the overt episode to maximize yield. Do not use capsule instead of resuscitation or acute localization/source control.
- If brisk ongoing bleeding with hemodynamic instability, activate GI/IR and use the acute hemorrhage pathway: catheter angiography/embolization may be required emergently; in a stable patient with active significant bleeding, CTA can localize and guide intervention. Capsule is not the acute test for an unstable patient. If bleeding is intermittent/slower and patient remains stable, capsule timing is coordinated with GI.
- Before capsule, assess retention risk (obstructive symptoms, known Crohn disease/stenosis, prior small-bowel surgery or radiation); choose cross-sectional enterography and/or patency capsule first when appropriate. If capsule is contraindicated or urgent tissue/therapy is needed, specialist-directed device-assisted enteroscopy or imaging is an alternative. A positive capsule should direct device-assisted enteroscopy for confirmation and possible endoscopic treatment.
- After a high-quality negative capsule, conservative follow-up is appropriate if bleeding has stopped and clinical suspicion is low; treat iron deficiency and monitor. Recurrent overt bleeding, persistent iron-deficiency anemia or strong suspicion warrants GI reassessment and further targeted testing (repeat capsule, enterography, enteroscopy or other modality according to presentation); a negative capsule does not exclude a mural mass or all lesions.
- Discharge only after bleeding has settled, stable reassessment and reliable follow-up; a low-risk score supports rather than replaces clinical judgment. Give explicit return instructions for recurrent bleeding, syncope, dyspnea or pain.

title: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Suspect ischemia with severe pain disproportionate to examination, atrial fibrillation, vascular disease or unexplained deterioration during shock. A normal early lactate or soft abdomen does not exclude it.
- Obtain urgent arterial/venous-phase CTA without oral contrast. Do not delay solely for renal dysfunction when suspicion is high. Activate general surgery, vascular surgery and interventional radiology immediately on strong suspicion, in parallel with CTA rather than waiting for its result; peritonitis requires urgent operative assessment.
- Keep nil by mouth, give titrated analgesia, restore perfusion with titrated fluids and frequent reassessment to avoid overload/abdominal compartment syndrome, correct electrolytes and start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly. Route exact antibiotic doses through `empiric-antibiotics` and current local renal/allergy guidance.
- Distinguish arterial embolism/thrombosis needing urgent revascularization, acute mesenteric venous thrombosis (MVT), and nonocclusive ischemia (NOMI). For acute arterial AMI, start therapeutic IV UFH promptly unless contraindicated, coordinating it with the vascular/surgical team; WSES supports full-dose anticoagulation before the procedure. Peritonitis alone is not a reason to automatically omit a bolus or defer anticoagulation. Active bleeding, HIT or other major contraindications require an immediate individualized decision. Never let anticoagulation or its monitoring delay reperfusion or laparotomy. Do not copy an ACS, PE or thrombolysis regimen automatically.
- Acute MVT: unless a major contraindication exists, start systemic therapeutic anticoagulation promptly. ESVS 2025 recommends UFH or LMWH first line (Class I, level C); WSES 2022 supports continuous UFH infusion (strong, moderate-quality evidence). Without peritonitis, anticoagulation plus supportive care is first-line. With peritonitis, perforation, deterioration or suspected necrosis, urgent operative assessment/source control; anticoagulation does not replace it. If imminent operation, active bleeding concern or severe renal failure makes rapid offset/reversal useful, UFH may be preferred because it is manageable and reversible with protamine; make this decision with the treating team. Worsening despite anticoagulation may prompt specialist consideration of endovascular therapy, not routine thrombolysis.
- MVT aftercare: ESVS recommends 3–6 months of VKA or LMWH (Class I, level B); a DOAC may be considered as an alternative (Class IIb, level C). Consider indefinite therapy for idiopathic MVT or persistent thrombosis risk factors after balancing bleeding risk. These duration recommendations apply to acute MVT, not automatically to arterial AMI or NOMI. Investigate relevant underlying causes/risk factors with the specialist team.
- Neither ESVS 2025 nor WSES 2022 provides a universal UFH loading dose, infusion rate or monitoring nomogram for this emergency pathway. Use the institution's therapeutic weight-based protocol, actual patient weight, baseline bleeding/coagulation context, renal function, platelet/HIT history, planned intervention and local aPTT/anti-Xa monitoring. Obtain baseline CBC/platelets, aPTT/INR, renal function and electrolytes. When the selected UFH nomogram uses aPTT, a common hospital reference is to recheck 4--6 hours after starting or changing the infusion, but the therapeutic target and stable-monitoring schedule must come from that laboratory/nomogram; do not adopt a universal rule of two stable tests. If baseline aPTT is unsuitable, obtain hematology advice on anti-Xa monitoring. Monitor bleeding and platelet/HIT risk. State the preparation, concentration, arithmetic, mL/h and monitoring when enough patient/formulary data exist; otherwise do not invent a pump rate. For NOMI, prioritize correction of low flow and cause, optimizing cardiac output and reducing vasoconstrictors when clinically feasible. In the absence of bleeding, systemic anticoagulation may be considered individually; neither prophylactic nor therapeutic IV UFH is a universal default for every NOMI presentation. Specialist intra-arterial vasodilator with protective heparinization is a separate conditional intervention, not the routine MVT regimen.
- Necrotic bowel requires surgery; consider staged reassessment. Anticoagulation or apparent pain improvement cannot replace reperfusion/source control. Monitor perfusion, abdomen, lactate trend and organ failure in critical care.
- ESVS 2025 recommendation 37 (IIa B): consider endovascular revascularization first for embolic/thrombotic superior mesenteric artery occlusion, according to anatomy and immediate expertise; this must not defer bowel assessment when peritonitis or necrosis is suspected. Recommendation 40 (IIa C) supports considering staged resection without primary reconstruction and second-look laparotomy when resection accompanies revascularization. Recommendation 41 (I C) supports antibiotics but does not specify a superior regimen; use local guidance. In nonocclusive disease, specialist intra-arterial vasodilators under protective heparinization may be considered (recommendation 45, IIb C); this is not a routine systemic vasodilator order.

title: Acute Abdomen
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Adult initial framework: exclude hemorrhage, perforation, ischemia, obstruction/strangulation, ectopic pregnancy, torsion, sepsis and aortic disease. Shock, syncope, peritonism/rigidity, sudden severe or disproportionate pain, gastrointestinal bleeding with compromise, persistent vomiting/distension or evolving organ dysfunction require urgent reassessment and escalation. Older, immunocompromised or anticoagulated patients may have subtle findings. Children use `pediatric-abdominal-surgical-emergencies`; pregnancy requires the obstetric pathway.
- Assess ABCDE, monitor physiology, obtain IV access and provide titrated analgesia and antiemetic treatment while resuscitating according to perfusion and hemorrhage risk. Keep nil by mouth when obstruction, intervention or surgery is suspected. Activate general/vascular surgery, gynecology or urology early according to the suspected cause, in parallel with investigation; do not wait for all tests before calling for shock or peritonitis. Use `sepsis-shock` and `empiric-antibiotics` for suspected abdominal sepsis and source control, and the hemorrhage pathway for active bleeding.
- Obtain pregnancy testing when pregnancy is possible, and targeted blood count, renal/electrolyte, liver, lipase, urine, blood gas/lactate and other tests according to the differential. Normal early labs or limited ultrasound do not exclude dangerous pathology; specifically, normal lactate does not exclude early mesenteric ischemia. Review prior surgery, anticoagulants, comorbidity, medication and extra-abdominal cardiac/metabolic causes.
- Select imaging by stability, pain site, pregnancy status and diagnostic question with radiology. ACR rates CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast usually appropriate for adult nonlocalized pain with fever and no recent surgery; this is not a universal CT prescription. Suspected biliary right-upper-quadrant disease usually starts with ultrasound. Suspected gynecologic pelvic disease generally starts with transabdominal/transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler and pregnancy context. Use selected MRI, often without contrast in pregnancy, when appropriate; a necessary emergency CT is not automatically prohibited by pregnancy.
- Strong mesenteric/vascular suspicion needs the dedicated `acute-mesenteric-ischemia` or `abdominal-aortic-aneurysm` pathway and appropriately timed CT angiography, not a routine low-risk abdominal study. In instability, bedside ultrasound can assist while definitive teams are activated; negative POCUS does not exclude rupture or ischemia. Move to CT only when transport/physiology permits and it will not delay necessary source control.
- Obstruction with suspected strangulation, ischemia or peritonitis requires urgent surgical assessment, not routine conservative waiting. Appendicitis risk assessment, imaging and selection for surgery versus antibiotics follow the WSES 2025 edition with the surgical team; selected uncomplicated appendicitis recommendations must not be generalized to all abdominal emergencies. Route pancreatitis and other established diagnoses to their specific modules.
- Repeat the examination, vital signs and response after analgesia/resuscitation; use observation and reassessment when diagnosis remains uncertain. Persistent severe pain, deteriorating physiology, inability to tolerate intake or unresolved surgical suspicion warrants admission, urgent specialty assessment or transfer rather than reassurance from one normal test.
- Discharge only after stable reassessment, adequate symptom control, an acceptable working diagnosis, appropriate oral intake and no unresolved emergency features. Arrange reliable follow-up and written return instructions for worsening/persistent pain, fever, repeated vomiting, bleeding, syncope or new symptoms. Document diagnostic uncertainty, investigations and the reassessment/return plan; improvement after analgesia alone does not establish benign disease.

title: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Suspect symptomatic or ruptured AAA with sudden abdominal, flank or back pain, syncope, hypotension, unexplained shock or limb ischemia, especially in an older patient or known aneurysm. Absence of a palpable mass does not exclude it.
- Activate vascular surgery, anesthesia, theatre/endovascular pathway and massive hemorrhage support immediately. Place two large-bore IV/IO lines, send crossmatch/coagulation/fibrinogen/renal function, warm the patient and blood products, and reverse anticoagulation when indicated.
- Use bedside aortic ultrasound to confirm an aneurysm when immediately available, but do not use POCUS to exclude rupture. Obtain CT angiography for operative planning only when physiology permits and it will not delay hemorrhage control; an unstable patient with a convincing diagnosis needs direct definitive-pathway discussion.
- Use restricted crystalloid and balanced blood-component resuscitation. Follow permissive hypotension while the patient remains conscious and perfusing rather than normalizing BP; set a patient-specific lower bound for coronary/cerebral perfusion and abandon permissive hypotension for traumatic brain injury or other competing indications.
- Provide titrated analgesia without obscuring deterioration. Do not delay repair for central access, invasive monitoring or nonessential tests. Definitive treatment is urgent EVAR or open repair according to anatomy, resources and vascular expertise.
- Reassess mental status, radial pulse/BP, abdominal/back pain, lactate, temperature, calcium, coagulation and distal limb perfusion continuously. Document ceiling-of-care decisions without allowing age alone to deny emergency vascular assessment.

title: Urologic Emergencies
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Threats: infected obstruction, torsion, retention with complications, Fournier gangrene, priapism and major hematuria with clot retention.
- Obtain urinalysis/culture, renal function, pregnancy test and targeted ultrasound/CT. Analgesia must not delay torsion or source-control pathways.
- Infected obstruction requires antibiotics, resuscitation and urgent drainage consultation; discharge only uncomplicated stable disease with follow-up and return precautions.

title: Endocrine Metabolic
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Adult recognition/routing framework: consider DKA/HHS, adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, myxedema coma, severe hypoglycemia and pituitary emergencies. Assess airway, ventilation, perfusion, mental state, temperature and bedside glucose immediately. Look for infection, interrupted replacement therapy, medication effects, pregnancy and other precipitants; children require pediatric protocols.
- Obtain targeted ketones, blood gas, electrolytes, renal function and osmolality, with cortisol/ACTH or thyroid tests when indicated. Draw samples promptly if feasible, but do not delay treatment of suspected adrenal crisis or severe hypoglycemia for laboratory confirmation. Modest glucose does not exclude SGLT2-associated/euglycemic DKA; use ketones and acid-base findings.
- Route to `diabetic-ketoacidosis-hhs`, `adrenal-crisis`, `thyroid-storm` or `myxedema-coma` for their actual criteria, treatment sequence and monitoring. Do not interchange DKA, isolated HHS and routine ICU hyperglycemia regimens. Verify potassium, weight, renal function and the exact insulin/electrolyte preparation before calculation; the umbrella does not enable blocked medication contracts. In suspected myxedema coma, preserve glucocorticoid cover before thyroid replacement as specified in its module.
- Hypoglycemia: give oral fast-acting carbohydrate only when the patient is alert enough to swallow safely; impaired consciousness, seizures or unsafe swallowing require the monitored parenteral rescue pathway. Use verified IV glucose, or an appropriate glucagon alternative when IV access is unavailable, with product-specific instructions. Recheck glucose after 10--15 minutes and repeat/escalate until recovered; glucagon may fail with depleted glycogen, liver disease or sulfonylurea-related events. Review recurrence risk, provide ongoing carbohydrate when safe, and arrange supervised diabetes-treatment adjustment rather than automatically omitting all basal insulin in type 1 diabetes. Severe/recurrent or long-acting drug-related events need observation/admission and specialist/toxicology advice.
- Suspect pituitary apoplexy with sudden severe headache plus visual loss, field defect, ophthalmoplegia or altered consciousness; exclude competing neurologic emergencies in parallel. Assess visual function, stabilize, obtain urgent pituitary MRI when feasible (CT if MRI cannot be performed), and discuss immediately with endocrinology/neurosurgery. Hemodynamic instability, altered consciousness or major visual compromise warrants urgent glucocorticoid cover; sampling/imaging must not delay it. Surgery is a specialist decision, not automatic for every suspected apoplexy.
- Reassess circulation, glucose, neurological status, urine output and electrolyte trends after treatment. Admit/escalate shock, respiratory failure, impaired consciousness, major electrolyte disturbance or suspected endocrine crisis; apparent correction of one value is not discharge clearance. Document the precipitant, ongoing replacement/insulin plan, handover and follow-up.

title: Adrenal Crisis
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Suspect adrenal crisis with unexplained shock, vomiting, weakness, hypoglycemia or hyponatremia, especially after steroid interruption or with known adrenal/pituitary disease. Hyperkalemia may be absent in secondary adrenal insufficiency. Draw cortisol/ACTH if immediately feasible; do not delay treatment for sampling or results.
- Adult treatment: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately (IM if IV access is delayed), then 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg IV/IM every 6 hours. If pharmacy confirms the product/diluent and stability, 200 mg to a final 100 mL = 2 mg/mL, delivering 8.33 mg/h at 4.17 mL/h; 200 mg/200 mL = 1 mg/mL at 8.33 mL/h. Confirm bag replacement interval; never assume 24-hour stability from this arithmetic.
- Restore circulation with isotonic saline; an adult without fluid-overload risk commonly receives 1 L in the first hour, then reassessment. Use smaller reassessed aliquots in cardiac/renal disease. Treat hypoglycemia promptly, monitor sodium correction, glucose, potassium, urine output and perfusion, and treat the precipitant.
- The intermittent hydrocortisone regimen is an alternative when a pump is unavailable. If hydrocortisone itself is unavailable, urgently obtain an endocrinology/pharmacy-verified parenteral glucocorticoid alternative; do not substitute milligram-for-milligram or assume equal mineralocorticoid effect. Admit, taper after recovery with endocrinology and provide sick-day education.

title: Thyroid Storm
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Suspect clinical thyrotoxic decompensation with fever, marked tachycardia/arrhythmia, CNS disturbance, heart failure or GI/hepatic dysfunction. Scores support diagnosis but should not delay ICU/endocrine treatment. Obtain thyroid tests, glucose, electrolytes, liver tests, ECG, cultures and cardiac assessment while treating the precipitant.
- Control hormone synthesis when due to hyperfunction: ATA adult reference regimens are propylthiouracil 500--1,000 mg enteral loading then 250 mg every 4 hours, OR methimazole/thiamazole 60--80 mg/day in divided enteral doses. Select around hepatic injury, pregnancy, contraindications and actual availability; do not combine automatically. Thyroiditis/exogenous hormone requires a different strategy.
- Both ATA 2016 and the 2026 joint thyroid-storm consensus specify iodine at least 1 hour after the thionamide. Verify iodine concentration and formulation before converting to drops; products are not interchangeable. Other guideline sequences require explicit specialist reconciliation.
- Give stress-dose glucocorticoid using one verified storm protocol. The 2026 ETA/BTA/Society for Endocrinology/Welsh Endocrine and Diabetes Society consensus proposes hydrocortisone 100 mg IV once, then 50 mg IV every 6 hours (or 200 mg over 24 hours by syringe driver in HDU/ICU). ATA 2016 lists a different regimen (300 mg IV loading, then 100 mg every 8 hours); do not combine or silently interchange regimens—follow the current specialist/local protocol. Monitor potassium after glucocorticoids, especially when thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is plausible. Do not confuse storm treatment with adrenal-crisis dosing. Provide external cooling and suitable antipyresis; avoid aspirin/salicylates. Manage fluids and oxygen according to cardiac status.
- Assess shock and ventricular function BEFORE beta-blockade. Decompensated low-output failure can collapse after propranolol or even esmolol. In a well-perfused patient, select/titrate a verified beta-blocker regimen with continuous monitoring. If esmolol is appropriate, use the existing preparation/calculation in `acute-aortic-syndrome`, but do not copy its aortic BP/HR targets. Avoid automatic loading in tenuous circulation; stop for worsening perfusion, bradycardia, block or bronchospasm. Diltiazem is not automatically safe in systolic failure either.
- If significant hepatic dysfunction is present (e.g. transaminases around >3 times the upper limit of normal or rising bilirubin), the 2026 consensus favours considering methimazole/carbimazole over PTU because of PTU hepatotoxicity risk, except where patient-specific factors such as first-trimester pregnancy alter selection. Observational data have not shown a clear mortality advantage for PTU. Once clinically improving, reduce thionamide dosing as directed by endocrinology. If not clinically stabilising within 24–48 hours, reassess precipitant, absorption, cardiac dysfunction and need for rescue. Cholestyramine, lithium, plasma exchange or thyroidectomy are specialist adjunct/rescue options, not automatic steps. If thionamides are unavailable/contraindicated or treatment fails, obtain urgent specialist rescue planning; do not replace them with an unrelated antihypertensive. Verify Portuguese products via the localization workflow.

title: Myxedema Coma
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Recognize severe decompensated hypothyroidism with altered consciousness, hypothermia, hypoventilation, bradycardia, hypotension and/or hyponatremia; coma is not required. TSH may not be elevated with central disease. Obtain TSH/free T4, cortisol, gas, glucose/electrolytes and precipitant assessment without delaying treatment.
- Give empiric stress-dose hydrocortisone BEFORE thyroid hormone while adrenal insufficiency is being excluded; the adrenal-crisis module supplies 100 mg IV followed by 200 mg/24 h or 50 mg every 6 hours. Reconcile ongoing doses with the endocrine team.
- Adult ATA reference: levothyroxine 200--400 micrograms IV ONCE as a loading dose, reduced for older/smaller patients, coronary disease or arrhythmia. Subsequent daily IV replacement is approximately 75% of an oral 1.6 micrograms/kg/day reference, individualized with specialist monitoring. Never repeat the loading dose as daily maintenance or confuse micrograms with milligrams.
- If IV levothyroxine is unavailable, arrange urgent endocrine/pharmacy-directed enteral treatment; absorption with ileus is unreliable and oral and IV doses are not equivalent. Liothyronine is a selected specialist adjunct, not a routine substitute; cardiac risk and local availability matter.
- Admit to ICU, support ventilation early if needed, use cautious fluids and passive warming, correct hypoglycemia and sodium safely, and treat infection/other triggers. Avoid aggressive peripheral warming and unnecessary sedatives. Follow consciousness, ventilation, temperature, ECG/perfusion and free hormone trends.
- The 2026 ETA/BTA/Society for Endocrinology/Welsh Endocrine and Diabetes Society joint consensus supports IV levothyroxine loading at 200–400 micrograms, reducing the dose in older/smaller patients and those with ischaemic heart disease or significant arrhythmia, plus empiric IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 50 mg every 6 hours (or 200 mg/24 hours by syringe driver). This agrees with the module's cautious loading and hydrocortisone schedule. The exact enteral fallback regimen when IV levothyroxine is unavailable still requires source-level and pharmacy/local-protocol confirmation; do not invent an oral/NG loading dose or claim it is dose-equivalent.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis Hhs
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Diagnose adult DKA only when all three domains are present: diabetes/history or glucose at least 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), ketosis with beta-hydroxybutyrate at least 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones at least 2+, and metabolic acidosis with pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L. Actively consider euglycemic DKA with SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy, fasting or partial insulin treatment; do not exclude DKA from glucose alone.
- Diagnose HHS only when all four domains are present: glucose at least 600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L), effective osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg or total calculated osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, beta-hydroxybutyrate below 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones below 2+, and pH at least 7.3 with bicarbonate at least 15 mmol/L. Classify significant ketonaemia/acidosis with hyperosmolality as mixed DKA/HHS.
- Obtain glucose, beta-hydroxybutyrate, venous blood gas, sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, urea/creatinine, magnesium, phosphate, measured osmolality when available, ECG, fluid balance and precipitant evaluation. Calculate anion gap, albumin-corrected gap when albumin is known, effective/total osmolality and corrected sodium. Prefer beta-hydroxybutyrate to urine ketones and use `scripts/acid_base_hyperglycemia.py` for deterministic arithmetic.
- Restore perfusion first. In adults without cardiac or renal compromise, give isotonic saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500--1000 mL/h for the first 2--4 hours, then individualize by hemodynamics, sodium, osmolality and fluid balance. In older adults, pregnancy, heart failure or kidney failure, use smaller aliquots such as 250 mL with frequent reassessment; do not apply a fixed large-volume protocol.
- Check potassium before insulin. If potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L, replace potassium at 10 mmol/h and delay insulin until potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L. One conditional reference preparation is potassium chloride 20 mmol in a compatible final volume of 100 mL = 0.2 mmol/mL, delivered at 50 mL/h = 10 mmol/h; use only when the local protocol permits that concentration for the verified access, with a controlled pump and ECG/electrolyte monitoring. Once potassium falls below 5.0 mmol/L, usually add 20--30 mmol potassium per litre of IV fluid to target 4--5 mmol/L; withhold initial potassium when elevated and monitor closely. Never IV-push potassium.
- For DKA or mixed DKA/HHS, use soluble/regular insulin IV at 0.1 units/kg/h after the potassium safety gate. A practical pump preparation is 100 units in a final volume of 100 mL compatible 0.9% saline = 1 unit/mL: the numeric units/h equals mL/h. Prime tubing according to local protocol. Do not routinely give an insulin bolus when the infusion can start promptly.
- When glucose falls below 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) in DKA, add 5--10% dextrose and reduce insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h, targeting glucose near 200 mg/dL while continuing insulin until ketoacidosis resolves. In euglycemic DKA, begin dextrose with the insulin pathway rather than withholding insulin because glucose is near normal.
- In HHS without significant ketosis/acidosis, prioritize controlled fluid/osmolality correction and use insulin IV at 0.05 units/kg/h; a fluid-only glucose fall may occur before insulin. Do not exceed a glucose decline of 90--120 mg/dL/h, a sodium fall of 10 mmol/L/24 h or an osmolality fall of 3--8 mOsm/kg/h. An initial sodium rise as glucose falls is expected and alone is not an indication for hypotonic saline.
- Check capillary glucose every 1--2 hours. Repeat electrolytes, creatinine, phosphate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous pH every 4 hours; in HHS also repeat osmolality every 4 hours. Recheck potassium 2 hours after insulin starts and at least every 4 hours, more often when unstable or actively replacing.
- Assess bleeding, renal function, weight and venous/arterial thrombosis. Unless thrombosis is suspected or anticoagulation is contraindicated, use prophylactic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin according to the locally available product and renal/weight protocol; do not escalate automatically to therapeutic anticoagulation merely because HHS is prothrombotic.
- Do not give bicarbonate routinely. Consider it only for severe DKA acidosis below pH 7.0 under a current protocol; if used, the 2024 consensus regimen is sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol in 400 mL sterile water every 2 hours until pH exceeds 7.0, with potassium and sodium monitoring. Do not replace phosphate routinely unless phosphate below 1.0 mmol/L is accompanied by respiratory/cardiac muscle weakness or another specific indication.
- Define DKA resolution by beta-hydroxybutyrate below 0.6 mmol/L plus venous pH at least 7.3 or bicarbonate at least 18 mmol/L; ideally glucose is below 200 mg/dL. Do not use anion gap or urine ketones alone because recovery hyperchloremic acidosis and ketone conversion can mislead. Consider HHS resolved when osmolality is below 300 mOsm/kg, cognition and hyperglycemia improve, urine output exceeds 0.5 mL/kg/h and glucose is below 250 mg/dL.
- Continue or initiate an appropriate basal insulin plan. For transition after DKA/HHS, administer the subcutaneous basal insulin 2--4 hours before stopping IV insulin (ADA 2026 section 16); verify the product, documented administration time and ongoing basal coverage, including any basal already given. This basal-specific rule replaces the older general 1--2 hour SC-overlap shorthand from the 2024 consensus in this pathway. Stop IV insulin only after crisis resolution and with a verified basal/nutritional/correction plan; glucose normalization alone is insufficient. Do not infer a universal transition percentage, extra basal dose or NPH-specific interval. Treat the precipitant, stop SGLT2 inhibitors during the event, and admit severe DKA, HHS, mixed crises, altered consciousness, shock or major comorbidity to a high-acuity setting.

title: Acid Base Emergencies
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Confirm sample type (arterial, venous or capillary), oxygen delivery/FiO2, collection time and clinical context. Venous pH/bicarbonate are often sufficient for DKA trending, but venous PO2 must not be used to assess arterial oxygenation; use pulse oximetry and an arterial sample when oxygenation or an arterial-venous discrepancy matters.
- Separate the current result, reference interval and comparative column before interpretation; do not infer a prior result's time from a pasted layout. Use actual plasma bicarbonate (cHCO3(P)), not standard bicarbonate (cHCO3(P,st)), for simultaneous gap/compensation calculations. Read pH, PCO2 and bicarbonate together. Then obtain sodium, chloride, albumin, lactate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, glucose, urea/creatinine and relevant toxins. A normal pH does not exclude a mixed disorder.
- **Units and gap convention:** gas pressures must be explicitly mmHg or kPa; 1 kPa is approximately 7.50062 mmHg. Electrolytes/bicarbonate are mmol/L. Albumin g/L must be divided by 10 before using a g/dL formula; hemoglobin reported in g/dL does not establish the laboratory's albumin unit. Calculate anion gap as `Na - (Cl + HCO3)` and, when albumin is known in g/dL, corrected gap as `AG + 2.5 x (4 - albumin)`. The alternative potassium-inclusive gap is `Na + K - Cl - HCO3` and requires its own verified reference interval. Never apply an unidentified analyzer gap interval to a calculation that excludes potassium. For established high-gap metabolic acidosis calculate the delta ratio `(corrected AG - matching normal AG) / (24 - HCO3)`; 12 mmol/L without potassium is a generic reference, not a verified local baseline. State whether albumin correction was possible. Omit the ratio when bicarbonate is >=24 or the corrected gap is not elevated; near-zero denominators and variable baseline gap make isolated cutoffs unreliable.
- After confirming a metabolic-acidosis component, calculate Winter compensation: expected PCO2 `1.5 x HCO3 + 8 +/- 2 mmHg`. A measured PCO2 above this range indicates an added respiratory acidosis; below it indicates an added respiratory alkalosis. Low bicarbonate alone may instead reflect compensation for primary respiratory alkalosis. The calculator exposes the Winter label as conditional unless `metabolic_acidosis_confirmed` is explicitly true. For metabolic alkalosis use expected PCO2 approximately `40 + 0.7 x (HCO3 - 24) +/- 5`.
- For respiratory disorders, compare acute and chronic expected bicarbonate responses instead of declaring chronicity from one gas: respiratory acidosis raises bicarbonate by about 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg acute and 3.5--4 chronic; respiratory alkalosis lowers it by about 2 acute and 4--5 chronic.
- A near-normal pH may conceal a double or triple disorder. Combine the primary clinical process, gap/albumin, delta relationship and respiratory compensation; an abnormal delta ratio is a clue, not an automatic extra diagnosis. Obtain missing albumin, sample type, medication/exposure history and trends rather than inventing them.
- Use `scripts/acid_base_hyperglycemia.py` for reproducible calculations with explicit unit fields; duplicate-unit fields, nonfinite values and mathematically impossible inputs are rejected. Conversion and arithmetic do not establish analyzer accuracy or diagnose the cause. Treat the patient and cause: restore perfusion/oxygenation, address sepsis, DKA, renal failure, diarrhea, vomiting, salicylate/toxic alcohol exposure or ventilatory failure. Do not administer bicarbonate solely because bicarbonate is low. Route treatment to the verified syndrome pathway. BICARICU-2 (2025) found no reduction in 90-day mortality with bicarbonate in severe metabolic acidemia plus moderate/severe AKI; this does not establish a universal bicarbonate indication or contraindication. Shock, DKA, toxicology and renal-replacement decisions retain their own criteria.
- In severe metabolic acidosis, avoid unnecessary intubation. If intubation is unavoidable, minimize apnea and match or initially approximate the pre-intubation minute ventilation; an abrupt PCO2 rise can cause profound acidemia and cardiovascular collapse. Obtain an early post-intubation gas and reassess ventilation.
- **Review14/11/2026 — reference framework:** the manually verified numerical pathway can be reviewed independently of a local analyzer profile. No analyzer identity or potassium convention is inferred from the owner's laboratory example. The local-profile mapping remains unverified; it must not be used as an automatically matched interval. The engine labels its default12mmol/L reference as generic and reports the potassium-inclusive gap separately; check the matching convention/reference before interpretation. GREEN denotes the unit-aware physiological reference and tested arithmetic, not calibration/OCR or validation of the local laboratory instrument.

title: Aki Nephrology
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Determine baseline, perfusion, obstruction, nephrotoxins, urinalysis findings and complications. Use bladder/renal ultrasound when obstruction is plausible.
- Treat shock and cause while avoiding both under-resuscitation and congestion; adjust renally cleared drugs.
- Escalate refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary edema, uremic complication or toxin indication for nephrology/dialysis; do not use creatinine alone to decide.
- **Version control14/11/2026:** the official KDIGO AKI/AKD page still describes2026 as a public-review draft under preparation for publication. Retain the published KDIGO2012 baseline; do not label draft biomarker definitions, treatment thresholds or recommendations as final2026 guidance.
- **Recognition:** AKI includes any creatinine rise>=0.3mg/dL (26.5micromol/L) within48h, >=1.5times baseline within7days, or urine output<0.5mL/kg/h for6h. Check trends and the actual baseline; oliguria can precede creatinine elevation.
- **Urgent management:** investigate obstruction, sepsis, hypoperfusion and nephrotoxins; review drug doses against changing renal function. Use diuretics for volume overload when indicated, not to reverse AKI itself; do not use low-dose dopamine for renal protection. Life-threatening electrolyte, acid-base or fluid complications require urgent renal replacement assessment without a creatinine-only threshold. Arrange post-AKI follow-up, including reassessment around3months for recovery/CKD.

title: Rhabdomyolysis
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Identify trauma/compression, exertion/heat, seizure, drugs/toxins and ischemia; check CK trend, potassium, calcium, phosphate, renal function and ECG.
- Give goal-directed isotonic crystalloid while tracking urine output, perfusion and congestion; a commonly used adult urine-output target is about 1--3 mL/kg/h (up to roughly 300 mL/h), but stop escalating fluid if oliguria persists with overload risk. Treat hyperkalemia urgently and trend CK until a clear peak/downtrend.
- Do not use bicarbonate, mannitol or loop diuretics routinely to prevent rhabdomyolysis-associated AKI; reserve them for another specific indication or specialist protocol. Do not chase CK with unlimited fluid.
- Evaluate compartment syndrome and dialysis indications; admit significant electrolyte disturbance, AKI, systemic illness or ongoing muscle injury.

title: Acute Liver Failure
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- Recognize acute liver injury with coagulopathy and encephalopathy; assess glucose frequently and seek toxins, viral, ischemic, autoimmune and pregnancy causes.
- Start N-acetylcysteine immediately for suspected acetaminophen toxicity without waiting for a level. For adult non-acetaminophen ALF, ACG 2023 supports early IV NAC with liver/transplant specialist review; the early-encephalopathy trial signal does not establish benefit in every cause/stage or justify pediatric extrapolation. NAC does not replace cause-specific therapy or transplant assessment. Obtain an accurate timeline, acetaminophen concentration, toxicology and serial hepatic, renal, glucose, lactate, ammonia and coagulation data.
- Manage cerebral/airway risk and avoid unnecessary correction of INR without bleeding or an invasive-procedure need because INR does not measure the full hemostatic balance and correction can obscure prognosis.
- Contact a transplant-capable liver center at first recognition rather than after deterioration; worsening encephalopathy, lactate, acidosis, hypoglycemia or multiorgan failure requires critical care and urgent transplant assessment.
- **Local circuit acceptance (2026-11-13):** the owner accepts the reviewed NAC/reference pathway and early contact/transfer to a transplant-capable center and requests GREEN. No receiving-center name, phone number, guaranteed transfer time or new specialist/pharmacy signature is inferred. Use the accepted local contact route immediately when ALF is suspected.

title: Pancreatitis
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Diagnose from compatible pain plus enzymes and/or imaging; seek biliary disease, alcohol, triglycerides, drugs and alternative surgical causes.
- Use analgesia, antiemetics and moderately aggressive, individualized lactated Ringer's resuscitation with frequent reassessment for overload, renal function and response; avoid fixed large volumes, especially with cardiac/renal disease.
- In mild disease, begin low-fat oral feeding within 24--48 hours as tolerated rather than waiting for enzyme normalization. Use enteral rather than parenteral nutrition when oral intake is not possible.
- Avoid routine prophylactic antibiotics or treatment of sterile necrosis. Arrange urgent ERCP for pancreatitis complicated by cholangitis; do not perform urgent ERCP routinely for all biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis or persistent obstruction.
- Assess organ failure and cholangitis/obstruction requiring urgent intervention. Admit persistent systemic illness, organ dysfunction or inability to tolerate oral intake.

title: Hematology Oncology
sharedPreamble: # Disposition and cross-cutting modules
sectionBody:
- Adult recognition/escalation framework: threats include neutropenic sepsis, leukostasis, tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), hyperviscosity, spinal cord compression, malignant hypercalcemia and major bleeding/thrombosis. Record cancer/transplant diagnosis, recent systemic therapy, immunosuppression, prophylaxis, central access and treating-team details. Assess ABCDE, organ dysfunction, glucose and neurological status; minimal local signs or absent fever do not establish safety.
- An unwell patient receiving anticancer treatment may have neutropenic sepsis. Obtain cultures, blood count/differential, renal/liver function, lactate and source-directed tests promptly, without waiting for the neutrophil count or culture results to start urgently indicated empirical antibiotics. Use `sepsis-shock` and `empiric-antibiotics`, with antipseudomonal coverage chosen for allergy, renal function, prior resistant organisms and local epidemiology. Do not discharge from a low-risk score alone; outpatient care requires a formal oncology risk assessment and reliable treatment/review pathway.
- Suspect spontaneous or treatment-related TLS with high disease burden, renal dysfunction or evolving potassium, phosphate, calcium, urate and creatinine abnormalities. Arrange ECG, serial biochemical monitoring, strict fluid balance and immediate hematology/nephrology involvement; hydration must account for renal/cardiac tolerance. Prevention and established TLS require different specialist regimens. Select urate-lowering therapy promptly by risk and product information; rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency and can falsely lower urate in mishandled samples. Follow the laboratory's specific sample-handling instructions. Do not routinely correct asymptomatic TLS-associated hypocalcemia; symptomatic or ECG-threatening disturbances need the relevant emergency protocol. Escalate refractory electrolyte/volume or renal complications for renal replacement assessment.
- New respiratory or neurological compromise with suspected acute leukemia/hyperleukocytosis, symptomatic hyperviscosity, major bleeding or coagulopathy requires immediate hematology/critical-care discussion and syndrome-specific treatment; do not wait for complete disease classification. A cell count alone cannot determine leukostasis or a universal cytoreduction/apheresis plan.
- Route new spinal pain/weakness/sphincter dysfunction to `acute-spinal-cord-compression`, significant hypercalcemia to `calcium-magnesium-emergencies`, and bleeding/thrombosis to the corresponding hemorrhage, reversal or thromboembolism module. These conditions must not wait for a routine outpatient cancer appointment.
- Reassess infection, perfusion, neurological function, renal/electrolyte trends and treatment toxicity. Admit/escalate organ dysfunction, suspected TLS/leukostasis, uncontrolled symptoms or inability to provide reliable monitoring. This framework does not authorize chemotherapy, apheresis or an unverified local drug preparation; document specialist decisions and transfer/handover needs.

title: Anticoagulation Reversal
sharedPreamble:
# Procedure and pharmacology modules

Shared gate: verify identity, indication, consent/capacity, monitoring, allergies,
weight, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function, anticoagulation, equipment, skilled help,
rescue plan and post-intervention reassessment.

- For oral liquid/drop formulations, always retain the dose in mg and calculate mL only from the exact verified concentration. If the exact marketed product is dispensed as drops, also display whole drops per dose only from a verified mg/drop or drops/mL factor; never assume a universal drop factor.
sectionBody:
### Principios
- Identificar **fármaco exacto, indicación, última dosis/hora, función renal/hepática, peso, sitio y gravedad del sangrado, posibilidad de control de foco y nivel farmacológico/anti-Xa si está disponible con rapidez**. Suspender el anticoagulante. No retrasar reversión de una hemorragia vital esperando una prueba que no vaya a llegar a tiempo.
- Revertir de forma farmacológica principalmente en hemorragia **vital, crítica/espacio cerrado, expansiva o no controlada**, o cirugía/procedimiento urgente de alto riesgo que no puede esperar aclaramiento. Evitar reversión en la mayoría de sangrados menores/estables.
- **PT/INR normal no excluye apixabán/rivaroxabán.** Para dabigatrán son más informativos TT/dTT/ECT cuando estén disponibles; para inhibidores Xa, anti-Xa calibrado específico. El INR guía la reversión de antagonistas de vitamina K, no la selección/dosis de PCC para un AOD. Distinguir reversión específica de apoyo prohemostático: el **PCC de cuatro factores no activado** aporta factores, no elimina el AOD ni debe monitorizarse esperando normalizar su concentración. No intercambiar PCC de cuatro factores, PCC de tres factores y PCC activado (aPCC).

### VKA: warfarina/acenocumarol y superwarfarinas
- Hemorragia vital/mayor: **vitamina K1 10 mg IV lenta + 4-factor PCC**. Para ICH, AHA/ASA 2022: si INR 1.3–1.9 considerar **4F-PCC 10–20 IU/kg**; si INR ≥2, **25–50 IU/kg** según INR/producto. Se mantiene **PCC de cuatro factores no activado, sin nombre comercial**. Farmacia de guardia comprobará en el producto dispensado la dosis por INR/peso, las UI de factor IX, dosis máxima, contraindicaciones, reconstitución y velocidad. No inferir equivalencia en mL entre productos. FFP si PCC no disponible.
- Hemorragia no vital o INR supraterapéutico sin sangrado: no aplicar automáticamente 10 mg IV + PCC; seguir protocolo específico por INR, riesgo y necesidad de procedimiento.
- **Superwarfarinas (brodifacoum y similares):** vitamina K1 puede requerirse durante semanas/meses con seguimiento de INR; PCC solo para sangrado grave/urgencia, no como sustituto de vitamina K sostenida.

### Dabigatrán
- Antídoto específico: **idarucizumab 5 g IV**, administrado como **2 × 2.5 g consecutivos** para hemorragia vital/no controlada o cirugía urgente indicada.
- Si no disponible y hay toxicidad significativa: considerar PCC/aPCC bajo protocolo y **hemodiálisis** en situaciones seleccionadas, especialmente insuficiencia renal/alta carga.
- Rebote de dabigatrán puede ocurrir en carga alta o IRA; repetir pruebas/clinica. Una segunda dosis de idarucizumab no es rutinaria y requiere criterios específicos del producto/hematología.

### Apixabán y rivaroxabán
- Antídoto específico con indicación en la ficha EMA para hemorragia vital/no controlada: **andexanet alfa (Ondexxya)**. La FDA comunicó el18/12/2025 que el riesgo tromboembólico grave hacía desfavorable su balance beneficio-riesgo y el fin de ventas en EE.UU. desde22/12/2025. Esto no equivale a retirada de la autorización EMA: el PRAC de junio de 2026 mantiene balance favorable dentro de la indicación autorizada. La posición BSH de abril de 2026 también distingue jurisdicciones. La decisión clínica debe documentar beneficio/riesgo y regulación aplicable, con consulta experta precoz; no uso automático por figurar como antídoto ni preferencia universal independiente del sitio de sangrado.
  - **Baja dosis:** bolo **400 mg IV** (objetivo ~30 mg/min), luego **4 mg/min durante 120 min** = 480 mg.
  - **Alta dosis:** bolo **800 mg IV**, luego **8 mg/min durante 120 min** = 960 mg.
- Selección EMA:
  - apixabán ≤5 mg y última dosis <8 h: baja; >5 mg y <8 h: alta; ≥8 h: baja;
  - rivaroxabán ≤10 mg y <8 h: baja; >10 mg y <8 h: alta; ≥8 h: baja.
  - Si dosis o intervalo son desconocidos, la ficha EMA no ofrece una regla universal: usar anti-Xa si llega a tiempo y consultar hematología/farmacia.
- Para hemorragia vital por inhibidores Xa, **PCC de cuatro factores no activado** es una opción prohemostática inespecífica/off-label tras valorar beneficio/riesgo, especialmente si andexanet no está indicado o no se selecciona tras evaluación individual: **4F-PCC 25–50 IU/kg** o estrategia fija del protocolo aceptado (frecuentemente **2,000 IU**). La evidencia no establece una dosis universal óptima: el médico debe seleccionar y documentar una estrategia, validada por Farmacia para el producto dispensado; no sumar dosis fija y ponderal ni repetir por rutina. Riesgo trombótico con ambas estrategias; no utilizar PCC rutinariamente en sangrado menor.

### Edoxabán y otros inhibidores Xa
- **Edoxabán:** andexanet no está autorizado por EMA específicamente para edoxabán. En hemorragia vital considerar **4F-PCC 25–50 IU/kg** según protocolo/hematología. No presentar andexanet como antídoto aprobado local sin verificación regulatoria.
- **Betrixabán** (donde exista): no extrapolar indicación de andexanet sin comprobar regulación local; PCC es opción inespecífica experta.
- **Fondaparinux:** **no existe antídoto específico aprobado**. Protamina no neutraliza fondaparinux. En hemorragia vital puede considerarse aPCC/4F-PCC bajo hematología/toxicología, con evidencia limitada y riesgo trombótico.

### Heparinas
- **Heparina no fraccionada (UFH): protamina**. Referencia: **1 mg de protamina por cada 100 U de UFH administradas en las 2–3 h previas**, ajustando a tiempo transcurrido; máximo habitual **50 mg**, IV lenta (p. ej. ≤5 mg/min) por riesgo de hipotensión/anafilaxia. Recontrolar aPTT/ACT según contexto.
- **Enoxaparina/HBPM: reversión parcial con protamina.**
  - si enoxaparina <8 h: **1 mg protamina por 1 mg enoxaparina**;
  - 8–12 h: **0.5 mg protamina por 1 mg enoxaparina**;
  - puede darse una segunda dosis **0.5 mg por 1 mg enoxaparina** si persiste sangrado/actividad.
  - >12 h puede no ser necesaria en muchos casos, salvo insuficiencia renal/actividad persistente. Anti-Xa y hematología si grave.
