- Otras HBPM (dalteparina/tinzaparina/nadroparina): protamina solo revierte parcialmente; usar ficha/protocolo del producto, no convertir unidades entre HBPM.

### Inhibidores directos de trombina parenterales
- **Argatrobán:** no existe antídoto específico; suspender, soporte y control de foco. Vida media corta pero se prolonga en hepatopatía.
- **Bivalirudina:** no antídoto específico; suspender, soporte. Vida media corta, prolongada en disfunción renal; hemofiltración/hemodiálisis puede aumentar eliminación en casos seleccionados.
- **Desirudina/lepirudina** donde existan: sin antídoto específico; manejo experto y eliminación dependiente del producto/riñón.

### Anticoagulantes poco frecuentes
- **Danaparoide:** no existe reversor específico fiable; protamina es ineficaz o muy incompleta. Hematología y control de foco.
- **Heparinoides/compuestos investigacionales:** no asumir reversibilidad por protamina o PCC; verificar mecanismo y ficha.
- **Trombolíticos/fibrinolíticos (alteplasa, tenecteplasa, uroquinasa):** no son anticoagulantes clásicos y no tienen un único antídoto. Hemorragia grave: suspender, medir fibrinógeno/coagulación y considerar **crioprecipitado/fibrinógeno**; antifibrinolítico (ácido tranexámico o aminocaproico) solo según protocolo y balance trombótico.

### Antiagregantes
- Aspirina, clopidogrel, prasugrel y ticagrelor: **no existe un antídoto de uso rutinario universal**. Suspender cuando corresponda, control de foco; transfusión plaquetaria no debe usarse de forma automática y puede ser perjudicial en ciertos ICH no quirúrgicos.
- Desmopresina puede considerarse en determinados sangrados/ICH bajo protocolo (p. ej. 0.3 microgramos/kg IV), pero no es un antídoto específico y la evidencia clínica es limitada.
- Con DAPT/recent stent, evitar suspender ambos agentes sin coordinación cardiología salvo necesidad vital.

### Medidas complementarias y límites
- Considerar carbón activado tras ingestión muy reciente sólo si es apropiado y la vía aérea es segura/protegida; no retrasar hemostasia o reversión indicada. En sobredosis, consultar toxicología para ventana y descontaminación individualizadas; una sonda por sí sola no protege de aspiración.
- Plasma/crioprecipitado/fibrinógeno y rFVIIa no son antídotos de los AOD. Los componentes pueden estar indicados para transfusión o coagulopatía concurrente; distinguirlo de neutralizar el anticoagulante. No añadir rFVIIa de rutina.
- **No extender tranexámico de rutina a toda hemorragia digestiva por AOD.** La recomendación amplia del texto aportado es opinión secundaria de baja certeza y no se traslada como orden universal: HALT-IT no mostró beneficio de mortalidad y observó más tromboembolismo venoso con el régimen estudiado. Usar antifibrinolíticos cuando corresponda a la indicación específica, p. ej. trauma, sin extrapolar entre sitios de sangrado.
- Evitar acumular antídotos/prohemostáticos o repetir PCC por persistencia de una prueba aislada. Reevaluar control anatómico, hemostasia y riesgo trombótico; las combinaciones requieren justificación experta. Tras andexanet, los ensayos anti-Xa comerciales no son adecuados para medir su efecto de reversión (ficha EMA).

### Tabla rápida
| Agente | Reversor | Dosis/observación |
|---|---|---|
| Warfarina/acenocumarol | Vitamina K1 + 4F-PCC | Vit K 10 mg IV en sangrado vital; PCC por INR/peso/producto |
| Superwarfarinas | Vitamina K1 | Curso prolongado guiado por INR; PCC si sangrado vital |
| Dabigatrán | Idarucizumab | **5 g IV = 2 × 2.5 g** |
| Apixabán/rivaroxabán | Andexanet alfa o 4F-PCC según evaluación | Andexanet: 400 mg + 4 mg/min×120 min o 800 mg + 8 mg/min×120 min según ficha; PCC: estrategia inespecífica descrita arriba, sin sumar alternativas |
| Edoxabán | Sin antídoto EMA específico | 4F-PCC 25–50 IU/kg según protocolo si hemorragia vital |
| UFH | Protamina | ~1 mg/100 U UFH recientes, ajustar por tiempo; máx habitual 50 mg |
| Enoxaparina | Protamina parcial | <8 h: 1 mg/mg; 8–12 h: 0.5 mg/mg; posible segunda 0.5 mg/mg |
| Fondaparinux | Ninguno específico | PCC/aPCC solo rescate experto; protamina no útil |
| Argatrobán | Ninguno específico | Suspender + soporte/control de foco |
| Bivalirudina | Ninguno específico | Suspender; soporte; depuración extracorpórea seleccionada |
| Danaparoide | Ninguno específico fiable | Hematología; protamina no revierte adecuadamente |
| Trombolítico | Ninguno único | Fibrinógeno/crioprecipitado ± antifibrinolítico según protocolo |

### Seguridad y reinicio
- PCC, aPCC, andexanet e incluso corrección rápida de anticoagulación aumentan riesgo trombótico. Documentar indicación, hora, dosis, respuesta y plan de tromboprofilaxis/reinicio.
- Reiniciar anticoagulación cuando exista hemostasia duradera y la indicación persista; no hay un día universal. Individualizar por sitio del sangrado, causa corregida, riesgo embólico, función renal, vida media del fármaco y procedimiento.
- **Evitar andexanet antes de una heparinización prevista** en cirugía cardiaca/vascular: puede causar falta de respuesta a heparina y pruebas engañosas. La reversión para cirugía urgente no es una indicación perioperatoria genérica validada; seguir ficha/hematología.
- **Circuito local aceptado (13/11/2026): cualquier médico puede activar el algoritmo actualizado con Farmacia de guardia.** La disponibilidad de antídotos ya está confirmada por el propietario. Mantener PCC por denominación genérica de cuatro factores no activado; no se exige registrar aquí un nombre comercial para cerrar la revisión del módulo. Farmacia verifica la ficha y características del producto efectivamente dispensado antes de prepararlo/administrarlo. Consulta a Hematología u otros especialistas según complejidad y en paralelo, sin convertir su autorización previa en un requisito de activación no acordado. Registrar indicación, dosis, hora, respuesta y plan de reinicio.
- Alcance: aceptación del protocolo de referencia y circuito por el propietario; no auditoría independiente de lotes ni firma nominal de Farmacia/Hematología. Los cálculos automáticos de PCC siguen bloqueados sin tabla de producto verificada; GREEN del módulo no certifica conversión a mL o preparación específica.

title: Medication Selection Safety
sharedPreamble:
# Procedure and pharmacology modules

Shared gate: verify identity, indication, consent/capacity, monitoring, allergies,
weight, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function, anticoagulation, equipment, skilled help,
rescue plan and post-intervention reassessment.

- For oral liquid/drop formulations, always retain the dose in mg and calculate mL only from the exact verified concentration. If the exact marketed product is dispensed as drops, also display whole drops per dose only from a verified mg/drop or drops/mL factor; never assume a universal drop factor.
sectionBody:
- Define the exact syndrome, therapeutic purpose, current value and target before selecting a drug. Distinguish treating the underlying disease from changing a physiologic number or treating a similarly named condition.
- When a user proposes an agent, state one of: recommended, not routinely indicated, conditional, contraindicated or uncertain. Give the decisive indication mismatch, contraindication or monitoring issue before offering a dose.
- For a recommendation, provide generic drug, route, initial dose, titration/redosing, maximum when applicable, organ-function adjustment, key contraindications, monitoring, hold/stop condition and reassessment interval. Do not imply a checklist is prescribing clearance.
- **High-alert medication gate:** WHO Medication Without Harm and the ISMP 2024 acute-care list identify high-risk situations and high-alert medicines as requiring stronger system controls. Treat insulin, anticoagulants/thrombolytics, opioids, neuromuscular blockers, concentrated electrolytes/hypertonic saline and other locally designated high-alert drugs as requiring extra verification before administration. Injectable tranexamic acid is also high-alert: verify the vial and IV route and segregate it from neuraxial local anesthetics; never administer it intrathecally or epidurally.
- **Unit/concentration safety:** explicitly distinguish mg, micrograms, units and mmol; never silently convert between them. Use a leading zero for doses below 1 (for example 0.5 mg), never a trailing zero, and avoid ambiguous abbreviations. Confirm whether a label expresses active base, salt, equivalent drug amount or units before calculating a patient dose.
- **Patient-product match before calculation:** verify patient weight when weight-based dosing is used, age/pregnancy where relevant, allergy, renal/hepatic function, current interacting drugs, last dose/time for anticoagulants or antidote-sensitive agents, and the exact locally available product strength/concentration. If any critical input is missing, stop at a symbolic/reference calculation.
- For every continuous infusion, state the total drug amount, compatible diluent, final volume and final concentration. Prefer a 100 mL or 200 mL final volume when clinically appropriate and compatible with the locally available formulation; do not invent compatibility or override a pharmacy/local standard concentration.
- Convert every continuous dose to a pump rate in mL/h. Show the arithmetic, the starting rate, each titration step in both dose units and mL/h, the titration interval, maximum or ceiling when applicable, and explicit hold/stop thresholds. For a weight-based infusion use: `mL/h = dose (mcg/kg/min) × weight (kg) × 60 ÷ concentration (mcg/mL)`.
- **Independent verification for high-risk infusions:** where local policy requires it, verify drug, patient, weight, dose units, concentration, final volume, pump library entry/channel and calculated mL/h independently before starting or after a material concentration change. A second check must not be described as a substitute for correct prescribing/pharmacy controls.
- If weight or formulation is missing, do not invent it: provide the symbolic formula and request the missing value before presenting a patient-specific pump setting. A clearly labelled reference table may be added, but never presented as the patient's rate.
- Do not force bolus or intermittent medication into mL/h. For those, state the dose, stock strength, dilution when needed, final volume in mL and administration time/rate.
- **Look-alike/sound-alike and duplicate-therapy gate:** use generic name plus concentration/route; compare with the active medication list and recent administrations before recommending a duplicate, interacting or similarly named drug. Medication reconciliation is especially important at ED-ICU/ward transfers.
- Prefer titratable IV agents for time-critical hemodynamic control. Define both upper and lower safety bounds when cerebral, coronary or renal perfusion could be harmed; avoid an isolated target number without the syndrome and current pressure.
- Do not transfer targets or drugs among subdural hematoma, intraparenchymal hemorrhage, aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and ischemic stroke. Nimodipine is disease-modifying treatment for aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, not a general antihypertensive or routine treatment for isolated subdural hematoma. Nitrates are not default blood-pressure agents when intracranial mass effect or raised pressure is a concern.
- When an IV antihypertensive is unavailable, do not offer a name-only substitution. Route to `iv-antihypertensive-selection` and select by the organ-injury syndrome, heart rate/conduction, ventricular function, bronchospasm, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function and local formulation. Give a feasible alternative when one is supported and explain why it fits; if none is suitable or availability is unknown, state that limitation and the escalation plan rather than inventing availability. Explicitly reject nimodipine as a nicardipine substitute.
- In traumatic intracranial mass effect, treat hypertension as potentially compensatory until perfusion and raised-ICP physiology are assessed. Do not reflexively target SBP 140 mm Hg. Hypertonic saline for an ICP crisis is a weight-based bolus over a defined time, not a routine continuous infusion; preserve its bolus order even when a pump is used for delivery.
- If the evidence is update-sensitive, the exact formulation is unavailable locally, or the proposed use is off-label, verify an authoritative current source and local protocol before presenting the regimen as definitive.

title: Ophthalmology Emergencies
sharedPreamble: # Disposition and cross-cutting modules
sectionBody:
- Adult initial framework: establish onset/last known normal vision, pain, trauma/chemical exposure, contact lenses, recent eye surgery/injection and systemic symptoms. Assess visual acuity in each eye when feasible, pupils/RAPD, fields, motility and relevant anterior/posterior findings without delaying immediate rescue. A photograph or a limited examination does not replace the required clinical eye assessment; use pediatric-specific advice for children.
- Chemical exposure: begin copious irrigation immediately, before detailed history, visual testing or photography; do not wait for a preferred solution if clean water is immediately available. Remove ongoing contamination/contact lenses or retained particles when safely feasible, continue irrigation and reassess ocular-surface pH to an appropriate physiological endpoint with specialist guidance. Do not attempt chemical neutralization with an opposite-pH substance. Suspected simultaneous open globe needs immediate ophthalmology-led trauma/decontamination decisions; avoid pressure or forced irrigation. Arrange urgent ophthalmology review according to injury severity; no fixed volume alone proves adequate decontamination.
- Suspected open globe/penetrating injury: protect with a rigid shield without pressure, avoid manipulation, tonometry and pressure-producing ocular ultrasound, and do not remove an embedded object. Give appropriate systemic symptom control, keep ready for urgent operative assessment and contact ophthalmology immediately; further imaging/antimicrobial/tetanus decisions follow the trauma and eye-specialist protocol. A small wound or retained vision does not exclude serious penetration.
- Sudden painless monocular visual loss, a new field curtain or new flashes/floaters with visual disturbance requires urgent retinal/vascular assessment, not routine follow-up. Suspected retinal arterial occlusion activates immediate ophthalmology and stroke assessment; record last known normal and assess associated neurological signs. Reperfusion decisions belong to the current stroke/eye team and evidence, not an automatic ocular massage, paracentesis or empiric thrombolysis order from this framework.
- A painful red eye with reduced vision, corneal change, headache/nausea or abnormal pupil may be acute angle closure or another sight-threatening disorder. Measure IOP only when open globe is not suspected and obtain urgent ophthalmology assessment. Mechanism matters: topiramate-associated or other secondary angle closure is not automatically treated like pupillary block; do not give a universal pilocarpine regimen. Verify specific pressure-lowering drugs, contraindications and actual preparation with the specialist/product protocol.
- Suspect endophthalmitis with a painful red eye and reduced vision after surgery/injection, and orbital infection with proptosis, painful/restricted movements, visual impairment or systemic illness. Escalate immediately for specialist imaging, antimicrobials and source control as indicated; do not treat these as uncomplicated conjunctivitis. New visual loss with symptoms suggesting giant-cell arteritis also needs an immediate specialist/systemic treatment pathway, without waiting for routine eye follow-up.
- Reassess vision, pain, pupils and physiology after initial treatment. Discharge only after dangerous causes have been addressed and required specialist assessment completed, with an appropriate treatment plan, explicit deterioration advice and reliable follow-up. Unresolved loss of vision, suspected open globe, chemical injury, acute angle closure, retinal vascular/detachment concern or orbital/intraocular infection requires urgent specialist care/admission/transfer according to the actual pathway; on-site ophthalmology availability is not presumed.

title: Ent Emergencies
sharedPreamble: # Disposition and cross-cutting modules
sectionBody:
- Adult recognition/escalation framework: prioritize airway compromise, major hemorrhage, deep-neck infection/supraglottitis, mastoid/orbital or intracranial spread, sudden sensorineural hearing loss and hazardous foreign bodies. Assess ABCDE and consider children separately; do not apply adult examination, sedation or drug pathways automatically to a child.
- Severe throat pain with drooling, voice change, stridor, respiratory distress, trismus or systemic illness warrants urgent senior ENT/anesthesia assessment. A normal visible oropharynx does not exclude supraglottitis. Avoid forced/distressing examination or transfer to imaging before a threatened airway is secured; use `airway-rsi` with a controlled difficult-airway/rescue plan. Bedside intervention and transfer depend on actual expertise and resources, not assumed on-site ENT availability.
- Suspected deep-neck abscess, Ludwig angina, Lemierre syndrome or spreading infection needs urgent ENT/maxillofacial and sepsis assessment. Obtain contrast imaging when clinically safe and it will guide care; start indicated IV antibiotics through `empiric-antibiotics` and arrange drainage/source control when required. Imaging and cultures must not delay airway stabilization or sepsis treatment.
- For epistaxis, assess airway, circulation, ongoing blood loss and anticoagulants; start appropriate local first-line measures, including sustained soft-nose compression and anatomy-directed hemostasis/packing by trained staff. Persistent, recurrent or suspected posterior bleeding requires ENT escalation and possible operative/interventional control. In non-life-threatening bleeding, do not automatically stop/reverse anticoagulation before local first-line treatment; life-threatening bleeding uses `anticoagulation-reversal` and the hemorrhage pathway with specialist coordination.
- Sudden hearing loss not explained by external/middle-ear disease needs time-critical ENT assessment. NICE NG98: onset over 3 days or less within the past 30 days requires review within 24 hours. New focal neurological findings also require the appropriate stroke pathway. Do not assume wax/otitis without assessment or defer to routine audiology.
- Button batteries, caustic material, airway/esophageal foreign bodies or objects threatening tissue need immediate appropriate specialty advice and controlled removal, not repeated blind attempts. Arrange urgent assessment for mastoid swelling, orbital signs, facial weakness or neurological deterioration. Discharge only after airway/bleeding stability, adequate swallowing/hydration, a safe symptom plan and explicit follow-up/return instructions; unresolved red flags need observation, admission or transfer.

title: Dermatology Severe
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Look for mucosal involvement, skin pain, blistering, purpura, necrosis, systemic toxicity, immunosuppression and drug timing.
- Threats include SJS/TEN, DRESS, necrotizing infection, meningococcemia, purpura fulminans and severe drug reaction.
- Stop suspected culprit drugs, stabilize temperature/fluids/analgesia, avoid traumatic skin handling and obtain early dermatology/burn/critical-care input. Verify syndrome-specific steroids or immunomodulators before use.
- **SJS/TEN:** stop suspected culprit/nonessential drugs immediately, record exposure timing and obtain urgent dermatology plus early ophthalmology review. Assess airway/mucosal involvement, fluid/electrolytes, temperature, nutrition, pain and organ dysfunction; arrange specialist-unit care when required. Skin biopsy supports diagnosis but must not delay stabilization. Use careful skin handling and organ-specific wound/ocular care.
- **Immunomodulators:** S3 epidermal-necrolysis guidance2024 and the Japanese2025 supplement use differing conditional/systemic strategies. Neither establishes one universal steroid/IVIG/biologic prescription for every blistering rash; document syndrome/severity and use dermatology-led treatment. Do not delay emergency antibiotics/surgery for suspected necrotizing infection while considering a drug eruption.
- **DRESS:** assess eosinophils, liver/renal function and other organ involvement; adult international consensus supports severity-stratified topical versus systemic corticosteroids, with systemic therapy for severe organ disease and a supervised taper. Do not transfer adult regimens automatically to children. Arrange delayed-organ/thyroid and medication-allergy follow-up; avoid re-exposure to the culprit drug. A score or photograph does not alone establish the diagnosis.

title: Soft Tissue Infections
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Distinguish uncomplicated cellulitis/abscess from necrotizing infection, deep-space infection, pyomyositis and device-related infection.
- Pain out of proportion, toxicity, bullae, crepitus, anesthesia or rapid progression requires immediate surgical consultation; imaging must not delay exploration when suspicion is high.
- Drain drainable collections and select antibiotics by severity, anatomy, host factors and local resistance. Mark progression, reassess perfusion and admit systemic, high-risk or function-threatening disease.

title: Orthopedic Emergencies
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Identify open fracture, compartment syndrome, neurovascular injury, septic joint, dislocation, threatened skin and spinal injury.
- Document neurovascular status before and after splinting/reduction; provide analgesia and tetanus/antibiotic care when indicated.
- For procedures, verify sedation, reduction technique and rescue plan; obtain post-procedure imaging as appropriate and arrange urgent specialty care for limb threat.
- **Open fracture (NICE NG37):** give IV prophylactic antibiotics immediately in ED if not already administered; cover with saline-soaked/occlusive dressing and obtain urgent orthoplastic review. Do not irrigate long-bone/hindfoot/midfoot open fractures in ED before operative wound excision. Limb ischaemia or severe contamination requires immediate specialist action rather than waiting for a routine theatre slot.
- **Compartment/neurovascular safety:** document serial pain, passive-stretch pain, motor/sensory findings and perfusion, before and after intervention. Preserved pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome; suspected acute compartment syndrome requires urgent surgical assessment. Consider pressure monitoring when the examination is unreliable. Do not let radiography delay reduction of a limb-threatening dislocation/vascular emergency by an appropriately skilled team.
- **Occult injury and discharge:** NICE NG38 supports considering first-line MRI after clinical assessment for suspected scaphoid fracture. Negative initial radiographs do not alone justify discharge without protection/follow-up when suspicion persists. Confirm safe immobilisation, post-reduction neurovascular status and written deterioration/compartment warnings. GREEN covers this reference framework, not every reduction procedure or image classifier.

title: Acute Musculoskeletal Pain
sharedPreamble:
# Trauma and surgical modules

Shared gate: use an organized primary survey, expose while preventing hypothermia,
identify anticoagulation and pregnancy, repeat examinations and involve definitive
surgical/interventional teams early.
sectionBody:
- Adult initial framework: screen trauma and nontraumatic pain for fracture/dislocation, open injury, infection, compartment syndrome, neurovascular compromise, malignancy and referred visceral/vascular disease. Spinal pain with weakness, saddle sensory change or sphincter dysfunction uses `acute-spinal-cord-compression`/`cauda-equina-conus-emergency`; a threatened limb or systemic illness needs urgent specialty care. Children and pregnancy require their own assessment and medication selection.
- Document mechanism/onset, examination, swelling/deformity, joint movement, function/weight bearing and distal motor, sensory and vascular status. Repeat neurovascular assessment after splinting/reduction and with deterioration. Use `orthopedic-emergencies` and the relevant procedure/sedation pathway for reduction; analgesia does not replace diagnosis or serial examination.
- Suspect compartment syndrome with pain disproportionate to injury, pain on passive stretch or increasing analgesic requirement; normal pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome. Obtain immediate senior orthopedic/surgical review. At-risk patients need documented hourly reassessment; unreliable/equivocal examinations may require pressure measurement by the surgical team. Release constricting circumferential dressings and reassess urgently. Established compartment syndrome requires immediate decompression; do not delay for routine imaging.
- An acutely painful hot/swollen joint with restricted movement may be septic even without fever. Arrange urgent joint aspiration and orthopedic assessment; send bacterial identification, cell count/differential and crystals. Crystals or normal blood inflammatory markers do not exclude infection. In a stable patient obtain diagnostic samples before antibiotics; in sepsis or septic shock start antibiotics promptly without waiting for aspiration and arrange source control. Follow `empiric-antibiotics` and the local resistance/renal/allergy context.
- Choose imaging for the site and clinical suspicion. Use validated Ottawa ankle/foot or knee rules only in eligible patients, not as a rule for every painful limb. A normal initial radiograph does not exclude an occult fracture; persistent focal suspicion needs protection, reassessment and targeted further imaging. NICE NG38 advises considering first-line MRI after thorough examination for suspected scaphoid fracture. Imaging must not defer treatment of neurovascular or compartment emergencies.
- ACP/AAFP 2020 recommends topical NSAIDs, with or without menthol, first line for acute non-low-back musculoskeletal injuries in adults. This is not a recommendation for every atraumatic pain syndrome, spinal pain or pediatric patient. Oral NSAIDs or paracetamol are alternatives after checking age, renal/hepatic function, dehydration, gastrointestinal/bleeding and cardiovascular risk, pregnancy, anticoagulant interactions, allergy and duplicate medicines. Use `medication-selection-safety` and the actual product instructions for dose/formulation; do not infer interchangeability of topical strengths or a universal combined-drug schedule.
- Avoid opioids, including tramadol, as routine first-line treatment for this eligible injury scope. Severe injury or intolerance of first-line options may justify individualized, titrated rescue with reassessment, the shortest suitable course and respiratory/sedation precautions; avoid automatic sedative combinations. Apply suitable protection/support with a mobilization and recovery plan, avoiding unnecessary prolonged immobilization.
- Discharge only after adequate pain control, acceptable neurovascular reassessment, a safe functional/weight-bearing or assisted-mobility plan, no unresolved limb/systemic red flags and reliable follow-up. Explain medicine limits and return urgently for increasing/disproportionate pain, tense swelling, fever, redness, numbness, weakness, coldness/color change or loss of function. Document suspected occult injury and its imaging/review plan rather than labelling every negative radiograph a sprain.

title: Emergency Procedures
sharedPreamble:
# Procedure and pharmacology modules

Shared gate: verify identity, indication, consent/capacity, monitoring, allergies,
weight, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function, anticoagulation, equipment, skilled help,
rescue plan and post-intervention reassessment.

- For oral liquid/drop formulations, always retain the dose in mg and calculate mL only from the exact verified concentration. If the exact marketed product is dispensed as drops, also display whole drops per dose only from a verified mg/drop or drops/mL factor; never assume a universal drop factor.
sectionBody:
El contenido canónico ampliado desde v1.41 vive en:
- `modules/emergency-procedures-index.md` — índice textual maestro (200 IDs: 196 procedimientos canónicos y 4 alias; no 200 técnicas independientes).
- `modules/emergency-procedures-visual.md` — arquitectura de ficha y reglas visuales.
- `modules/procedures/01-*.md` a `16-*.md` — desarrollo textual por familia.

Reglas transversales:
- Confirmar indicación, alternativas, contraindicaciones, anatomía y asepsia; realizar time-out salvo que la urgencia inmediata lo impida.
- Preparar analgesia/sedación desde los módulos farmacológicos canónicos, monitorización, equipo de rescate y plan explícito de fallo.
- Confirmar éxito por método clínico/capnográfico/ecográfico/radiológico apropiado y repetir evaluación neurovascular, respiratoria o hemodinámica postprocedimiento.
- Las imágenes son material de apoyo y permanecen no validadas hasta superar Visual QA; nunca sustituyen la ficha textual ni la fuente clínica.
- Antes de iniciar, verificar paciente, procedimiento, sitio/lateralidad, consentimiento o fundamento de actuación urgente, alergias, anticoagulación, capacidad del operador y material disponible. Realizar la pausa de seguridad con el equipo; abreviarla a lo esencial si la demora amenaza la vida y documentar la situación. Una lista completada no acredita competencia técnica.
- Usar higiene de manos, técnica aséptica, protección y barreras apropiadas al procedimiento; para catéteres, consultar las recomendaciones OMS periféricas2024/centrales2026 y la ficha específica. Seleccionar acceso/material según riesgo y necesidad, mantener asepsia durante el uso y revisar diariamente la necesidad del dispositivo. Estas reglas no sustituyen la revisión de cada técnica ni prescriben un antiséptico incompatible con edad, piel o producto.
- Elegir analgesia/sedación desde `sedoanalgesia`, `airway-rsi` o el protocolo pediátrico pertinente, con preparación farmacológica verificada, personal, monitorización y rescate acordes al riesgo. Definir antes del intento cuándo detenerse, cambiar de estrategia o pedir ayuda; evitar intentos repetidos sin reevaluación anatómica y clínica.
- Documentar indicación, evaluación previa, operador, técnica, intentos, fármacos realmente administrados, confirmación de éxito y complicaciones. Establecer vigilancia posterior, cuidado/retirada del dispositivo, destino y criterios de consulta urgente; una mejoría transitoria no sustituye la confirmación apropiada de posición o función.
- GREEN corresponde únicamente a este marco transversal. No promueve las 196 fichas individuales, sus imágenes, competencias del personal ni recursos locales, y no habilita contratos farmacológicos bloqueados. Cada procedimiento conserva su fuente, estado, criterios de fracaso y plan de rescate.

title: Geriatric Emergencies
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- Establish pre-illness cognition, mobility, activities of daily living, frailty, nutrition, sensory/communication needs and social support using patient and carer information. Distinguish baseline dependency from acute deterioration; chronological age or a frailty score alone must not determine treatment limitation or destination. Discuss goals, decision-making capacity and existing care plans without delaying reversible emergency treatment.
- Expect atypical and multifactorial illness: assess ABCDE, glucose, pain, hydration, medication toxicity, infection, bleeding and occult injury. New functional decline or hypoactive confusion may be the presenting emergency even without fever or a dramatic vital-sign abnormality. Route delirium to `delirium` and collapse/falls to `syncope-falls-frailty`; a positive screen requires clinical assessment.
- Reconcile prescriptions, recent changes, over-the-counter drugs and adherence, especially anticoagulants, insulin/sulfonylureas, sedatives, anticholinergics, diuretics and nephrotoxic agents. Check renal function, interactions and actual weight/product where relevant. Use cautious individualized dosing and fluid reassessment without delaying effective treatment; avoid reflex sedation for agitation and unnecessary urinary catheters/restraints.
- For falls, investigate injury and the cause, including syncope, orthostatic hypotension, neurological disease and medicines. Assess gait/mobility, safe lying/standing BP, vision/hearing, footwear, nutrition and environmental hazards when appropriate. NICE NG249 supports comprehensive assessment for higher-risk fallers; a falls score or the label 'mechanical fall' is not a substitute. Arrange multidisciplinary/geriatric assessment according to need.
- Do not diagnose or treat UTI from delirium/fall plus bacteriuria alone when there are no urinary symptoms or systemic infection signs; search for other causes and observe. This restriction does not apply to an unstable patient with suspected sepsis, who needs prompt assessment and treatment. Assess retention, constipation, hypoxia and unmet sensory/basic needs rather than attributing all confusion to dementia.
- Reassess pain, cognition, hydration and function; preserve orientation, glasses/hearing aids, food/drink when safe, mobility and carer involvement. Disposition requires a feasible medication/feeding/mobility plan, capacity/support assessment, reliable follow-up and understandable written handover/return advice. Admit or arrange supported care when function, monitoring, safeguarding or caregiver capacity makes discharge unsafe, even if one acute test is reassuring.

title: Delirium
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- **Adult framework:** recognize acute/fluctuating inattention or cognitive/arousal change, including hypoactive presentations. Establish baseline and timing with family/carers, records and staff. Check immediate airway/oxygenation, glucose, circulation and neurological threats; confusion is a syndrome requiring a cause search.
- **Detection:** use **4AT** in appropriate general hospital/ED settings; **CAM-ICU or ICDSC** in critical care/recovery. A positive screen requires clinical assessment. Assess arousal first: deep sedation/coma can make CAM-ICU assessment inappropriate, not a negative delirium result. Repeat assessment when the clinical state changes and use communication/hearing/language support.
- **4AT boundaries:** >=4 suggests delirium;1--3 suggests cognitive impairment;0 does not definitively exclude delirium. Poor/refused attention performance is not the same as an explicitly **untestable** item. Use the validated scoring categories, not an improvised numerical substitute; the software's arithmetic is not bedside diagnostic validation.
- **Precipitants:** urgently look for hypoxia/hypercapnia, infection, glucose/electrolyte disturbance, dehydration/renal or hepatic illness, medication toxicity/anticholinergic burden, withdrawal, pain, urinary retention, constipation and acute neurologic disease. Several causes can coexist; do not assume dementia, intoxication or bacteriuria alone explains an acute change.
- **First treatment:** correct causes and pain, provide reorientation/reassurance, family contact, glasses/hearing aids, hydration/nutrition, appropriate mobility and protected sleep. Reduce unnecessary lines, transfers and restraint; document the least restrictive safe plan, capacity and safeguarding.
- **Medication is conditional:** severe distress or immediate danger after ineffective/inappropriate de-escalation may justify a short course of haloperidol under the selected RCM, lowest appropriate dose and cautious reassessment; NICE generally describes **1 week or less**, with earlier stopping when possible. Do not prescribe an antipsychotic routinely for every positive screen or leave it on discharge without an explicit indication/review plan. Benzodiazepines are reserved for withdrawal or another specific indication, not routine non-withdrawal delirium.
- **Haloperidol safety:** do not use in **Parkinson disease or dementia with Lewy bodies**. Review QTc, cardiac disease, interacting QT-prolonging medicines, K/Mg and other contraindications; obtain baseline ECG/correct electrolytes and repeat monitoring as clinically indicated. Monitor sedation, hypotension, extrapyramidal effects and dysphagia/aspiration; stop/reassess adverse effects. Verify the exact oral/IM product and route; no generic IV preparation or dose is inferred.
- **ICU evidence boundary:** PADIS 2025 could not recommend for or against antipsychotics versus usual care for ICU delirium because evidence is insufficient. Do not equate emergency control of dangerous behavior with proven shortening of delirium. ICU sedation/dexmedetomidine decisions follow the relevant sedation pathway rather than a universal prescription for confusion.
- Persistent or unexplained delirium, unstable physiology, inability to maintain hydration/therapy or unsafe supervision requires monitored admission/escalation. Communicate the diagnosis, suspected causes, serial assessment and medication stop/review plan at handover. GREEN is the accepted reviewed framework, not prospective accuracy validation of every cognitive score.

title: Syncope Falls Frailty
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- Separate syncope from seizure, mechanical fall and unexplained collapse. Obtain history/witness account, examination, 12-lead ECG and standing BP when safe; evaluate bleeding, structural/electrical heart disease, medication effect and neurologic findings.
- Do not order routine broad laboratory panels, EEG or head CT for uncomplicated syncope without findings that indicate them. Continuous monitoring and urgent cardiac assessment are warranted for high-risk ECG, exertional/supine syncope, persistent hypotension, major structural heart disease, family history of sudden death or serious injury.
- In older/frail patients, assess occult head/hip injury, anticoagulation, gait, cognition and home support.
- Do not discharge based on a risk score alone; integrate cause, recurrence risk, function and reliable follow-up.
- Establish the event sequence and witness account, prodrome, posture/exertion, palpitations, recovery, medications and family history; brief jerking can occur in syncope and does not alone establish epilepsy. Examine for alternative causes of transient loss of consciousness. Check orthostatic BP when safe, but a postural drop does not automatically exclude a concurrent cardiac or bleeding cause.
- Match targeted glucose, hemoglobin, pregnancy or other tests to the suspected cause; do not use one risk score to replace the history/ECG or routinely perform neurological imaging without a neurological/traumatic indication. Unexplained exertional/supine events, cardiac warning features or serious injury need monitored urgent assessment. Use `geriatric-emergencies` and the relevant injury module for functional decline, anticoagulation and occult fracture.
- A clear uncomplicated reflex/postural diagnosis may support discharge after stable reassessment, appropriate trigger/medicine advice and reliable follow-up. Recurrent unexplained or suspected arrhythmic events need appropriate ambulatory/specialist investigation. Discuss driving and hazardous activities according to the actual diagnosis and applicable Portuguese rules; do not invent a universal restriction interval. Document event uncertainty, test/result ownership and return advice.

title: Psychiatric Emergencies
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- Adult assessment framework: establish immediate danger, ABCDE, glucose, temperature, oxygenation and injury, then history/onset, medications/substances and collateral baseline information. Exclude delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, neurologic disease, metabolic illness and trauma before attributing symptoms to primary psychiatric disease. New fluctuating attention, abnormal physiology, focal findings or unexplained first presentation require targeted medical evaluation; a psychiatric history does not exclude physical illness.
- In alert, medically stable adults, testing is guided by history and examination rather than a universal laboratory/toxicology panel. This does not justify withholding tests in delirium, poisoning, instability or a concerning first presentation. Route relevant causes to `delirium`, `altered-consciousness`, `alcohol-withdrawal` or `toxicology` and treat reversible threats in parallel with behavioral safety.
- Use verbal de-escalation, personal space, a calm environment, clear choices and trained assistance; offer voluntary/oral treatment when appropriate. Aim for the least restriction and sedation needed for safety and assessment. If imminent danger requires parenteral medication or temporary restraint, provide an adequately staffed monitored setting with immediate airway/hemodynamic rescue. Do not use coercion as punishment or convenience; minimize duration, avoid pressure compromising the neck/chest/airway, continuously assess breathing/circulation and document repeated need and release as soon as safe.
- Medication must match cause, route and patient factors: check prior doses, intoxication, respiratory reserve, QT/cardiac disease, interacting drugs, renal/hepatic function, frailty and Parkinson/Lewy-body risk. Obtain ECG/electrolytes when indicated and feasible without delaying life-saving rescue. ACEP severe-agitation recommendations concern a defined adult emergency population; they do not establish a regimen for children, pregnancy or adults older than 65. Do not copy procedural-sedation doses from `sedoanalgesia` into a psychiatric-tranquillisation order. Verify the actual product-specific/local regimen through `medication-selection-safety`; no universal drug combination or new dose schedule is supplied here.
- Product-specific warning: simultaneous IM olanzapine and parenteral benzodiazepine is not recommended. If a parenteral benzodiazepine is needed after IM olanzapine, wait at least 1 hour; if the benzodiazepine came first, assess carefully before IM olanzapine and monitor closely, rather than assuming a symmetric automatic interval. The EMA product requires close BP/pulse/respiration/consciousness observation particularly during the first 4 hours after IM olanzapine, continued when clinically indicated. This is not a general waiting rule for every antipsychotic and does not confirm local stock.
- After medication/restraint, reassess airway, ventilation, oxygenation, pulse/BP, temperature, consciousness and adverse effects, including QT-related arrhythmia, dystonia and oversedation. Use ongoing direct observation and monitoring appropriate to the depth/risk; improvement in agitation alone is not medical clearance or permission for unmonitored transfer. Re-evaluate the cause as cooperation improves.
- Assess decision-making capacity for the actual decision, self-harm/suicide, violence, self-neglect, safeguarding and available supports. Use `suicide-risk`; do not use a risk score or a no-suicide contract to decide discharge. In Portugal, apply the current mental-health law and local urgent psychiatric/legal pathway, including the necessity, proportionality, physician oversight and documentation requirements of Lei35/2023; diagnosis or a family request alone does not establish compulsory treatment. No local form, court deadline or psychiatric-bed availability is assumed.
- Medical instability, unresolved delirium/intoxication, significant injury, unsafe post-sedation recovery or diagnostic uncertainty needs medical observation/admission with psychiatric input as indicated. Arrange psychiatric admission/transfer when risk cannot be managed safely by less restrictive care. Discharge only after appropriate assessment, safe recovery, a collaborative safety/support plan, treatment/follow-up ownership and explicit crisis/return advice; document the rationale, capacity/consent and receiving-team handover.

title: Suicide Risk
sharedPreamble:
# Special-population modules

Shared gate: adjust thresholds, communication, consent, safeguarding, doses and
disposition to physiology, developmental stage, pregnancy and baseline function.
sectionBody:
- Ask directly about thoughts, intent, plan, access to means, recent acts, substance use, psychosis, supports and protective factors.
- Treat medical consequences and maintain a safe environment with observation proportional to immediate clinical need. Do not use a risk scale, global low/medium/high label or protective-factor count alone to predict suicide, decide discharge or deny psychosocial assessment.
- Arrange timely psychosocial/specialist assessment, collaborative safety planning, lethal-means restriction and named follow-up. Do not use a no-suicide contract as disposition; confirm a safe transfer and provide explicit crisis/return instructions.

title: Alcohol Withdrawal
sharedPreamble:
# Renal, metabolic and toxicology modules

Shared gate: obtain glucose, ECG, electrolytes, acid-base status, renal function,
medications/toxins and volume/perfusion assessment. Repeat critical values and
verify whether results are affected by sampling error.
sectionBody:
- **Adult reference:** children and pregnancy need specialist-specific management. Establish reduction/last intake, usual consumption, prior seizures/delirium tremens, concurrent sedatives/opioids, pregnancy, trauma, infection, liver disease, nutrition, glucose and electrolytes. Intoxication and withdrawal risk may coexist. Exclude alternative causes of agitation, seizure or confusion; alcohol attribution must not delay resuscitation or other urgent diagnosis.
- **Use scores appropriately:** CIWA-Ar measures symptoms, not a stand-alone diagnosis. Reliable reporting and trained assessment are prerequisites. Delirium, critical illness or inability to communicate requires a monitored clinician-directed/objective approach such as RASS/MINDS rather than CIWA-Ar-driven dosing.
- **Benzodiazepines are first-line:** choose symptom-triggered treatment only when a reliable validated assessment can be performed with trained staffing, or a prescribed fixed/front-loading regimen with frequent reassessment. Individualize for age, liver disease, previous sedatives and respiratory risk; lorazepam/oxazepam may be preferable when long-acting active metabolites are problematic. Do not apply a routine unsupervised reducing schedule to severe complicated withdrawal.
- **ASAM monitored adult example:** diazepam **20 mg orally every 2 h for 3 doses**. Reassess before each dose; hold for oversedation, hypoventilation or hypotension. This is **not a compulsory 60 mg course** or universal maximum; do not stack loading regimens. Frailty, liver disease, unsafe swallowing or cardiorespiratory risk requires individualization.
- **Thiamine phases, UK acute-hospital guidance 2025/updated 2026:** lower-risk prophylaxis **50 mg orally four times daily**; high-risk prophylaxis **200--300 mg IV or IM once daily for 3--5 days**, with daily review. Suspected/established Wernicke encephalopathy requires **300--500 mg IV three times daily for 3--5 days**; if still symptomatic after the first 5 days, continue 300--500 mg IV daily for a further 3--5 days and while improvement continues, under review. Do not substitute prophylaxis for treatment of suspected Wernicke disease or wait for a complete classic triad. Follow parenteral treatment with appropriate oral supplementation.
- Give thiamine promptly but **do not delay glucose for hypoglycemia**. Check/correct Mg, K and phosphate as indicated and watch refeeding/fluid risk. Verify the actual parenteral thiamine product, dilution and administration time, with anaphylaxis treatment available; do not invent ampoule counts, IV push timing or a local formulation from the guideline dose.
- **Adjunct boundaries:** phenobarbital requires experienced staff, close monitoring and a cumulative-dose/airway plan; avoid unstructured benzodiazepine stacking. Antipsychotics, clonidine or dexmedetomidine do not replace seizure/delirium prevention. Active seizures follow the status pathway; phenytoin is not routine without another indication.
- **Monitor and escalate:** reassess symptoms, consciousness/sedation, respiratory rate, SpO2, BP/HR, temperature, fluids and electrolytes; review before/after doses and use continuous cardiorespiratory observation for severe illness or parenteral sedative escalation. Delirium tremens, recurrent seizures, refractory/high-dose requirements, respiratory depression, unstable physiology or serious comorbidity needs senior/ICU assessment and airway capability. Do not wait for a score threshold when complications occur.
- Discharge requires controlled symptoms, adequate observation after sedatives, nutrition/thiamine and a safe follow-up plan; severe/high-risk withdrawal is not routine outpatient detoxification. Offer ongoing alcohol-use-disorder treatment/support rather than treating withdrawal as the whole intervention. No new sedative infusion or automated drug contract is approved by this guide.

title: Environmental Emergencies
sharedPreamble: # Disposition and cross-cutting modules
sectionBody:
- Adult initial framework: stop exposure while protecting rescuers, assess ABCDE, trauma, glucose, ECG, electrolytes and organ injury, and obtain a reliable core temperature when relevant. Document exposure duration, exertion, immersion, medications/toxins and treatment already given; use pediatric-specific pathways for children.
- Heat stroke is suspected with heat/exertion exposure and CNS dysfunction; do not postpone cooling for a perfect temperature reading or a rigid diagnostic cutoff. Start rapid active cooling while supporting airway/perfusion. Cold-water immersion is effective when feasible with airway protection and continuous supervision; adapt the method to patient/context. Monitor core temperature and prevent overshoot. Antipyretics do not treat heat stroke. Distinguish exercise-associated hyponatremia, intoxication and malignant hyperthermia; their treatments differ. Suspected heat stroke needs monitored assessment for renal, hepatic, coagulation and muscle injury.
- In hypothermia, remove wet exposure, insulate, handle gently and use severity-appropriate active rewarming with core-temperature/ECG monitoring. For an unconscious hypothermic patient, assess signs of life for up to 1 minute. Use the 2025 temperature-modified resuscitation protocol rather than an unchanged normothermic drug/shock schedule; discuss severe instability or arrest early with an extracorporeal-rewarming center. Availability and transport feasibility must be confirmed, not assumed.
- Drowning prioritizes safe rescue, ventilation and oxygenation. For adult resuscitation use the ERC/RCUK 2025 sequence, beginning with 5 rescue breaths then standard CPR when indicated. Suspected spinal injury precautions must not delay essential extrication/resuscitation. Assess associated hypothermia and evolving respiratory failure; route ongoing respiratory support to `acute-respiratory-failure` and monitor symptomatic patients rather than clearing them from one normal initial finding.
- Use `toxicology`, `anaphylaxis`, `major-burns` and `smoke-inhalation-toxic-injury` for relevant exposures; electrical injury, decompression/altitude illness and bites/envenomation need their own expert assessment and disposition. Do not generalize one cooling, rewarming, antidote or hyperbaric plan to all environmental emergencies.
- Reassess mental state, temperature, oxygenation, hemodynamics, urine output and laboratory trends. Escalate persistent neurological/respiratory abnormalities, shock or organ injury; discharge only after syndrome-appropriate observation/recovery, reliable follow-up and clear deterioration warnings. This review covers the initial environmental framework, not every specialist exposure-treatment regimen.

title: Emergency Infectious Diseases
sharedPreamble:
# Infection, allergy and respiratory modules

Shared gate: assess airway, breathing, circulation, immune status, recent healthcare
exposure, cultures, source control, allergies and prior resistant organisms. Do not
delay stabilization for diagnostic certainty.
sectionBody:
- Adult initial framework: define the likely syndrome/source, immune status, pregnancy, travel/exposures, recent healthcare/antibiotics, prior resistant organisms and organ dysfunction. Assess ABCDE and perfusion promptly; absence of fever does not exclude serious infection. Children, neutropenic/transplant patients and pregnancy need their specific pathways.
- Apply standard precautions to every patient and add contact, droplet or airborne precautions according to the suspected syndrome/pathogen at triage, without waiting for confirmatory testing. Coordinate isolation, respiratory protection and exposure management with infection prevention/public health; communicate required precautions during transport and handover. A negative early or inappropriate test does not by itself end a necessary isolation pathway.
- Obtain blood/source cultures and targeted microbiology promptly when they will guide care, before antibiotics if this causes no clinically important delay. Route sepsis/shock to `sepsis-shock`, CNS infection to `cns-infection`, and neutropenic illness to `hematology-oncology`; treat time-critical infection and arrange source control without waiting for complete diagnostic certainty. Assess severe malaria urgently in a compatible travel/exposure context with appropriate specialist testing/treatment rather than routine fever follow-up.
- Choose initial therapy through `empiric-antibiotics` using syndrome severity, allergy, organ function, prior microbiology, exposure and local resistance patterns. Do not wait for the current antibiogram to treat an emergency, but local resistance data can change the initial empirical choice. Obtain infectious-disease/microbiology advice for unusual pathogens, immunosuppression, resistant infection or diagnostic uncertainty; no universal antibiotic regimen fits this whole module.
- Reassess clinical response and diagnostic alternatives, review culture results and narrow/stop unnecessary agents when appropriate. Normalizing one biomarker is not a substitute for perfusion, source control and organ-function assessment. Avoid treating colonization or asymptomatic bacteriuria as the sole explanation for nonspecific symptoms; preserve immediate sepsis care when clinically indicated.
- For Portugal, consult the current DGS SINAVE notifiable-disease list/case definitions and coordinate with the relevant local/regional public-health authority. Notify suspected or confirmed conditions as required by that disease's current rules; do not invent one notification deadline or assume mainland response arrangements apply unchanged to the Azores. Notifications must not delay stabilization.
- Admit/escalate organ dysfunction, unsafe oral intake, unresolved high-risk infection or unreliable monitoring/support. Document the working diagnosis, treatment/review timing, pending tests, isolation advice and explicit return precautions for any outpatient plan. GREEN covers this framework, not validation of every pathogen-specific regimen or local laboratory/public-health capability.

title: Non Coronary Chest Pain
sharedPreamble:
# Cardiovascular modules

Shared gate: establish ABC status, perfusion, symptom onset, ECG timing, vascular
access, glucose, pregnancy possibility, bleeding risk, renal function and current
antithrombotic therapy. Use serial examinations; a single normal ECG, troponin or
POCUS study does not exclude time-critical disease.
sectionBody:
- Adult assessment framework: 'non-coronary' is not an initial rule-out diagnosis. Exclude ACS, acute aortic syndrome, PE, pneumothorax, tamponade, esophageal rupture and dangerous abdominal causes before assigning a benign explanation. Assess ABCDE, onset/time course, exertion, radiation, syncope, dyspnea, fever, bleeding and vascular risks; chest-wall reproducibility, pleuritic character, anxiety or response to analgesia alone cannot exclude serious disease.
- Instability, severe ongoing pain, hypoxemia, neurological/vascular deficit, shock or a concerning ECG needs immediate monitored escalation and cause-specific treatment. Obtain/review an ECG within 10 minutes of arrival for acute chest pain and repeat with persistent/recurrent symptoms or evolving concern. A single normal ECG does not exclude ACS.
- Use `acute-coronary-syndrome` when ACS remains possible. Apply an assay-validated hs-troponin clinical decision pathway with symptom timing, required serial measurements/delta and the local assay's limits; do not invent one threshold or interval for every assay or use an early negative value as universal clearance. Intermediate or inconclusive results need further observation/testing rather than a low-risk label from symptoms alone.
- Route suspected aortic disease to `acute-aortic-syndrome`, PE to `pulmonary-embolism`, tension pneumothorax to `tension-pneumothorax` and pericardial compromise to `cardiac-tamponade-pericardial-emergency`. Obtain imaging tailored to stability and pretest probability; a normal chest X-ray or limited POCUS cannot exclude PE, dissection or other high-risk causes. Suspected esophageal rupture needs urgent surgical/thoracic assessment and source-control planning, not a reflux trial as reassurance. Antithrombotic treatment must follow the actual diagnosis and bleeding context rather than a generic chest-pain order.
- Consider myocarditis/pericarditis when compatible pain, recent infection, troponin change, ECG abnormalities or effusion are present. ESC2025 supports initial ECG, biomarkers and echocardiography with further cardiac imaging/specialist assessment as indicated. Hemodynamic compromise, significant arrhythmia, ventricular dysfunction or other high-risk features requires admission/escalation; do not assume every inflammatory chest-pain syndrome is uncomplicated outpatient pericarditis or automatically copy its drug regimen.
- Reassess vital signs, examination, symptoms and test evolution; consider pulmonary, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal and other causes only within a defensible differential. Not every patient needs every advanced test, but a test chosen for one diagnosis does not clear the others.
- Discharge only after the appropriate pathway is completed, serious alternatives are reasonably addressed, serial physiology is stable, symptoms/function are acceptable and follow-up is reliable. Document the working diagnosis and uncertainty, pending-result ownership and explicit return advice for recurrent/worsening pain, syncope, dyspnea or new neurological symptoms. Use `observation-discharge` when further reassessment is needed; no risk score alone establishes safety.

title: Acute Heart Failure
sharedPreamble:
# Cardiovascular modules

Shared gate: establish ABC status, perfusion, symptom onset, ECG timing, vascular
access, glucose, pregnancy possibility, bleeding risk, renal function and current
antithrombotic therapy. Use serial examinations; a single normal ECG, troponin or
POCUS study does not exclude time-critical disease.
sectionBody:
- Use the acute bridge recommendations in ESC 2026 heart-failure guidance and the 2026 ACVC/HFA/EUSEM emergency consensus. Identify pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, shock, ACS, arrhythmia, mechanical/valvular cause and precipitant.
- Use lung/cardiac POCUS, ECG, radiography and biomarkers in context. NIV may help appropriate pulmonary edema; avoid it when airway protection or shock makes it unsafe.
- Give oxygen for hypoxemia rather than routinely. Use IV loop diuretic for clinically significant congestion; consider a titratable vasodilator when BP is adequate, especially in hypertensive pulmonary edema. Do not use inotropes routinely: reserve them for low-output hypoperfusion after correcting reversible causes; use norepinephrine preferentially when vasopressor support is required.
- Before nitrates, diuresis or positive-pressure ventilation, look for critical aortic stenosis, right-ventricular infarction, obstructive shock and preload dependence. Choose therapy from congestion, blood pressure and perfusion rather than the label of heart failure alone.
- Track work of breathing, urine output, renal function, electrolytes and perfusion; admit high-risk patients and escalate shock or respiratory failure. After stabilization, arrange congestion reassessment, appropriate disease-modifying treatment review and a safe follow-up/disposition plan; the initial resuscitation pathway alone is not a discharge clearance.

title: Cardiogenic Shock
sharedPreamble:
# Cardiovascular modules

Shared gate: establish ABC status, perfusion, symptom onset, ECG timing, vascular
access, glucose, pregnancy possibility, bleeding risk, renal function and current
antithrombotic therapy. Use serial examinations; a single normal ECG, troponin or
POCUS study does not exclude time-critical disease.
sectionBody:
- Recognize shock from hypoperfusion plus a primary cardiac pump problem; hypotension may be absent early. Record a SCAI stage and trend mental status, skin/peripheral perfusion, urine output, lactate, acid-base state and vasoactive requirement rather than relying on one blood-pressure value.
- Activate a shock/cardiology pathway early. Obtain ECG, serial troponin, blood gas/lactate, full blood count, electrolytes, renal/hepatic function and urgent echocardiography. Use POCUS to identify ventricular phenotype, congestion and a possible mechanical lesion, but obtain expert echocardiography and invasive hemodynamics when the phenotype or response remains uncertain.
- Treat the cause immediately: activate reperfusion for acute MI; correct unstable arrhythmia; seek urgent structural/cardiothoracic treatment for papillary-muscle, septal, free-wall or valve catastrophe; and distinguish obstructive shock (PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax) because its definitive treatment differs.
- Give oxygen only for hypoxemia and choose ventilatory support cautiously because induction and positive pressure can precipitate collapse. Do not give automatic large fluid boluses. If true hypovolemia or preload-dependent right-ventricular shock is plausible, use a small test bolus (for example 250 mL balanced crystalloid) with immediate lung, venous-congestion and perfusion reassessment; stop if congestion worsens or perfusion does not improve.
- When hypotension threatens perfusion, norepinephrine is a reasonable first inopressor while the cause is treated. Example preparation: norepinephrine 8 mg to a final volume of 100 mL = 80 micrograms/mL (or 8 mg/200 mL = 40 micrograms/mL). A local starting range of 0.02--0.1 micrograms/kg/min must be individualized. Pump rate = dose (micrograms/kg/min) x weight (kg) x 60 / concentration (micrograms/mL). At 80 kg and 0.05 micrograms/kg/min: 3 mL/h with 8 mg/100 mL or 6 mL/h with 8 mg/200 mL. Titrate every 2--5 minutes to an individualized MAP/perfusion target (often initially MAP at least 65 mm Hg), recording rhythm, extremity perfusion, urine output and lactate; use the local maximum and central/peripheral-line policy.
- Add an inotrope only for persistent low-output hypoperfusion after pressure, rhythm, preload and reversible cause have been addressed. Example dobutamine: 250 mg/100 mL = 2,500 micrograms/mL (or 250 mg/200 mL = 1,250 micrograms/mL); 2.5--5 micrograms/kg/min is a common starting range. At 80 kg, 2.5 micrograms/kg/min = 4.8 mL/h with 250 mg/100 mL or 9.6 mL/h with 250 mg/200 mL. Titrate to perfusion/cardiac output and stop or reduce for tachyarrhythmia, ischemia or worsening hypotension. Milrinone is not a default substitute in hypotensive or renally impaired patients because vasodilation and accumulation can be harmful.
- Do not use epinephrine, dopamine, dual inotropes or temporary mechanical circulatory support reflexively. Escalate deteriorating SCAI C--E shock to a multidisciplinary shock team/advanced center for phenotype-guided invasive monitoring and device selection; device benefit and harm depend on cause, timing, ventricular phenotype, bleeding/vascular risk and recovery or destination strategy.
- Reassess at least every 5--15 minutes during escalation: MAP and pulse pressure, rhythm, oxygenation/ventilation, capillary refill/temperature gradient, urine output, lactate trajectory and drug/device complications. Transfer to a cardiac ICU or shock-capable center; a transient BP response is not resolution.

title: Vasoactive Inotrope Infusions
sharedPreamble:
# Cardiovascular modules

Shared gate: establish ABC status, perfusion, symptom onset, ECG timing, vascular
access, glucose, pregnancy possibility, bleeding risk, renal function and current
antithrombotic therapy. Use serial examinations; a single normal ECG, troponin or
POCUS study does not exclude time-critical disease.
sectionBody:
- Scope: adult continuous vasopressor/inotrope reference (draft v1.35, human review pending). Pediatric infusions are out of scope. Choose the agent from the shock phenotype and cause using `undifferentiated-shock`, `sepsis-shock`, `cardiogenic-shock` or `acute-heart-failure`; this module supplies drug position, preparation, arithmetic and safety only and does not replace those pathways. Always apply `medication-selection-safety`.
- Universal rules: confirm the ampoule strength and whether it is expressed as base or salt, diluent, final volume and concentration before every calculation. Rate formula: `mL/h = dose (micrograms/kg/min) x weight (kg) x 60 / concentration (micrograms/mL)`; for fixed doses `mL/h = dose per hour / concentration per mL`. Use a dedicated lumen/line, a smart pump with the local drug library, arterial pressure monitoring when escalating, and double-check preparation. Worked examples below use 70 kg and are arithmetic references, not a patient's prescription. Where a local/pharmacy standard concentration exists, it overrides these examples.
- Peripheral versus central: SSC 2026 suggests starting vasopressors peripherally to restore MAP rather than delaying for central access (conditional, very low certainty); SSC 2021 qualified this as a short period through a well-functioning vein at or proximal to the antecubital fossa. Some product labels (for example the UK noradrenaline SmPC) state central venous access, and US labels say to infuse into a large vein. Therefore: peripheral start is acceptable only in a large proximal vein, with site checks at least hourly per local policy and a plan for central access if requirements persist or rise; angiotensin II labelling recommends a central line.
- Extravasation of a catecholamine vasopressor: stop the infusion at that site, restart via another line without interrupting support, and per US norepinephrine/dopamine labelling infiltrate phentolamine 5--10 mg in 10--15 mL sodium chloride 0.9% as soon as possible (most effective within 12 hours). Mark the area, escalate to plastic surgery/local extravasation protocol, and document.
- Monitoring for all agents: continuous ECG, arterial pressure when escalating or on more than one agent, SpO2, mental status, capillary refill/skin mottling, urine output, lactate trend, glucose and potassium, limb/digital/mesenteric ischemia, and echocardiographic phenotype when the response is inadequate. Reassess every 5--15 minutes during titration.
- **Norepinephrine (noradrenaline)**, position: SSC 2026 recommends it first-line in septic shock over dopamine, epinephrine or selepressin (strong; high certainty versus dopamine) and suggests it over vasopressin or angiotensin II (conditional). It is also the usual first vasopressor when hypotension threatens perfusion in cardiogenic shock (see `cardiogenic-shock`). Starting dose varies by source: US label 8--12 micrograms/min then 2--4 micrograms/min maintenance; UK SmPC 0.4--0.8 mg/h base initially; ESC 2021 heart-failure table 0.2--1.0 micrograms/kg/min, a starting dose criticised as unnecessarily high, with AHA-cited 0.05 micrograms/kg/min for cardiogenic shock. Draft reference start 0.05--0.1 micrograms/kg/min, individualized. Preparation: **8 mg norepinephrine base to a final volume of 200 mL = 40 micrograms/mL** (the UK SmPC standard concentration is 40 mg/L base, in glucose 5%, sodium chloride 0.9% or glucose-saline; US labelling uses dextrose-containing diluents). Fluid-restricted alternative 8 mg/100 mL = 80 micrograms/mL. **Critical check: never infer a base/salt conversion from the word bitartrate/tartrate alone. Use the product label's declared norepinephrine-equivalent amount/concentration. Some current products are explicitly labelled as milligrams equivalent of norepinephrine even though supplied as norepinephrine bitartrate. Portugal/Azores presentation remains a local QA gate.** 70 kg at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min: 0.05 x 70 x 60 = 210 micrograms/h; 210 / 40 = 5.25 mL/h (2.6 mL/h at 80 micrograms/mL). 70 kg at 0.1 micrograms/kg/min = 10.5 mL/h at 40 micrograms/mL. Titration: BP every 2 minutes until target, then every 5 minutes (US label); adjust in small steps (for example 0.02--0.05 micrograms/kg/min) every 2--5 minutes to an initial MAP 65 mm Hg in septic shock (60--65 mm Hg is suggested at age 65 years or older). No absolute labelled maximum: at about 0.25--0.5 micrograms/kg/min SSC 2021 describes adding vasopressin rather than escalating alone, and rising requirements should prompt reassessment of cause, volume, cardiac function, adrenal insufficiency and source control. Wean gradually, never abrupt stop (label/SmPC).
- **Vasopressin (argipressin)**, position: add in septic shock on escalating norepinephrine rather than escalating norepinephrine alone (SSC 2026 conditional, moderate certainty; SSC 2021: usually started at norepinephrine 0.25--0.5 micrograms/kg/min). Not first-line. Fixed dose, not weight-based. Doses differ: the US Vasostrict label starts septic shock at 0.01 units/min and titrates by 0.005 units/min every 10--15 minutes to a maximum of 0.07 units/min (post-cardiotomy start 0.03 units/min, maximum 0.1 units/min), while guideline practice and trials commonly use a fixed 0.03 units/min. Preparation (label): **100 units to a final volume of 100 mL = 1 unit/mL** (fluid restriction) or 50 units/500 mL = 0.1 unit/mL, in sodium chloride 0.9% or glucose 5%. At 1 unit/mL: 0.03 units/min x 60 = 1.8 units/h = 1.8 mL/h; 0.01 units/min = 0.6 mL/h; each 0.005 units/min step = 0.3 mL/h; 0.07 units/min = 4.2 mL/h. At 0.1 unit/mL, 0.03 units/min = 18 mL/h. Watch digital/mesenteric ischemia, hyponatremia and reduced cardiac output; label taper after 8 hours at target without catecholamines: reduce 0.005 units/min every hour as tolerated. Diluted solution: discard after 18 hours at room temperature or 24 hours refrigerated (label).
- **Owner-selected local Empressin standard (14 November 2026):** **40 units (2 mL of 20 units/mL) + 38 mL NaCl 0.9% = 40 mL FINAL at 1 unit/mL**. A 50 mL syringe contains only 40 mL of this mixture; do not top up to 50 mL. At **0.01 / 0.02 / 0.03 units/min**, the pump rates are **0.6 / 1.2 / 1.8 mL/h**. Dose units are units/min, not units/kg/min. Titrate to response every 15--20 min according to the Empressin dose reference with catecholamine support; above 0.03 units/min is emergency-only in that label, not a routine maximum imported from Vasostrict. CIMA83405 describes 0.8 units/mL (2 mL + 48 mL saline to 50 mL); that is a separate manufacturer reference, not the selected local pump table. Keep unopened stock at 2--8 C. Start immediately after opening/dilution. The owner sets mandatory local container/tubing replacement by 24 h from preparation, earlier if a shorter applicable limit or completion requires it. This local ceiling is not a claim of manufacturer-certified 24 h chemical stability at 1 unit/mL and does not authorize delayed storage.

| Selected Empressin dose (units/min) | Dose (units/h) | Pump rate at 1 unit/mL (mL/h) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.01 | 0.6 | 0.6 |
| 0.02 | 1.2 | 1.2 |
| 0.03 | 1.8 | 1.8 |

- **Epinephrine (adrenaline)**, position: third agent when MAP is inadequate despite norepinephrine plus vasopressin in septic shock (SSC 2026 conditional, very low certainty); in septic shock with cardiac dysfunction norepinephrine or epinephrine may be first-line (SSC 2026 new, very low certainty), and epinephrine alone is an alternative to norepinephrine plus dobutamine for persistent hypoperfusion. In cardiogenic shock do not use it reflexively (see `cardiogenic-shock`). Label: 0.05--2 micrograms/kg/min, titrated every 10--15 minutes in steps of 0.05--0.2 micrograms/kg/min; after stability wean incrementally, e.g. every 30 minutes over 12--24 hours. Preparation: **4 mg to a final volume of 100 mL = 40 micrograms/mL** (or 8 mg/200 mL; US label uses glucose 5% and a 1 microgram/mL dilution, so confirm local diluent/concentration). 70 kg at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min: 0.05 x 70 x 60 = 210 micrograms/h; 210 / 40 = 5.25 mL/h; each 0.05 micrograms/kg/min step = 5.25 mL/h. Monitor tachyarrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, hyperglycemia and a beta-2-mediated lactate rise that must not be misread in isolation as worsening perfusion.
- **Dopamine**, position: not first-line in septic shock (SSC 2026 recommends norepinephrine over dopamine, strong, high certainty); consider only as an alternative when norepinephrine is unavailable, in selected patients at low tachyarrhythmia risk, or as a chronotropic bridge in bradycardia per the adult bradyarrhythmia pathway. Do not use low-dose dopamine as renal protection. Label: start 2--5 micrograms/kg/min, titrate in 5--10 micrograms/kg/min steps to response, not more than 50 micrograms/kg/min; into a large vein; wean gradually. Preparation: premixed **400 mg/250 mL = 1,600 micrograms/mL** (labelled premix; 250 mL is the common standard). 70 kg at 5 micrograms/kg/min: 5 x 70 x 60 = 21,000 micrograms/h; 21,000 / 1,600 = 13.1 mL/h. Stop for tachyarrhythmia or ischemia; extravasation as above.
- **Dobutamine**, position: inotrope for persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac dysfunction after MAP, rhythm, preload and cause are addressed (SSC 2026 conditional; ESC 2021 advises against routine inotropes without cardiogenic shock). It can lower BP; add or increase norepinephrine rather than accept hypotension. Label: start 0.5--1 micrograms/kg/min, usual 2--20 micrograms/kg/min, maximum 40 micrograms/kg/min; the label does not fix a titration interval, so use small steps (e.g. 2.5 micrograms/kg/min) with perfusion/cardiac-output reassessment per local protocol. Preparation: **250 mg to a final volume of 100 mL = 2,500 micrograms/mL** (or 250 mg/200 mL = 1,250 micrograms/mL). 70 kg at 2.5 micrograms/kg/min: 2.5 x 70 x 60 = 10,500 micrograms/h; 10,500 / 2,500 = 4.2 mL/h (8.4 mL/h at 1,250 micrograms/mL). Reduce or stop for tachyarrhythmia, ischemia or worsening hypotension.
- **Milrinone**, position: PDE-3 inodilator for low-output states, e.g. beta-blocked patients or right-ventricular/pulmonary-vascular load under specialist guidance; not a default substitute in hypotension or renal impairment (vasodilation and renal accumulation). Label: optional loading 50 micrograms/kg over 10 minutes, maintenance 0.375--0.75 micrograms/kg/min; in shock or hypotension the loading dose is commonly omitted (practice, not label). Renal adjustment (label, CrCl mL/min/1.73 m2): 50 -> 0.43, 40 -> 0.38, 30 -> 0.33, 20 -> 0.28, 10 -> 0.23, 5 -> 0.2 micrograms/kg/min. Preparation (label): **20 mg to a final volume of 100 mL = 200 micrograms/mL** in sodium chloride 0.45%/0.9% or glucose 5%. 70 kg at 0.375 micrograms/kg/min: 0.375 x 70 x 60 = 1,575 micrograms/h; 1,575 / 200 = 7.9 mL/h; loading 50 x 70 = 3,500 micrograms = 17.5 mL over 10 minutes if used. Long half-life: a rate change takes hours to reach steady state; monitor BP, arrhythmia, renal function and platelets.
- **Levosimendan**, position: calcium sensitizer for selected low-output heart failure under cardiology/ICU direction; SSC 2026 suggests against it in septic shock with cardiac dysfunction (conditional, low certainty). EU SmPC (Simdax): loading 6--12 micrograms/kg over 10 minutes (6 micrograms/kg or omit when already on IV inotropes/vasodilators or BP is low, per SmPC caution), then 0.1 micrograms/kg/min (range 0.05--0.2) for a recommended 24 hours. Contraindicated with severe hypotension/tachycardia, CrCl below 30 mL/min or severe hepatic impairment; active metabolites peak about 48 hours after stopping, so monitor for at least 3 days (5 days with mild-moderate renal/hepatic impairment). Preparation (SmPC): **12.5 mg (5 mL) in 500 mL glucose 5% = 25 micrograms/mL** (500 mL is the labelled volume; 0.05 mg/mL is the alternative). 70 kg at 0.1 micrograms/kg/min: 0.1 x 70 x 60 = 420 micrograms/h; 420 / 25 = 16.8 mL/h. Optional 6 micrograms/kg load = 420 micrograms = 16.8 mL over 10 minutes (100.8 mL/h for 10 minutes).
- **Phenylephrine**, position: pure alpha-agonist with limited role; not a first-line shock vasopressor in SSC; may be considered when tachyarrhythmia limits beta-agonists or for dynamic outflow obstruction under specialist direction. It can reduce cardiac output and cause reflex bradycardia. US label (hypotension from vasodilation during anesthesia): infusion start 10--35 micrograms/min, titrate to effect, not above 200 micrograms/min. Preparation (label): **10 mg in 500 mL = 20 micrograms/mL** (proportionally 2 mg/100 mL gives the same concentration); diluted solution use within 4 hours at room temperature or 24 hours refrigerated. 20 micrograms/min x 60 = 1,200 micrograms/h; 1,200 / 20 = 60 mL/h. This dilute concentration is volume-heavy; higher concentrations only per pharmacy/local protocol.
- **Angiotensin II** (only if authorised, supplied and in local protocol; EU/Portuguese availability not verified here): SSC 2026 suggests norepinephrine over angiotensin II (conditional, very low certainty).
